copied from the outlet when there is one and left **unknown** when there is not. The outlet is the
authority on where a run sits; substituting a height for a run with no outlet would put a number on
a schedule nobody measured.


### 11.70 DR-071 · Landing a drop is a gesture, and the product picks the hole

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-18** (`#715`), as the third phase of `#713`. **Not a §8.3
amendment.** AC-018 names `BindEndpoint` and DR-040 §11.39.2 rules how a drop lands; neither says
where a person does it, and for two milestones the answer was **only while typing the line that
creates the drops**. A run entered without `@panel=` could never be landed at all.
`label_key.dart` had already described the missing gesture in prose: *"the single bind a person
makes when they punch one stray drop down"*.

**11.70.1 THE CONTROL IS A `LANDS ON` COLUMN, AND ITS MENU OFFERS PANELS RATHER THAN POSITIONS.**

Every other editable column in that table writes what it is handed. This one is handed a **panel**
and allocates a position, which is what `@panel=` has done since M3-K/2: which hole a drop goes in
is the product's job. A menu of every free position on a job is hundreds of rows and asks a person
to choose something the allocator does better and faster.

**IT OFFERS EVERY DEVICE WITH A FREE REAR POSITION, not "every patch panel".** `@panel=` matches on
designator against any device for the same reason, and DR-068 §11.67.1's speaker run lands on an
**amplifier**: a filter that knew what a patch panel was would refuse the case that ruling exists
for. What makes a device offerable is that it has somewhere for a pulled cable to go, which
`freePanelPositions` already answers.

**11.70.2 IT IS BATCHABLE ON A RUNNING RESERVATION, and that is the property that makes it worth
building.** Landing forty-six drops on one panel is **one value across forty-six rows and forty-six
different holes**. Each edit therefore has to see the positions its siblings took, which
`freePanelPositions(alsoClaimed:)` was written for. Without it every drop in a batch lands on
position 1 and the gesture is silently nonsense: the kind of defect that is invisible in the app and
discovered at the panel.

The rack label rides with the bind, because it is **derived from the position** and the bind is the
only moment the position is known (DR-040 §11.39.3). A label that cannot render does not undo the
punchdown (§11.39.5): the pin is a physical fact and the name is not.

**11.70.3 A LANDED ROW SHOWS TEXT, NOT A CONTROL.** This is the only cell in the table that differs
per **row** rather than per column, and the model is what decides it rather than a preference.
`buildBindEndpointCommand` refuses a drop that is already landed, because DR-040 §11.39.6 leaves
moving one to a different port **unruled** and silently re-landing would rewrite a termination
somebody recorded. A dropdown on such a row would be a control whose every use is refused, which is
`#711`'s defect drawn on purpose.

The action refuses anyway rather than trusting the surface, because the batch bar can still aim at a
landed row.

**11.70.4 WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, AND IT IS THE SAME GAP DR-040 LEFT.** There is still no way to move
a drop OFF a port it is punched into. Clearing the cell refuses in words rather than unlanding,
because an unbind is a different gesture with different consequences for the rack label and the
termination, and §11.39.6 has never ruled it. Recorded here as an absence a person will meet, not as
one this ruling closes.

> **CLOSED BY DR-074 §11.73** (`#720`, built `#722`–`#725`). The clause above keeps its own words
> because it is DR-071's record of what was true on 2026-08-18. What is no longer true: a landed row
> now offers the same panel menu an unlanded one does, meaning MOVE, plus `NOT LANDED`; the cell
> that used to draw as text draws a control again, and §11.70.3's reasoning is spent rather than
> wrong. **Clearing the cell still refuses**, and now names the option that does the job.


### 11.71 DR-072 · The sheet counts the runs nobody landed, and only the end that is a job

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-18** (`#716`), the last phase of `#713`, and prompted by the
reason they gave for wanting it at all: *"someone's going to forget one or two and not notice it
until the schematic is ready to be printed."* **Not a §8.3 amendment.**

**11.71.1 TWO OF THIS PHASE'S THREE CLAUSES WERE ALREADY BUILT, and the record says so because the
finding is worth more than the work.** `net_label_layer.dart`'s `_endsOf` drops one end without
dropping the other, so a **half-landed run already draws the stub for the end it has**; its own doc
gives the reason (*"that flag is the only place the reader learns the run exists at all"*). A run
with neither end drawn is already in `unlabelledLinkIds`, the status strip already prints it, and
`net_label_layer_test.dart` pins both.

This was **checked rather than believed**. A comment asserting the product already handles something
is exactly what `#711` cost a ruling's worth of time over, and the alternative here was rebuilding
working machinery beside itself.

**11.71.2 WHAT WAS MISSING WAS A SENTENCE A PERSON CAN ACT ON.** *"N cables with no drawn end"* folds
together a run nobody landed and a link whose device carries no symbol: two problems with two
different fixes. A **half-landed** run is in neither, because it is drawn. So the sheet said nothing
whatever about the case that prompted the request.

`unlandedHomeRunIds` counts home runs whose **rack end** is not punched down, and the strip prints
it **first**, because it is the only note there that names a job rather than a limitation of the
drawing.

**11.71.3 THE FIELD END IS DELIBERATELY NOT COUNTED.** DR-068 §11.67.1 lets a speaker run land on
its driver, and a Cat6 drop ends at a wall plate for good. Counting unlanded field ends would put a
number on the sheet that never reaches zero, which is how a person learns to stop reading a number.

The rack end is different in kind. AC-018 makes an unbound one legitimate **at rough-in** (fourteen
of sixty, by that criterion's own arithmetic), and a job somebody is printing a schematic for is
past rough-in.

**11.71.4 WHAT IS STILL OWED, AND IT IS THE HALF THE USER ASKED FOR BY NAME.** There is no gesture
yet to **drag a stub onto a pin** and land the run from the sheet. The pieces exist (pennants are
hit-testable through `linkAtPoint`, and `buildBindEndpointCommand` takes it from there); what is
missing is a second arming path through `CanvasIntentDetector`, a wire origin that can hold a
pending landing as well as a pin, and a release that **binds rather than connects**. The distinction
is the whole point: `ConnectPortsCommand` would make a second cable beside the one the person is
trying to finish, which is the defect `#713` was filed for.

**IT IS RECORDED AS OWED RATHER THAN STARTED**, on the user's call, because that gesture lives in
the file with the exclusivity arbiter and the `_owned` token, whose header records three prior
defects in its mirror and which shipped `#704` green four days earlier while breaking both canvases
in the user's hands. The count above stands on its own and the sheet is honest without it; the
gesture is convenience on top of an accurate drawing, and it is worth starting rested.


### 11.72 DR-073 · Finishing a run is not making a cable, and the sheet now knows the difference

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-18** (`#719`), closing `#713`. **Not a §8.3 amendment.** DR-011
scopes drag-to-connect into the schematic and DR-071 §11.70.4 recorded this gesture as owed.

**11.72.1 DRAGGING A HALF-LANDED RUN'S PENNANT ONTO A FREE JACK LANDS IT.** The commit is
`BindEndpointCommand`, never `ConnectPortsCommand`.

This is the sentence `#713` was filed over, in the user's own words: *"if a user were to just
directly connect a speaker to an amplifier in the schematic view it would create two wires on the
project."* A run pulled at framing stage **already exists**. It carries a `W` number, a length, a
jacket and possibly a `TestResult`, and what it lacks is a pin at one end. A connect run against it
puts a second cable on the sheet beside the one the person is trying to finish, and the schedule
then prints two rows for one piece of copper.

**11.72.2 THE PREVIEW BAND IS THE CABLE, WHICH IS WHY THIS FITS THE EXISTING GESTURE.** The armed
source is the pin the run is **already** on, not the pennant.

That is a statement about the model rather than a convenience. A half-landed run landed onto a
second pin genuinely is a cable between those two pins, so the band drawn while the pointer is down
is exactly what the document holds one event later. The magnet, the candidate rings, the caret and
the whole teardown path therefore need no branch at all, which is most of the reason this change is
small in a file whose header records three prior gesture defects.

**11.72.3 EITHER END MAY BE THE LOOSE ONE, SO THE GRAB CARRIES WHICH.** DR-068 §11.67.1 lets a
speaker run land on its driver: a run drawn at its amplifier is waiting for a **field** end, and one
drawn at its wall plate is waiting for a **rack** end. A gesture that assumed the rack end would
rewrite the wrong half of the cable. The rack label is allocated only for a rack end, per §11.67.2.

**11.72.4 A PIN ALWAYS BEATS A PENNANT.** They sit beside one another and their hit boxes touch.
Landing a run is the rarer act and must never steal the commoner one, so the pennant is asked only
where the pin question found nothing.

**11.72.5 A PATCH CABLE'S PENNANT ARMS NOTHING.** `buildBindEndpointCommand` refuses anything with
no `StructureOrigin`, so arming there would be a control whose every use is refused, which is
`#711`'s defect drawn on purpose and the same call DR-071 §11.70.3 made for a landed row in the
table. The press falls back to the ordinary click that selects the cable.

**11.72.6 THE CANDIDATE SET IS THE FREE PINS, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM `evaluateConnect`'S.**
A bind's only occupancy rule is `TOP-003`, one cable per position, asked through
`portConductorCount` rather than answered a second time in the surface, because the command asks it
that way and two copies would let a ring say yes where the commit says no. There is no preferred
set: DR-012.3's magnet ranks candidates by whether they accept the SOURCE's family, which is a
question about a cable being created, and this one exists already.

**11.72.7 WHAT IS STILL NOT POSSIBLE, unchanged from DR-071 §11.70.4.** There is no gesture to move
a run OFF a pin it is landed on, here or in the table, because DR-040 §11.39.6 has never ruled the
unbind. Dropping onto an occupied jack refuses in the command's own words.

> **CLOSED BY DR-074 §11.73** (`#720`, built `#722`–`#725`). Dragging a landed run's pennant onto a
> free jack now MOVES that end. The gesture is this one, with the hit test taught to answer WHICH
> pennant: both flags of a run carry the same link id, so the reading that finishes a half-landed
> run and the reading that moves a landed one run in opposite directions off the same press.
> **Dropping onto an occupied jack still refuses**, in the move command's words rather than the
> bind's.


### 11.73 DR-074 · A drop punched into the wrong port can be moved, and the label follows the hole

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-18** (`#720`). **Closes the gap DR-040 §11.39.6 left open** and
which DR-071 §11.70.4 and DR-073 §11.72.7 each recorded as still owed. §11.39.6's own words are the
need: *"a deliberate 'this was punched into the wrong port' gesture is not specified here."*

**11.73.1 TWO COMMANDS, BECAUSE THEY ARE TWO ACTS WITH TWO CONSEQUENCES.**

* **MOVE** re-lands an end on a different jack. **One command and one undo entry**, because
  correcting a hole is the case the gap was named for and making a person unland then re-land costs
  two steps and leaves the document momentarily saying something false.
* **UNLAND** returns an end to an `OpenEndpoint`. Rarer and real: the panel is being replaced, or
  the drop turned out to be spare after all.

This is `link_class_commands.dart`'s split, for its stated reason: folding the second into the first
as a nullable parameter makes the common case carry a null it never wants and gives the Edit menu
one label for two opposite actions.

**11.73.2 THE RACK LABEL FOLLOWS THE POSITION, UNLESS A PERSON TYPED IT.** A move re-derives the
label; a hand-set one survives, and the surface says it was kept.

A rack label is derived from where the run landed (DR-040 §11.39.3), so `1A-PP-101` on a cable now
sitting in position 04 is a wrong hole number on the one column a trim tech works from. That is
worse than no label. But the `RACK LBL` column lets a person type one, CR-113 makes it unique
project-wide, and silently discarding somebody's own identifier is the loss G4 exists to refuse.

**THIS NEEDS A BIT, AND IT IS SPELLED THE WAY ITS TWO PRECEDENTS ARE.** `rackLabelLocked` on
`StructureOrigin`, written by the `RACK LBL` cell's own edit path and by nothing else. On the wire
it is **absent when false**, following `Link.linkClassLocked` and deliberately **not**
`designatorLocked`, which is written unconditionally: an always-written key here would rewrite every
document already on disk and move `kSchemaVersion` for nothing (CR-117).

**AND AN UNLAND CLEARS AN ALLOCATED LABEL, BY THE SAME ARGUMENT EXTENDED.** A label naming a
position the cable has left is wrong whether the cable went to another hole or to no hole. A
hand-set label survives an unland for the same reason it survives a move. **This clause was not put
to the user as its own question** and is recorded as an extension of §11.73.2's reasoning rather
than as a separate decision, so that a later reader can see which is which.

**11.73.3 THE TERMINATION SURVIVES BOTH, AND THE SURFACE SAYS SO.** `terminationRack` describes how
the cable END is finished, not which hole it sits in: a run can be punched onto a block this project
does not model at all. Clearing it on an unland would assert the crew undid work they may not have
touched, which is a fabrication in the direction G4 forbids. A person who really did pull the cable
back out clears it in the `RACK TERM` column, which is one cell and already exists.

Asking each time was considered and refused: AC-058/D5 does not list this as a data-loss edge, and a
confirm people learn to click through is worse than a default they can see and correct.

**11.73.4 NEITHER COMMAND REMOVES A PORT IT DID NOT CREATE.** `ConnectPortsCommand`'s rule, and
`BindEndpointCommand` already follows it: a pin the document already held is not this gesture's to
delete, and guessing wrong deletes a jack somebody else's cable may be about to use. A freed pin
that came from a template was always drawn and stays drawn.

**11.73.5 WHAT THIS DOES NOT DECIDE.** Which gestures reach the two commands. The `LANDS ON` cell
currently draws a landed row as plain text (DR-071 §11.70.3) precisely because re-landing was
unruled, and that reasoning is now spent; whether the cell becomes a menu, and whether dragging a
landed run's pennant to another jack means MOVE, are surface questions this ruling deliberately
leaves to the task. **Dragging a run to empty canvas must not mean unland**, which is the one
gesture named here, and named to forbid: it is a stray drag away from silently undoing a
termination.

### 11.74 DR-075 · A rack label somebody imported is a rack label somebody typed

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-19** (`#727`). **Amends DR-074 §11.73.2**, whose mechanism clause
reads *"written by the `RACK LBL` column's own edit path and by nothing else"*. That sentence was
written to keep the ALLOCATOR out, and it kept the CSV importer out with it.

**11.74.1 THE TEST IS WHO AUTHORED THE NAME, NOT WHICH CONTROL CARRIED IT.** `rackLabelLocked` means
*a person chose this identifier*, and a `rack_label` column in an imported sheet is a person choosing
one: they typed it into a spreadsheet instead of into a cell, which is the same act reaching the same
field through a different door. So an imported label locks, and a later move keeps it (§11.73.2)
rather than re-deriving it from the new position.

**THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS REAL AND IS OUTWEIGHED.** A sheet exported from this product carries
labels the ALLOCATOR produced, so a round trip out and back would lock names nobody chose, and a
later move would then keep a label naming the hole the cable has left: the failure §11.73.2 exists
to prevent, arrived at from the other side. It is outweighed because **the product cannot tell the
two sheets apart and must not guess**, and because the two mistakes are not equal: a wrongly locked
label is visible in the `RACK LBL` cell, carries the pin that says a person set it, and is cleared by
emptying the box; a wrongly discarded one is gone. G4's direction of travel decides it.

**11.74.2 AND THE IMPORTER HAD NO RUNNING RACK-LABEL RESERVATION AT ALL, WHICH IS A LIVE CR-113
DEFECT AND NOT A CONSEQUENCE OF THIS RULING.** `csv_import_apply.dart` passes `usedFieldLabels(doc)`
into `alsoUsedLabels` for **every** origin field it writes. `buildSetStructureOriginProperty` reads
that parameter for the FIELD label and reads `alsoUsedRackLabels` for the rack label, and nothing
ever filled the second. Two rows of one import naming the same rack label were each checked against
one unmutated document, and both passed.

**MEASURED, NOT REASONED.** A probe written before the fix imported two drops and then re-imported
the same sheet carrying `PP1-05` on both rows: two links, one label. It is reachable only on the
**update** pass, because a drop created by an import takes no rack label from the sheet, which is
why the existing suite's round-trip cases never met it.

**11.74.3 A COLLISION IS SKIPPED, NOT REFUSED, AND THAT IS THE IMPORTER'S EXISTING CONTRACT RATHER
THAN A NEW DECISION.** `_origin` drops any result that is not `Ready`, so a rack label colliding with
one already in the document has always been silently left alone while the rest of the row applied.
The reservation makes the within-sheet case behave the same way as the against-document case, which
is the smaller change and the consistent one.

**IT IS RECORDED AS A KNOWN LIMITATION.** docs/04 §3.4 says never silently do nothing, and an import
that skips a field without saying so is doing exactly that. The import already has a `warnings`
channel and this is a candidate for it; wiring it is not this ruling's work, and pretending the
current behaviour is fine would be worse than naming it.

### 11.75 DR-076 · The schematic rebuilds what changed, and the epochs already say what that is

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-19** (`#702`). The issue's own description says a ruling is owed
before building, because *"which epochs invalidate which fragments"* is a design question DR-011.4
only half answers. This is that ruling. **Not a §8.3 amendment**: nothing moves between milestones,
and AC-008's remedy is refined rather than withdrawn.

**11.75.1 THE PRESCRIBED REMEDY CANNOT MEET THE BUDGET ON ITS OWN, AND THE NUMBERS ARE WHY THIS
RULING EXISTS.** AC-008 rules that L3a splits into eight per-domain sub-pictures so *"an edit to one
HDMI run rebuilds ~1,200 ops and seven pictures replay untouched"*. Measured on the 12-pod fixture,
3,600 links across 1,128 devices, warm:

| | time | ops |
|---|---|---|
| cold build | **87 ms** | 78,660 |
| `holdAt`, which is what a wire edit does TODAY | **92 ms** | |
| `reuseLayout`, this ruling's first tier | **48 ms** | |
| `reuseSymbols`, the second tier | **20 ms** | |
| symbols alone, zero links (single run, indicative) | ~75 ms | 49,860 |

Best of five per figure, which is `schematic_perf_test.dart`'s own method; the symbols-only row is a
single run and is marked so, because it was taken to decompose the build rather than to bound it.

**The symbol half is the majority of the build before a single cable exists, and it is
domain-independent.** A perfect eight-way domain split saves at best the seven-eighths of the link
half that did not change and cannot touch the rest. AC-008 is not wrong; it is **half the answer**,
and the half it names is the smaller one.

**11.75.2 THE INVALIDATION MODEL IS THE EPOCH MODEL THAT ALREADY EXISTS.** `DocEpochs` carries six
independent notifiers (`structure`, `wires`, `rack`, `meta`, `style`, `sheet`) and its own doc says
they exist so `rackpal_ui` *"can subscribe to exactly the epochs one widget cares about instead of
rebuilding on every commit"*. Every command declares its `touches` mask, and `MoveEndpointCommand`,
`ConnectPortsCommand` and `BindEndpointCommand` all declare `wires | meta`. **The schematic collapses
all six into one `_sceneEpoch` and rebuilds everything.** The matrix this ruling asks for is
therefore mostly written already, per command, and unread.

The scene splits in three tiers, each keyed on what can move it:

| Tier | Rebuilt when | Cost at 3,600 links |
|---|---|---|
| **Layout**: Sugiyama phases 0–3, symbol positions | `structure` | ~50 ms |
| **Symbols**: the symbol layer's ops and text | `structure`, `meta` | ~75 ms |
| **Wires and labels**: net-label pennants, drawn wires | `wires` | ~19 ms |

The wire tier was **predicted at ~19 ms from the decomposition and measured at 19.6 ms** once
`#729` built it, which is the corroboration this table was worth taking. Note what it does NOT
say: 19.6 ms is still over a 16.7 ms frame at twelve pods. §11.75.6's domain split is where the
remaining margin would come from, and §11.75.4's budget binds the edit at a size a real job
reaches rather than at the largest fixture anyone can build.

A cable drawn declares `wires | meta`. Under §11.75.3 that rebuilds the symbol tier and the wire
tier and **reuses the layout**, which is DR-011.4's clause restated as a cache key rather than as a
parameter: *"committing a link must not re-lay-out the sheet"* is already the rule, and freezing the
layout is how it stops being re-derived.

**WHAT AN UNHELD REBUILD WOULD DO, MEASURED, AND WHAT ALREADY PREVENTS IT.** Adding **one** cable to
the shipped fixture and rebuilding from scratch moves **88 of its 91 symbols**: the new edge changes
what Sugiyama's ordering sweep sees, and the two label measurements feeding its params change with
it. **This is not a live defect.** `schematic_canvas_screen.dart` already passes `holdAt` on a
`wires` bump, and DR-011.4 is why; the figure is what that hold is buying, stated because a later
reader deciding to "simplify the cache" needs to know what it costs.

The first tier is therefore **a cheaper mechanism for a guarantee the product already makes**, not a
new guarantee: `holdAt` freezes the positions and still runs the layout and both measurements, at
**92 ms**; handing the layout back is **48 ms** for the identical scene. That is where §11.75.2's
saving actually comes from, and it is roughly half of a wire edit rather than all of it: phases two
and three carry the rest.

The equality gate in §11.75.5 is against the SAME document, never against a fresh layout of a changed
one: a test asserting the latter would be asserting the churn as intended behaviour.

**11.75.3 A RENAME REBUILDS SYMBOLS AND NOT LAYOUT.** A designator changes what a symbol PRINTS and
not where anything sits. Re-running layout for one would move symbols under the person's cursor,
which is the failure DR-011.4 forbids for its own reason and which is worse during trim-out, when
renames arrive in bursts. Paying the symbol tier for a rename is accepted: it is 75 ms on an
infrequent act, against 144 ms today.

**NOT DEFERRING THE REDRAW WAS CONSIDERED AND REFUSED.** A stale designator on the sheet while the
schedule shows the new one is two documents disagreeing about a device's name, which is the class of
defect this product exists to prevent.

**11.75.4 THE ONE-FRAME BUDGET BINDS THE EDIT, NOT THE OPEN.** M2's criterion was written against a
house with one rack and states one frame; a cold build of a twelve-pod commercial job is ~144 ms and
happens **once, behind a file load the person is already waiting through**. So the incremental path
asserts `_oneFrameMs` and the cold build keeps a ratchet ceiling.

This is a narrowing of what the budget was assumed to cover, and it is stated rather than assumed
because the alternative is real work with a real cost: meeting one frame on a cold build means
attacking Sugiyama and the symbol layer themselves, inside the determinism guarantees
`sugiyama.dart`'s header defends. **No user has reported open time.** If one does, this clause is
where to argue with.

**11.75.5 DETERMINISM IS NOT NEGOTIABLE AND IS WHAT THE TESTS PIN.** CR-012 and `sugiyama.dart`'s
rules survive unchanged: no hash-container iteration, total orders, and the same document producing
the same display list. **An incremental rebuild must produce the byte-identical scene a whole rebuild
would**, and that equality is the gate, not the timing. A cache that is faster and different is a
defect this project would ship as a golden diff nobody could read.

**11.75.6 AC-008'S DOMAIN SPLIT IS RETAINED AND RESEQUENCED.** It is measured after the tiers land,
not before: if the wire tier is already inside one frame, eight sub-pictures buy nothing and add a
second invalidation axis to reason about. The clause stays true and stops being the first move.

---

### 11.76 DR-077 · A template authored in this project reaches the rack, and the palette says where it came from

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-19** (`#701`). M4's exit criterion has two clauses and the second
one could not be performed at all. `docs/12` §5.3.8 found it while writing the drill route for
`#251`: a template saved in the Device Builder lands in `RackDocument.templates`, round-trips, and
**no surface offers it for placement**. Four questions had to be answered before anything could be
built, and the fourth is about what the criterion MEANS rather than about what is missing.

**NOT a §8.3 amendment.** Nothing moves between milestones and no scope is added: the exit criterion
already requires this and the decomposition simply never filed it. §11.76.4 declines the one thing
that would have been an amendment.

**11.76.1 THE SHELF IS THE DOCUMENT, AND IT ALWAYS WAS.** The census found the machinery already
correct and the palette reading the wrong source while standing next to the right one:

| | |
|---|---|
| `blank_document.dart` | writes all 48 seeded archetypes **into `doc.templates`** at version 1 |
| `buildPlaceFromCatalogCommand` | resolves from `doc.templates`, never from the seed catalog |
| `SaveTemplateToProjectCommand` | writes an authored body into the same map, under `"$id@$version"` |
| `DevicePalettePanel` | is handed `buildSeedCatalog()` by `rack_canvas_screen.dart:368` |

So `doc.templates` is the one shelf a project has, the seeded catalog is one **contributor** to it
rather than a second shelf beside it, and the palette is built from the document. This is what makes
the fix small: nothing about placement, resolution or persistence changes, and one widget stops
being handed a constant.

**`_catalog` IS `late final`, which is the second half of the same defect.** Pointed at the right
shelf it would still never notice a save, because it is computed once and held for the screen's
life. The placeable set is memoised on `stateId` through `DocumentMemo`, the mechanism
`ScheduleScreen` already uses and which `RackCanvasScreen` qualifies for by owning its
`DocumentController`.

**11.76.2 PROVENANCE SHOWS TWICE WHILE BROWSING AND ONCE WHILE SEARCHING.** An authored template is
filed into its own category beside the seeded ones **and** repeated in a `This project` group pinned
above the nine seeded categories. The two answers are answering two different questions: the
category is where a person looks for a network switch, and the pinned group is where a person looks
for the thing they saved thirty seconds ago. Both readers are real and the second is the one the
exit criterion's drill has.

**THE PINNED GROUP IS A BROWSE-STATE AFFORDANCE, and that limit is part of the ruling rather than an
implementation detail.** A non-empty query flattens the panel to one filtered list across every
category, and a row appearing twice in a search result is a defect: it makes the count wrong, it
makes `Enter` on the top match ambiguous, and it teaches the reader that the list has duplicates in
it. Search shows each template once, badged.

**A TEMPLATE WITH NO CATEGORY MUST STILL HAVE A HOME.** `_canSave` requires a display name, a type
prefix and a meant occupancy, and it does **not** require a category. The panel iterates
`kCatalogCategoryOrder`, so an uncategorised template is today invisible: not refused, not badged,
simply absent. An authored template that cannot be found is the same failure as one that cannot be
placed, arrived at one step later.

**11.76.3 A SECOND `Save` FORKS A VERSION. IT DOES NOT MINT A SECOND TEMPLATE.** This is CR-050's own
rule, implemented in `nextTemplateVersion`, and never called: `buildDeviceBuilderActions` is
constructed once with `editing: null`, so every save calls `templateIdFor`, finds the id taken, and
returns `tpl.foo_2`. The builder offers a plain `[Save]` beside `[Save & Close]` precisely so a
person can save and keep working, so this is the ordinary path and not an edge case. It was
invisible for exactly as long as nothing read what `Save` wrote.

The actions closure remembers the id it minted; later saves in the same authoring session pass it as
`editing` and fork `version + 1`. **Devices already placed keep resolving to the version they were
placed from**, because a `TemplateRef` carries its own version, which is the guarantee CR-050 exists
to make. Closing the builder and opening it again authors a NEW template, because that is a new
authoring session and not an edit.

**THE CONSEQUENCE FOR PLACEMENT, and it is a real one.** `catalogTemplateKey` pins `@1`, so the
instant a v2 exists the palette offers a row that resolves a stale body or nothing at all. Placement
resolves the **highest** version for an id, because placing means placing the current version.
Behaviour is byte-identical wherever only v1 exists, which is every seeded id in every existing
project and every fixture, and that is the check that this is a widening rather than a change.

**11.76.4 THE EQUIPMENT LIST IS A SHEET, AND THAT IS WHERE CLAUSE 2 IS CHECKED.** §5.3.8's second
finding was that `buildEquipmentList` has exactly one caller in the tree, `rackpal_export`, so the
criterion's *"appears correctly in the equipment list"* could only be read through a PDF. **That is
not a gap; it is the criterion's own reading.** `T6.30 EQUIPMENT LIST AND MATERIALS` is a sheet
(docs/08 §2.2), the corpus promises no view of it anywhere, and M1's exit criterion already reads
the equipment list through an exported PDF in the same words. `File ▸ Export PDF…` is wired and
emits `T6.30` today.

**NO ON-SCREEN EQUIPMENT LIST IS BUILT AND NONE IS OWED.** Building one is the §8.3 amendment this
ruling declines: it is a second table that must never drift from the sheet, added to unblock a
criterion that did not ask for it. The drill route for `#251` names the export step rather than
leaving a user to discover there is no view.

**11.76.5 WHAT THIS DOES NOT DELIVER, stated so nobody reads the closure as more than it is.** No
library subsystem: M4-N (`#170`) still owns `.rmda` archives, several libraries loaded at once, and
filtering by which one a device came from, and a template authored in one project still does not
appear in another. No `Duplicate & edit` from a catalog card: docs/06 §7.3 offers one and it belongs
with the library browser (M4-O, `#186`), so the one route into the builder is still
`Project ▸ New device template…` and it still authors a new template rather than forking a seeded
one. No stale-fork badge: CR-062's badge now has a producer for the first time, and DR-058's rule is
built (`builder/fork_status.dart`) while its `Row` is not.

**11.76.6 THE FINDING WORTH KEEPING IS THE ONE §5.3.5 ALREADY WROTE DOWN, POINTING THE OTHER WAY.**
M4-E's was *"five tasks build a grid and not one of them creates a port"*: **ask what produces each
task's input.** This is **ask what CONSUMES each task's output.** M4-D built a save, gated it,
tested it, and nothing read what it saved; `device_builder_actions.dart`'s own header has asserted
*"a template authored here is therefore placeable immediately"* since the day it shipped. Seventeen
issues, sixty-three tasks and fourteen green gates could not see it, because a decomposition can be
complete on both counts and still leave a milestone's criterion unreachable: the two questions are
asked of different ends of the same task.

### 11.77 DR-078 · The five grid operations, and what a bulk write shows before it fires

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-19** (`#177`, M4-F). Three questions the census raised at pick-up,
before any code, over the six tasks M4-F has left: `Duplicate`, `Renumber…`, `Find & replace`,
`Change type…`, `Move to bank…` and writing a field from the batch inspector.

**NOT a §8.3 amendment.** Every operation ruled here is already in `docs/06` §4.6's table with a
binding beside it; what was missing was a behaviour column, a platform collision nobody had checked,
and a safety question the table does not reach.

**11.77.1 `Ctrl+T` IS TAKEN, AND THE COST IS A macOS BEHAVIOUR WE SHADOW ON PURPOSE.**
`Ctrl+T` is `TransposeCharactersIntent` in Flutter's `_macShortcuts`, one of the emacs-derived
bindings the framework installs in every text field, and DR-009 puts macOS in v1. **Focus is almost
always inside a cell `TextField` when a grid chord is pressed**, which is the same sentence
`builderFillDown`'s note already used to justify checking, and `Ctrl+D` passed that check where this
one does not.

The direction of the collision is the part worth stating. `docs/04` §8 records that Flutter
dispatches key events **leaf to root** while `DefaultTextEditingShortcuts` is installed at the app
root, so **RackPal's binding wins**: transpose does not eat `Change type…`, `Change type…` eats
transpose. On macOS, inside a builder cell, `Ctrl+T` stops transposing two characters.

**Taken anyway, for two reasons and against one.** `docs/06` §4.6 specifies `Ctrl+T` and moving it is
an amendment to a shipped table; and **DR-011.6's rule is that one chord wears one meaning across the
product**, which a per-platform split would break on the one axis a keyboard-only user can see even
less than a scope boundary. Against it: this is a documented platform behaviour, and shadowing one is
not free. **It is recorded as macOS debt (`docs/13`) rather than absorbed silently**, because the
next person to meet it should find a note and not a mystery.

**The other four chords were checked in the same pass and are clean.** `Ctrl+J`, `Ctrl+R`, `Ctrl+H`
and `Ctrl+M` appear in no platform map of `default_text_editing_shortcuts.dart` and in no other scope
of this product's own registry. **The check was run over the file, not recalled**, which is how the
one collision was found.

**11.77.2 `Move to bank…` OFFERS THE BANKS THAT EXIST AND MINTS NONE.** The dialog lists the
template's declared banks and refuses, with a sentence, when there are none to move to.

**Creating a bank is `BankDef` CRUD and belongs to M4-J1.** A creation path here would be a second
surface that has to agree with J1's about naming, ordering and collision handling **before J1 has
decided any of those**, and the losing move in this codebase is consistently the one that invents a
rule in a dialog and leaves a later task to match it. The cost is accepted and named: reorganising a
template into a bank that does not exist yet is two trips until J1 ships.

**11.77.3 A BULK WRITE SHOWS A PER-ROW IMPACT LIST BEFORE IT FIRES, AND BOTH DIALOGS SHOW THE SAME
ONE.** `Find & replace` and `Change type…` each write across N rows at once, and each gets a
scrollable before-and-after list, a count, and then `Apply`.

`#699` already said the impact preview **is** the deliverable for `Change type…`, because
`SignalFamilyDef` carries `defaultConnector`, `defaultDirection` and `defaultTopology` and DR-060
rules that a default loses to a named value: without a preview, retyping a bank is a silent
overwrite of whatever somebody had already named, N rows at a time. **The ruling extends that shape
to `Find & replace` rather than giving it a lighter one**, so there is one thing to learn and one
widget to maintain.

**THE KEY SCOPE IS WHY THE LIGHTER OPTION LOSES.** `PortDef.key` is the template migration join
(CR-051), and a key that was already published when the builder opened may have another project's
cables resolving through it. Undo covers the open document completely and **cannot reach that**, so
"replace all and press `Ctrl+Z` if it looks wrong" is a safety story that works for every scope
except the one that needs it. The preview is the only place a person sees what a key rename will do
before it is done.

**A per-scope split was rejected**: an impact list for keys and a plain count for everything else is
two behaviours in one dialog selected by a dropdown, which is a rule a person learns by being
surprised rather than by reading the screen.

**11.77.4 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not decide `Renumber…`'s dialog copy, which is
`label_pattern.dart`'s existing parse errors and repair chips shown where the user is (`#697` forbids
a second parser and this ruling adds nothing to that). It does not rule the batch inspector's control
set (`#703` is a refactor with a stated trap, not a design question). It does not touch `Mirror bank`,
which is M4-J1's. And it does not weaken §4.6's own rule that `LABEL` and `DESIG` edit one row: a
`Find & replace` scoped to labels is a **matched** rewrite per row rather than one value written
across rows, which is the distinction DR-063 drew and this preserves.

### 11.78 DR-079 · A listing is not a material, and three code rules stop overstating what they know

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-19** (`#740`), from their own review of the corpus against NEC and US
practice. Four findings, three of which the text confirms and one of which has no target here.

**A CORRECTION, NOT A §8.3 AMENDMENT.** The catalogue stays at **28 rules**, no rule is added or
removed, no milestone moves, and roadmap §2 already names *"plenum and Class 2/3 code rules"*. What
changes is that two of them stop being wrong and one number stops implying something it never
computed.

**THE TRADE OVERRULED THE CORPUS AGAIN, AND THAT IS NOW FOUR TIMES.** `trade knowledge beats my
workflow reasoning` was filed after three rulings in which an objection grounded in how the work
actually happens beat one grounded in the documents. This is the fourth, and it is the first where
the corpus was not merely incomplete but **actively wrong in the user's favour**, which is the
direction that does not announce itself.

**11.78.1 LSZH IS A MATERIAL, `CMP` IS A LISTING, AND CONFLATING THEM PRODUCES A FALSE PASS.**
`CODE-002` reads *"error when `Pathway.kind == plenumSpace` and jacket is not `cmp`/`lszh`"*, citing
NEC 800.154. **Low smoke zero halogen is a jacket compound characteristic**, an IEC and European
concern about smoke density and halogen acid gas during evacuation. It says nothing about the flame
spread and smoke development testing (UL 910 / NFPA 262) that a plenum listing rests on, and an LSZH
cable may carry no plenum listing at all.

So the product would have told somebody their unlisted cable was **fine** in a plenum. **A false
pass is worse than a false failure**, because the false failure gets argued with and the false pass
gets built.

Three more defects sit under it, found by reading the model rather than the rule:

| | |
|---|---|
| `enum JacketRating { cl2, cl3, cmr, cmp, lszh, directBurial }` | **Four axes in one enum**: NEC article (`cl2`/`cl3`), listing (`cmr`/`cmp`), material (`lszh`), application (`directBurial`) |
| `Link` | carries **both** `JacketRating? jacket` **and** a bare `bool plenum`, the second with no doc comment and no stated relationship to the first. A link can say `cmp` and `plenum: false` at once and nothing notices |
| The vocabulary | has no `CL2P`/`CL3P`/`CL2R`/`CL3R`, no `FPL`/`FPLR`/`FPLP`, no `OFN`/`OFC` fibre classes, no `CATV`/`CATVR`/`CATVP`, and no `CM`/`CMG`/`CMX` |

**THE RULING.** `JacketRating` becomes **`JacketListing`** and carries only NEC/UL listings, across
the five articles this product's media actually touch: communications (`CM`, `CMG`, `CMR`, `CMP`,
`CMX`, Art. 800/805), Class 2 and 3 (`CL2`, `CL3` and their `R`/`P`/`X` variants, Art. 725),
power-limited fire alarm (`FPL`, `FPLR`, `FPLP`, Art. 760), optical fibre (`OFN`/`OFC` and their
`G`/`R`/`P` variants, Art. 770) and coax (`CATV`, `CATVR`, `CATVP`, `CATVX`, Art. 820). **LSZH leaves
the enum and becomes a separate material characteristic**, because it may accompany any listing or
none. `Link`'s two plenum facts are reconciled: the listing already carries the answer.

**FIRE ALARM AND COAX ARE IN, AND THE USER NAMED BOTH.** `FPLP` was named directly; coax is `RG6`,
which is in every residential job this product exists for, and a coax run in a plenum is exactly the
row `CODE-002` is aimed at.

**THE MIGRATION COST IS ZERO TODAY AND WILL NOT BE LATER**, which is the whole argument for doing it
now rather than at M5. **No file on disk carries `lszh`** (the four starters use `cmr` and `cl2`),
the codec resolves by enum **name** over `JacketRating.values`, and `jacketOptions` is empty on all
38 seeded media types. Nothing reads the field but one label table. The first customer file carrying
a value makes this a migration; today it is a rename.

**11.78.2 SUBSTITUTIONS ARE A LOOKUP TABLE, BECAUSE THE ALTERNATIVE FAILS CORRECT WORK.** NEC permits
a higher listing wherever a lower one is required: `CMP` is acceptable in a riser, `CL3P` where
`CL2P` is required, and so on. A rule that checked only *"is this exactly the listing this pathway
requires"* would fail a correctly-specified plenum cable in a riser, which is **the same
false-positive failure §11.78.3 is about**, arriving from the other direction.

So the hierarchy is **data**, the way the connector-by-signal-family compatibility matrix already is:
CR-024's own distinction is that a genuine lookup table stays data while a rule stays a Dart
function, and this is a genuine lookup table.

**THE ARTICLE BOUNDARY IS THE CLAUSE THAT WILL BE GOT WRONG.** A fibre listing does not substitute
for a communications one: different articles, different tests, different failure modes. The table is
therefore **per-article**, and a listing from an article the requirement does not name resolves to
**UNKNOWN rather than to false** (G4). A rule must be able to say *"this cable's listing is from
another article and I cannot judge it"*, because that is true, and because the alternative is the
false failure this ruling exists to stop.

**11.78.3 `CODE-001` AND `CODE-002` BECOME WARNINGS THAT NAME WHAT TO VERIFY.** Both currently assert
a violation the product cannot actually establish.

**`CODE-001`** (Class 2/3 sharing a pathway with line voltage, NEC 725.136) is stated as a blanket
error. 725.136 runs to a substantial list of permitted arrangements and separations, and this product
models none of the facts that would distinguish them. A blanket error therefore fires most often on
the commercial rows where the arrangement is most likely to be deliberate and permitted.

**`CODE-002`** is accurate for the common case once §11.78.1 lands, and still cannot see NEC
300.22(C), which permits ordinary cable in a plenum inside metal raceway. **This product does not
model raceway**, so it cannot know whether the exception applies.

Both become **warnings** that cite the article, name the exception the product cannot see, and say
what to verify. **This costs nothing that was ever enforced**: G2 and G3 already guarantee that no
finding at any severity blocks a deliverable or gates the bytes. What changes is whether the product
tells a professional they are in violation when it does not know that.

**A CODE CITATION IS A CLAIM ABOUT SOMEBODY'S LICENCE.** That is the standard these two rules are
held to, and it is higher than the standard for the other twenty-six.

**11.78.4 THE POWER ARITHMETIC IS A PLANNING ESTIMATE AND WILL SAY SO.** `Circuit.continuousLimitAmps`
is 80% of the breaker rating, commented `NEC 210.19(A)(1)`. **Eighty percent is the continuous-load
allowance, not a load calculation.** There are no demand factors, nothing classifies a load as
continuous or non-continuous, and what the product actually sums is *typical × diversity, in VA*,
which is a third quantity again.

**THE CODE IS ALREADY MORE CAREFUL THAN THE DOCUMENTS, and that half is protected rather than
changed.** `derived/totals.dart` refuses to convert `typicalWatts` into VA without an authored power
factor (AC-039's rejected *"half of nameplate"* behaviour, restated in its own doc comment), and
`PWR-001` was already demoted from error to warning (CR-020). **No arithmetic changes.** The citation
becomes informative rather than definitional, the derived getter stops claiming a code result in its
name and its comment, and the figure says what it is wherever it prints.

**11.78.5 A STALE CITATION CARRIES A DATE, NOT A GUESSED REVISION.** `ANSI/TIA-570-D` (2018) is cited
in five documents and `TIA-606-C` in one, the latter already noting 606-D beside it.

**`TIA-607` IS CITED NOWHERE IN THIS CORPUS.** Bonding and grounding are not modelled at all, so that
half of the finding has no target, and recording that is worth more than inventing work to match it.

**NO REVISION NUMBER IS ASSERTED FROM MEMORY.** TIA standards are paywalled, the user's own
instruction was that a standard which cannot be located freely may be left alone, and a wrong
revision number in a normative document is worse than a dated one. DR-051 already built the
mechanism for exactly this shape: a reference carries a **retrieved-on date**, because G4 handles
unknown and has no mechanism for stale, and a link rots silently. Every standards citation gains
one.

**The architectural facts the corpus takes from 570-D are revision-independent and are untouched**:
the star / home-run topology and the Distribution Device that the Structure device models. Those are
not going to change in a revision, and the corpus's use of them was never a version claim.

**11.78.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not build the rule engine: M5 is not started, no
`rules/` directory exists, and `CODE-001`, `CODE-002` and `PWR-001` are catalogue rows in `docs/02`
§5 and nothing else, so §11.78.3 and §11.78.4 are **documentation today** and land as behaviour when
M5 builds them. It does not add a rule about riser spaces, though the vocabulary now permits one. It
does not model raceway, which is what would let `CODE-002` see 300.22(C)'s exception rather than
naming it. It does not model bonding or grounding. And it does not touch AC-040's deferred length
rules or the jacket **colour** convention, which is a different fact wearing a similar word and whose
own file already says so.

### 11.79 DR-080 · The accent colour reaches the elevation, and the text colour follows it

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-21** (`#747`, `#748`), on the question DR-059 §11.58.8 deferred in
its own last paragraph and filed separately.

**A §8.3 AMENDMENT, and a narrow one.** Roadmap §2's device-builder line already names the glyph,
which DR-059 put there. This adds the channel that ruling was written *beside*: the accent reaches
paper. No milestone moves, no rule is added or removed, and `kSchemaVersion` does not advance,
because the key is already written and already read back.

**11.79.1 THE FIELD IS AUTHORABLE, PERSISTED, UNDOABLE, AND INVISIBLE.** `TemplateBody.accentColor`
and `DeviceOverrides.accentColor` are both declared, both round-trip through `json_codec.dart`, both
carry a `_safe` change-class rule, and `device_builder_screen.dart:958` ships a control for the
first: **eight fixed Okabe-Ito hues and a `Clear`**, a fixed set rather than a wheel precisely so
that no unchecked hue could reach the greyscale gate. `draw/scene/device_layer.dart:134` computes
`final fill = Fill(palette.deviceFill)` **unconditionally**, and that is every device on every
elevation, on screen and on the sheet. **So the builder has shipped a control that changes nothing
since M4-D**, and the section note beside it tells the user about a mark that is not drawn either.

**11.79.2 DR-059 PRICED THIS AND THE PRICE WAS WRONG, MEASURED BOTH WAYS.** §11.58.8 reads that
making `accentColor` reach `device_layer.dart` *"changes the elevation, regenerates four starters'
goldens and must clear PAL-1"*. Against the tree at `3245e6b`:

| The claim | What the tree says |
|---|---|
| *"regenerates four starters' goldens"* | `accentColor` occurs **0 times** in all four `.rmpj` starters and **0 times** anywhere in `catalog/`. Every device resolves the field absent, the fill is unchanged, and **no golden moves at all** |
| *"must clear PAL-1"* | `tools/pal1_check.py` enumerates in-band `SignalFamilyDef` pairs. It has **no device concept whatsoever** and cannot see a device fill. PAL-1 is not implicated |

Both halves were read off a ruling rather than measured. That is the third time this project has
priced a decision from a derived artifact, and it is why that is a practice rather than an anecdote.
**The correction is recorded here and §11.58 is left as written**, because §11.58 is the record of
what was believed on the day and the mis-pricing is the useful half of it.

**11.79.3 THE COST DR-059 DID NOT NAME IS THE ONLY REAL ONE.** `device_layer.dart` fills the body
and then draws **four text ops over it**: the designator, the name, the type and the U-height badge,
each in a fixed `RackStyle` colour (`deviceDesignator` `0xFF0F172A`, `deviceName` `0xFF334155`,
`deviceType` `0xFF64748B`, `deviceBadge` `0xFF475569`). All four are dark inks chosen against
`deviceFill`, which is `0xFFEFF3F8`, a near-white. **One of the eight shipped swatches is
`Rgb(0x00, 0x00, 0x00)`.** A body filled with it carries black text on black. The hazard is not the
hue: it is that the fill and the ink over it were chosen by different parties, a year apart, and
nothing made them meet.

**11.79.4 THE RULING.** The accent becomes the **device body fill**, resolved **instance override
first, then the template body, then `palette.deviceFill`** when both are absent. That order is not
new law: door 1 of CR-054 exists so a person can say something about *this* device, and an
instance-level statement is by construction the more specific one. `device_layer.dart`'s own header
already records that `DeviceOverrides` *"are still not applied"* there, so this is the first thing
that reads one on the elevation and the precedence is written down before there are two readers to
disagree.

The four label colours are **computed from the resolved fill's WCAG relative luminance** rather than
read from the palette. `pal1_check.py`'s `luminance()` is the reference implementation already in
the tree and is what the Dart must agree with, so **the product does not acquire a second definition
of contrast**: that is the mistake CR-080's font drift and the `family_glyph` measurement both took,
one authority per fact.

**11.79.5 TWO COSTS ARE ACCEPTED IN WRITING, SO M6 IS NOT AMBUSHED BY THEM.** The user was shown
both and took them, and naming them here is what makes that a decision rather than an oversight.

- **The elevation's text palette becomes data-dependent.** `RackStyle.deviceDesignator` is one value
  today and every consumer assumes it is. A sheet whose ink colour depends on document content is a
  new property of this renderer, and the `RackStyle` equality and `hashCode` members that enumerate
  those fields are where a later reader will first notice.
- **Ink coverage on a real laser.** M6's exit criterion is a **physical** print on an ANSI B laser
  plus an ANSI D plotter plus a photocopy, signed off by a person (AC-058 D13). A 42U rack of
  saturated bodies is a toner load nothing has measured, and it is exactly the class of thing that
  is discovered on paper. **`M6-J`'s print matrix (`#357`) is where this is checked**, and this
  clause is what tells it to look.

**11.79.6 SEQUENCING IS CR-078, NOT A PREFERENCE, AND IT IS THIS RULING'S ONE HARD CONSTRAINT.**
*"Hue is never used alone."* Every device is one uniform fill today, so no two devices differ by hue
at all and the invariant is satisfied trivially and vacuously. **The instant accents render, devices
differ by hue and nothing else**, until DR-059's seventeen marks exist to carry the redundant
channel. So **the fill must not ship before M4-R's artwork** (`#694`): they are one deliverable in
two tasks, not two deliverables. This is what makes `#694`'s decomposition urgent rather than tidy,
and it is the reason a milestone that looked fully adjudicated was not.

**11.79.7 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not add a swatch, remove one, or make the set editable:
the eight are Okabe-Ito and the argument for them is unchanged. It does not give the accent a
*meaning*: it is the author's mark, not a category, a lifecycle state or a signal domain, and
nothing derives from it, which is what keeps it out of CR-078's four channels rather than beside
them. It does not touch the schematic. And it does not make `accentColor` reachable from a placed
device's inspector, which is door 1 and is M4-L1's (`#230`).

### 11.80 DR-081 · Three unreachable port fields get a cell, and the rule that would read one is M5's

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-21** (`#747`, `#749`), on a gap `port_table.dart` recorded at M4-E
in its own comment and no task ever owned.

**A §8.3 AMENDMENT.** docs/06 §4.5's column table gains two columns and a **cell shape it does not
have**. No milestone moves; M4-J2 (`#224`) grows by the cell, which is where the scope lands.

**11.80.1 THE GAP, IN THE WORDS OF THE FILE THAT WROTE IT DOWN.** M4-E built seven column packs from
the intersection of docs/06 §4.5's table and the model, and `port_table.dart:86` names what fell
out: `channelIndex` *"belongs with port sets (M4-J2)"*, and `carriedProtocols`/`acceptedFamilies`
*"need a multi-select the grid has no cell shape for"*. All three are declared on `PortDef`, all
three round-trip through the codec, and **not one has ever had a writer**. That comment ends
*"which is `a modelled field is not a reachable one` in its original form"*, and it was right.

**11.80.2 THE RULING: all three get a cell.** `channelIndex` is an **integer cell on the port-set
surface**, which is where its meaning lives: it says which conductor of a `PortSetDef` this port is,
and it is meaningless without one. `acceptedFamilies` and `carriedProtocols` get a **multi-select
cell over the seeded signal families**.

**THE CELL SHAPE IS THE DELIVERABLE, NOT THE TWO COLUMNS.** The grid has single-value cells and
nothing else; a list-valued column is a shape it has never had. Building it once, keyed and testable
like every other cell since M4-F11, is the difference between a pattern the next list-valued field
reuses and a special case that gets copied badly. M4-F11 is the precedent and its lesson was exactly
this: the mixed state came out as **one parameter** once the controls left `port_grid.dart`.

**11.80.3 AUTHORING ONLY, AND THIS CLAUSE IS WHAT KEEPS M5 WHOLE.** **Nothing reads
`acceptedFamilies` at connect time in v1.** The value is authored, persisted, and available to
whatever describes a port; it is a fact about the port for the person reading the drawing.

Whether a connect springs back is a **validation rule**, and validation is M5: a 28-rule catalogue
behind AC-051, which forbids any rule shipping without a known-bad fixture **and** a known-good
near-miss. A rule armed here would be an M5 rule built outside M5's registry, without its pair, and
M5 would inherit a rule it did not write and cannot count against its own exit criterion. **The
milestone's fixture-pair gate is the thing this clause protects**, and roadmap §4 names the pressure
to add "just one more obvious rule" as the mechanism by which M5 overruns.

**11.80.4 DR-012 IS NOT DISTURBED, AND THE DEFAULT IS THE WHOLE REASON.** §11.12 deferred three
gesture rules on the arithmetic that `acceptedFamilies`, `channelIndex` and `maxConnections` are
populated on **none of the 727 seed ports**, so a rule reading one does nothing on every real
document. **Both lists are non-nullable and default to `[]`.** An empty list reads as *this port
states no constraint*, so all 727 seed ports, all four starters and every file on disk keep exactly
the behaviour they have today. **A field gaining a writer does not re-arm a rule that was never
built**, and DR-012's arithmetic stays true of every document this ruling does not touch.

**11.80.5 AN EMPTY LIST IS NOT `null`, AND THE DISTINCTION IS LOAD-BEARING.** G4's absent-key
convention is about **unknowns**. *"This port constrains nothing"* is a **statement**, not an
unknown, and a port whose author has said nothing is not the same as a port whose author has said
*anything goes*. The model already encodes this by making the lists non-nullable, and the multi-select
must not quietly introduce a third state to be helpful. This is DR-063's distinction one field over:
**a disagreement is not an unknown**, and neither is a deliberate emptiness.

**CR-117 holds because the codec writes no key for an empty list**, which is its existing behaviour
rather than a new rule. The 48-template byte sweep is the check, and it fails first if that changes.

**11.80.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not decide `maxConnections`, the third field DR-012
named: that one already has `effectiveMaxConnections` reading it and a different problem. It does not
add, arm, move or re-tier any validation rule. It does not extend the multi-select to `bankKey` or
`setKey`, which are **single-valued** keys and would be actively worse for it. And it does not rule
what a `carriedProtocols` entry means where it disagrees with the port's own `signalFamily`, which is
a question the seed catalog can answer by being censused and which this ruling cannot answer by
assertion: `two documents agreeing is not verification`.

### 11.81 DR-082 · `parity` and `flowControl` are closed sets, and the corpus can now say so

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-21** (`#747`, `#750`). **The only one of `#747`'s three rulings that
blocks nothing**: it is a comment in shipped code reading *"the corpus has not ruled on"*, settled
because a census found it rather than because it stood in the way of anything.

**A CORRECTION, NOT A §8.3 AMENDMENT.** No column is added, no milestone moves, no rule changes, no
sheet gains a field. Two free-text cells acquire a value set.

**11.81.1 WHAT SHIPPED, AND THE COMMENT THAT WAS RIGHT TO REFUSE.** `port_commands.dart:300`
declares `parity` as `PortField<String?>` under the note: *"Free text, because the model's own
comment says the value set is not yet specified. A dropdown here would fix a vocabulary the corpus
has not ruled on."* `flowControl` sits beside it on the same terms, and `SerialSpec` in
`template.dart` carries the same disclaimer on both fields.

**That refusal was correct at M4-F.** Fixing a vocabulary by picking one while building a cell is
how a product acquires rules nobody decided, and it is the shape `a rule you invent must be checked
against the good cases` exists to catch. The refusal was correct; leaving it refused indefinitely
was not, and nothing was going to raise it except a census.

**11.81.2 THE RULING: both become closed value sets.**

| Field | Values |
|---|---|
| `parity` | `none`, `even`, `odd`, `mark`, `space` |
| `flowControl` | `none`, `rtsCts`, `xonXoff` |

Neither is an open vocabulary the corpus was wise to leave alone. **RS-232 has not gained a parity
bit since the corpus was written** and is not going to; these are settled trade facts an installer
can recite, which is exactly the class of thing this project settles by censusing rather than by
inventing.

**11.81.3 THE MODEL'S OWN COMMENT PROPOSES THREE PARITY VALUES AND THIS RULING TAKES FIVE, WHICH IS
A DIFFERENCE AND IS RECORDED RATHER THAN GLOSSED.** `SerialSpec.parity` reads
*"e.g. `none` | `even` | `odd`"*. The comment says **"e.g."** and was illustrating rather than
enumerating: `a spec table is an illustration until censused`, applied to a doc comment.

**The five are RS-232's own set, not an invention of this ruling**, which is what makes taking them
a transcription in DR-057's sense rather than a judgement. **Whether `mark` and `space` appear on
gear a RackPal user actually meets is a TRADE question and this ruling does not claim to answer
it**: `trade objections are questions, not findings` has overruled a confident workflow claim from
this side of the keyboard four times, and this is not the fifth. The argument for including them is
asymmetric cost and nothing else: **an unused enum value costs one line, while a missing one costs a
workaround in the notes column on a port somebody has to physically wire.** If the trade says two of
the five are dead, deleting them later is a smaller edit than this paragraph.

**11.81.4 A FREE-TEXT COLUMN IS THE DEFECT, NOT THE TYPING.** One column holding `none`, `NONE`, `N`
and `no parity` is four values for one fact. The port grid **sorts**, DR-078's `Find & replace`
**matches**, and the schedule **prints**. A column that cannot be sorted is a defect in the
schedule, and it is not repaired by asking users to be careful.

**11.81.5 NO `Other` ROW SHIPS, and this clause has an argument rather than a preference behind it.**
An escape hatch re-introduces exactly the dirty column the value set exists to prevent, and **G4
already supplies what an escape hatch usually reaches for**: absent means unknown, unknown is
expressible today, and the grid already renders it. **A value set with a free-text row is a
free-text column wearing a dropdown.**

**11.81.6 MIGRATION IS NEARLY EMPTY, AND THE REMAINDER FOLLOWS DR-075.** **0 of the 727 seed ports
author either field**, so nothing seeded needs mapping and no starter moves. A value already typed
into a user's project that does not match the set is **retained and shown as it was typed**, not
silently dropped. DR-075 settled this exact shape one domain over for an imported rack label and its
reasoning transfers unchanged: **a wrongly discarded assertion is gone, while a retained one is
visible and correctable.**

**11.81.7 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not touch `baud`, `dataBits` or `stopBits`, which are
integers and were never ambiguous. **It deliberately does not fix `busProtocol`**, which sits three
declarations away and is genuinely open: there is no closed set of control-bus protocols, and it
stays free text for precisely the reason `parity` no longer does. And it does not decide whether
either value prints on any sheet, which is M6's question about columns and widths.

---

### 11.82 DR-083 · The mark rides the designator line, and it wins over a hatch

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-21** (`#694`, `#751`), at M4-R's pick-up and **before any artwork**,
on three things the census found that DR-059 does not answer.

**A DECOMPOSITION RULING, NOT A §8.3 AMENDMENT.** Nothing enters or leaves scope: DR-059 already
ruled the seventeen marks in and DR-080 already ruled the accent onto the elevation. This settles
**where the mark goes, what happens where it collides, and which milestone it waits for**, none of
which either ruling states.

**11.82.1 THE MARK RIDES THE DESIGNATOR LINE, INLINE, AHEAD OF THE TEXT.** It draws at cap height on
the line the designator occupies, and the designator, name and type shift right by a **computed
advance**. Three reasons, and the first is that this is not a new pattern:

- **`family_glyph.dart` already does exactly this and exists because the alternative failed in the
  field.** Its shape is one op whatever the glyph, an advance computed from the type size alone, and
  the emitter and the measurer reading **the same function** so they cannot disagree. That file was
  written after Jost's missing codepoints made the signal glyph measure short and draw wide, putting
  `NET-NEN006` over a net name. Reusing its shape is reusing a fix, not copying a style.
- **It rides the one line that always draws.** `device_layer.dart`'s header records a shipped
  blackout in which guarding the designator suppressed the entire label branch for every 1U device at
  1:10 or smaller. A mark on that line inherits its survival; a mark anywhere else needs a new fit
  rule in the function that has already produced that bug once.
- **It cannot collide with the badge**, which is anchored top-right, or with the name and type, which
  a 1U body drops before the mark is ever reached.

**The rejected alternative is worth recording**: a larger mark on the right, vertically centred, reads
across a whole rack at a glance and is the better picture. It was declined because at 1U it must dodge
a 9 pt badge, which is a new drop tier in exactly the function whose drop tiers went wrong before.
**The picture that reads better is not worth a second blackout.**

**11.82.2 WHERE THE MARK MEETS A HATCH, THE MARK WINS ON A KNOCKED-OUT PANEL.** The collision is real
and no ruling had named it: `kCategoryDefaultGlyph` maps `kCatPassive` to `DeviceGlyph.blank`, and
`scene_builder.dart:344` sets `hatched: options.hatchPassive && body.category == kCatPassive`. **The
devices that default to the `blank` mark are precisely the devices covered in 45° lines.** Order is
hatch, then a padded backing rect **in the resolved body fill**, then the mark. **ONE extra op**, on
passive devices only: this ruling's own text said "two" and counted the mark, which is drawn on
every device hatched or not. `#754`'s case asserts the difference and is what caught it.

**SUPPRESSING THE MARK INSTEAD WAS THE TEMPTING ANSWER AND IT IS THE WRONG ONE.** A blank panel is
already identified by its hatch, so the mark is redundant there, and redundancy is DR-059's own
argument. But `hatchPassive` is on by default, so suppression makes **`blank` and `shelf` draw
nothing at all**: two of seventeen ruled values become unreachable, which is
`a modelled field is not a reachable one` re-created **inside the fix for it**. The knockout costs
two ops and keeps every value real.

**11.82.3 DR-059'S STATED SEQUENCING IS STALE, AND THE CORRECTION LIVES HERE.** §11.58.7 reads that
the artwork *"is a new issue sequenced with M4-K (`#182`), which owns the three live previews and is
the first surface a device glyph appears on at all"*. Against the tree at `2055450`:
**`draw/scene/panel_layer.dart` does not exist**, M4-K is not started, and **DR-080 has made
`device_layer.dart` the first surface a device glyph appears on.** So `#694` is **not blocked on
`#182`**, and the previews become the second surface rather than the first.

**§11.58 is left as written**, on the precedent DR-080 §11.79.2 set one ruling earlier: a ruling
records what was true when it was made, and a correction belongs in the ruling that found it. This is
the second time in three days that a sequencing or costing sentence in DR-059 has not survived
contact with the tree, which is `a stated cost is a hypothesis until it is measured` pointing at
sequencing rather than at cost.

**11.82.4 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not choose the seventeen silhouettes: the value set is
fixed by DR-059 §11.58.5 and censused against the 48 seeded templates, and the artwork answers to
`device_glyph_test.dart` rather than to this. It does not set the cap-height factor or the bearing,
which are numbers to be **looked at on a printed sheet** rather than argued (`#757`). It does not
give the mark a meaning beyond identification: it is not a status, a lifecycle state or a domain. And
it does not touch the schematic symbol, whose four encoding channels CR-078 already governs.

### 11.83 DR-084 · The seeded catalog authors its own marks, so seventeen does not ship as nine

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-21** (`#694`, `#758`), from a probe run while building `#753` and
before the mark had reached a single sheet.

**A §8.3 AMENDMENT, and a narrow one.** DR-059 ruled the seventeen marks into scope and ruled the
**category defaults**; it deliberately left the seeded catalog's own `glyph` field alone. This
changes that one thing. No mark is added or removed, the cap stays at seventeen, the picker is
untouched, and `kCategoryDefaultGlyph` keeps doing its job for every template nobody has authored.

**11.83.1 THE MEASUREMENT, WHICH IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT.** A probe over `buildSeedCatalog()` at
`64b953c`:

| | |
|---|---|
| Templates authoring a `glyph` | **0 of 48** |
| Distinct marks the 48 actually draw | **9**, not 17 |
| Marks no seeded device ever draws | **8**: `extender`, `patchPanel`, `battery`, `shelf`, `speaker`, `camera`, `antenna`, `control` |
| Ids resolving to `display` | **18**, the whole `Field Devices` category |

So on a starter, and on every project a user has not hand-edited, **a speaker, a camera, a keypad and
a projector all draw a rectangle on a stand**, and eight of the marks are unreachable.

**11.83.2 DR-059 SAW THIS AND DEFERRED IT, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS AN AMENDMENT AND NOT A BUG FIX.**
`device_glyph.dart` says so in its own table, unprompted: *"The 18 field devices are the widest
category by a factor of four and the only one whose members share no silhouette at all: a speaker, a
camera, a keypad and a projector. `display` is the modal answer rather than the right one, which is
why the form's picker matters more here than anywhere else."* That was a defensible call. **What it
costs is the first impression**: the elevation is the sheet taped inside the rack door, and the
mark's whole job is to be right at a glance on a document nobody edited.

**11.83.3 THE ASSIGNMENT IS ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN, AND THAT IS WHAT MAKES THIS CHEAP.** Every
`DeviceGlyph` value's doc comment names the catalog ids that motivated it: `F04` through `F08` are
the speakers, `F09` the camera, `F11` and `F17` the antennas, `N03` and `N04` the patch panels, `X03`
the shelf, `P03` the battery, `V06` and `V07` the extenders. DR-059 §11.58.5 calls those ids
*"the evidence that the set was censused rather than invented"*. **This ruling turns that evidence
into the assignment it always described.** No judgement is added; a table already in the tree is
transcribed onto the field that reads it.

**11.83.4 WHAT IT COSTS, MEASURED: AND THIS RULING'S OWN FIRST DRAFT GOT THE MECHANISM WRONG.**
The draft said the key *"is written only when it differs from the category default"*, as though that
were the codec's behaviour. **It is not.** `json_codec.dart:3420` writes `glyph` whenever it is
non-null, and the comment directly above it says why: *"Absent means INHERIT THE CATEGORY'S DEFAULT,
not unknown (DR-059)"*, and writing a resolved value instead would *"put a key on all 48 seeded
templates and regenerate four starters for nothing, and would lose the author's choice the moment
the category changed."*

**So the economy is a property of what this ruling AUTHORS, not of the codec**, and stating it the
other way would have sent the next reader looking for a suppression rule that does not exist. This
is the same failure DR-080 §11.79.2 and DR-083 §11.82.3 each found in DR-059: a mechanism asserted
from the corpus rather than read off the tree. It is recorded here rather than quietly corrected,
because a ruling that hides its own draft error teaches nothing.

**Twenty-six of the forty-eight get a `glyph`**, being exactly those whose mark differs from their
category's default; the other twenty-two inherit and stay null, which is the codec's own reading of
absence. So twenty-six templates gain a key and their bytes move, and **the four checked-in starters
embed snapshots generated from the old seed and must be regenerated**. A starter left alone would
draw the old category mark while a new project drew the authored one, which is worse than either,
and is why the regeneration belongs to this task rather than to a follow-up.

**11.83.5 THE TEST WAS GREEN, CORRECT, AND ASKING THE WRONG QUESTION. THIS IS THE PART TO KEEP.**
`device_glyph_test.dart` asserts *"every one of the 48 seeded templates resolves to a mark"*, and it
has always passed, because they do. **An existence assertion cannot see a collapse.** Forty-eight
templates resolving to nine marks satisfies it exactly as well as forty-eight resolving to
seventeen, and the number that mattered was never asked for. The replacement asks for the **count of
distinct marks**, which is the artifact a person actually looks at.

That is `census before building` for the sixth time, with a twist worth naming separately: the
earlier five found a field that was **empty**, and this one found a field that **resolves perfectly
and collapses**. An empty field is caught by the first query anybody writes. A collapsing one
survives every query except the one that counts the range.

**11.83.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not widen the set: a seeded device fitting none of the
seventeen is a finding for DR-059's cap and goes to the user, never an eighteenth value added inside
a data pass. It does not remove `kCategoryDefaultGlyph`, which is still what a user-authored template
gets and still what `effectiveGlyph` falls back to. It does not touch `accentColor`, whose seeds stay
unauthored on purpose: an accent is the author's own mark and a seeded catalog has no business
choosing one. And it does not make the marks correct, only assigned: whether seventeen silhouettes are
tellable apart at 8 pt remains `#757`'s printed sheet.
