### 11.94 DR-095 · A milestone closes on clauses discharged or parked, and parking costs a ruling

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-26.** In DR-017's lineage (§11.16), which roadmap §8.7 records as
the first ruling to govern **process rather than product**. No count of such rulings is written
here: §8.7's own `DR-001` through `DR-087` range is already stale by several IDs, which is the
liability a written-out count always becomes.

**11.94.1 THE PRACTICE HELD FOR TWO TRANSITIONS AND WAS NEVER A RULE.** The user's account was that
M1 through M3 each finished before the next opened. Checked against the record, that is true of two
transitions and false of two others:

| Transition | Held | The record |
|---|---|---|
| M0 to M1 | no | M0 stands at six of eight clauses, `PARTIAL`, weakest mark `VACUOUS`, today |
| M1 to M2 | yes | M1 eight of eight, weakest mark `CONFIRMED`, drill 2026-07-27 and 2026-07-28 |
| M2 to M3 | yes | M2 five of five, weakest mark `CONFIRMED`, drill 2026-08-01 |
| M3 to M4 | no | M3's subject-tagged work ran 2026-08-05 to 2026-08-10; M4 opens at `e964e28`, 2026-08-13 |

The habit was real and it was a habit. Nothing named it, so nothing noticed when it lapsed, and the
lapse was invisible for thirteen days because the thing that would have shown it (docs/12 §5.2's
header row) is itself stale and has `#92` filed against it.

**11.94.2 THE DEFINITION ALREADY EXISTED. WHAT WAS MISSING WAS A PLACE IT HAD TO BE TRUE.** §8.1
rules that the exit criterion is the unit of truth and that done means demonstrated. docs/12 §0
rules that `DEMONSTRATED` and `CONFIRMED` are the only two of the seven marks that discharge an exit
clause. Between them, "complete" has been precisely defined since the board was written: **every
exit clause of the milestone carries `DEMONSTRATED` or `CONFIRMED`.** No new definition is created
here and none was needed. What is created is a **boundary** at which that definition is checked.

**11.94.3 A STRICT READING DEADLOCKS, AND DR-027 HAD ALREADY BUILT THE WAY OUT.** Some clauses
cannot be discharged by the milestone that owns them, because the thing they name belongs to a
later one. M3's exit criterion asks for a Pull Sheet export; `SheetRole` carries no such value and
building it is M6's work. DR-027 resolved that by **splitting the clause**: M3 owes the derivation,
M6 owes the sheet. AC-018's PRINTS limb is parked on M6 the same way, as `#574`.

M6 is itself a join on M2, M3 and M5 (docs/12 §5.5). So a rule reading *"every clause discharged
before the next milestone opens"*, applied without that split, requires M3 to wait on M6 and M6 to
wait on M3. **The mechanism that avoids the cycle is therefore not an exception to this ruling; it
is half of it**, and DR-027 is its precedent rather than its violation.

**11.94.4 THE RULE.** A milestone may not **open** while the milestone before it holds an exit
clause that is neither:

* **discharged**, carrying `DEMONSTRATED` or `CONFIRMED` under docs/12 §0; nor
* **parked**, reassigned by ruling ID to a **named later milestone**, with the structural reason it
  cannot be discharged where it sits.

A milestone may not **close** while it holds an undischarged clause that is not parked. The two are
one rule read at two moments, and the second is the load-bearing one: opening is a soft edge that
`M5-0a` and `M8-F1` both crossed usefully, whereas closing is the act the version number and the
board both key off.

**11.94.5 PARKING COSTS A RULING ID, AND THAT PRICE IS THE POINT.** A park is an amendment to what a
milestone owes, so it is §8.3's machinery and not a note: an ID, a named destination, and the
reason. Without the price, "parked" becomes the word for every clause nobody wants to do, and the
board goes back to being a list of things believed. With it, a milestone's open work reads as a
number a person can act on: *n discharged, m parked on a named milestone, k owed*, and only `k`
blocks.

**11.94.6 THE MARKS ARE THE VOCABULARY, AND NOT EVERY CLAUSE TABLE USES THEM.** M0 §2.2 and M6 §5.5
mark clauses with the seven. M3's current clause table (§5.2, against `01c698d`) does not: its
states read `BUILT`, `needs a person`, `NOTHING ALLOCATES ONE` and `M6's`. Those are honest and they
are informative, and none of them is a mark. §0 already rules that *"a mark that reads 'demonstrated
in spirit' or 'demonstrated but' is not a mark, it is a negotiation"*, and `BUILT` is that sentence
with the negotiation left out: it says code exists, which is `BELIEVED`, while reading as though it
discharges.

**Normalising every clause table to the seven marks is a prerequisite of this ruling and not a
tidy-up.** It is not formatting. `BUILT` resolving to `DEMONSTRATED` or to `BELIEVED` is the
difference between M3 owing one clause and owing four, and no reader can tell which from the word.

**11.94.7 THIS APPLIES RETROACTIVELY TO M0, WHICH IS A DEPARTURE FROM §8.8 AND IS DELIBERATE.** §8.8
adopted its record-keeping rule forward-only, on the ground that a hash reconstructed months later
is a guess wearing the costume of a record. That reasoning does not transfer: a clause's mark is not
archaeology. The evidence for every clause is in the tree right now and can be re-run, so applying
this backwards recovers facts rather than inventing them.

The retroactive reading surfaces this much, and the cost is stated rather than discovered later:

| Milestone | Clause | Today | Disposition this ruling forces |
|---|---|---|---|
| M0 | 4a, `templates.keys` (AC-015) | `VACUOUS`, but no longer for the stated reason | **Owed, and small.** §2.4 said it *"becomes real the day M4 or M1's copy-on-place lands"*. M4-S landed `SaveTemplateToProjectCommand`, which mutates `doc.templates`, so the precondition is met and the clause is a generator change rather than a park |
| M0 | 5, epoch-mask letter (AC-014) | `VACUOUS`, and drifting (§4.5) | **Owed.** Cheap today, dearer with every derived consumer added |
| M3 | 1, sixty drops under fifteen minutes | `UNPERFORMED` | **Owed.** A drill, a person and fifteen minutes. Nothing else discharges it, and it is M3's only remaining build-independent debt |
| M3 | 2b, one `rackLabel` each | **built** | **No action.** DR-040 (§11.39), shipped as M3-K `#661` with all four tasks Done on 2026-08-11 |
| M3 | 4, fourteen unbound far ends | **reachable** | **No action.** Same ruling: `@panel=` lands forty-six and leaves fourteen open, which is what the clause asks |
| M3 | 4c, prints | `M6's` | **Already parked**, by DR-027 as `#574`. No action |

**11.94.8 THE TWO ROWS ABOVE THAT NOW READ "NO ACTION" SAID "OWED" WHEN THIS RULING WAS WRITTEN, AND
THE MISTAKE IS THE POINT.** As first published, §11.94.7 recorded M3's clause 2b as *"owed, and the
expensive one"*, and this subsection carried the consequence in a heading: **that M4 could not close
until landings existed in the model.** It said the rack-label pattern could not render because
`{PANEL}` and `{PORT}` are facts about a landing and nothing in the product recorded one, and that
`allocateOutletRackLabel` had four callers all inside its own test.

**Every sentence of that was true on 2026-07-27 and false when it was written.** DR-040 (§11.39)
settled it on 2026-08-11: `BindEndpoint` is built, `@panel=` lands a drop on a panel's rear port,
and the rack label is allocated through the one format engine rather than typed. It shipped as M3-K,
board `#661`, with `#663` through `#666` all Done. The allocator's callers today include
`bind_endpoint_command.dart` and `home_run_commands.dart`.

**THE SOURCE WAS docs/12 §5.2's CLAUSE TABLE, WHICH CARRIED ITS OWN DATE AND WAS OBSOLETE THE NEXT
DAY.** Its caption read *"against `01c698d`"*, a commit of 2026-08-10; DR-040 settled on
2026-08-11. **The table was accurate for one day**, and `#92` is already filed to sweep it. It was
read as current, and a ruling was written on top of it. CLAUDE.md states the rule that would have
prevented this in one line: **read the ruling, not only the derived sentence**, and it gives the
precedent, *"a stale sentence in docs/09 once produced a board task instructing weeks of work that
a ruling had abolished."* The same failure has now produced a **ruling clause** asserting a
milestone was blocked on work that had shipped a fortnight earlier, which is worse: a board task
is discarded when someone opens the code, and canon is quoted.

**What this costs the rule itself: nothing, and that is worth saying plainly.** §11.94.4 is
unchanged, and so is the retroactive reach in §11.94.7's heading. What changed is the WORKLIST, and
a worklist that shrinks on inspection is the rule behaving correctly: the gate blocks on clauses
neither discharged nor parked, and two of them turned out to be discharged. **M4's closure is not
blocked by M3.** M3's own remaining debt is a drill.

**AND THE GENERAL LESSON FOR §11.94.9's SCRIPT.** The mechanical gate is blocked on normalising the
clause tables to the seven marks, and this subsection is the argument for why that normalisation is
a correctness prerequisite rather than tidying. A table whose states read `BUILT` and `nothing
allocates one` cannot be dated by a machine, and a human reading it cannot tell a current row from
one describing a tree that is six weeks gone. **The sweep must date every clause row against the
ruling that last touched it**, not against the commit the section was written at.

**11.94.9 THE MECHANICAL GATE IS SEQUENCED BEHIND THE NORMALISATION, NOT SHIPPED WITH THIS RULING.**
This ruling is enforced by review on the day it lands. A CI gate reading docs/12's clause tables and
failing on an undischarged, unparked clause in any milestone before the current one is filed as
`#780` under `#92`, **blocked on the §11.94.6 normalisation**, and joins the family in `tools/`.
Precedent for a gate that parses the corpus is `pal1_check.py`, `palette_parity.py` and
`registry_parity.py`.
Shipping the script first would have it read `BUILT` and either crash or, far worse, guess.

**11.94.10 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not change any milestone's exit criterion; every
criterion stands verbatim as written, and a park moves who owes a clause rather than what it says.
It does not forbid work landing against a later milestone: `M5-0a` and `M8-F1` both did so
usefully, the version rule in docs/14 §14.0 already contemplates it, and §11.94.4 gates **closing**
rather than touching. It does not make CI mechanical for anything else (§4.1 stands). It does not
rule on whether M0's epoch-mask clause is discharged by extending `epoch_mask_test.dart`, which is
§4.5's question and is unchanged. And it does not backfill closed **tasks**, which remains §8.8's
forward-only rule: this ruling reaches clauses, which are re-runnable, and not hashes, which are
not.

### 11.95 DR-096 · The product is RackPal, and the wordmark is the one thing this repository cannot re-cut

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-26.** The name **RackMate** is withdrawn and the product is
**RackPal**. Both searches are the user's; both results are recorded below rather than assumed.

**NOT A §8.3 AMENDMENT**, on DR-089's own reasoning (§11.88): §8.3 governs moving an item between
v1, v1.1, v1.2, v2 and not-doing, and nothing moves here. The scope list is untouched, every exit
criterion stands verbatim, and no milestone gains or loses a clause. What changes is an identifier.
It still takes a ruling ID, because §8.2 wants one for a change this size and because the sweep it
authorises would otherwise be a large untraceable diff.

**11.95.1 THE SEARCH THAT FOUND THIS IS THE SEARCH RJ-017 SCHEDULED, AND IT RAN IN TIME.** RJ-017
put *"a trademark search before any certificate or domain is bought"* into hardening under
AC-058/D9, and DR-089 §11.88 restated it while shipping the wordmark. It ran. **A company producing
homelab-focused hardware is using RackMate, and the user assesses the likelihood of a cease and
desist as high.**

Nothing had been bought and nothing had been signed when that came back. DR-006 had already made
signing self-signed with no OV/EV reputation ramp (§11.6), so there is no certificate to reissue and
no SmartScreen history to lose. **This is the cheapest moment at which the finding could have
arrived**, and it arrived there because a rule said it had to arrive before the purchases rather
than with them. Recorded as a rule that paid, since the board's opening table is otherwise a list of
the ones that did not.

**RackPal has cleared its own search** (user, 2026-08-26), which is why it is ruled here and not
merely proposed. A second name adopted on assumed availability would repeat the failure at twice the
cost, the sweep below having already run once.

**11.95.2 THE SWEEP IS MECHANICAL EXCEPT WHERE THE STRING IS A QUOTATION, AND THAT EXCEPTION IS THE
WHOLE RISK.** Measured at `21b42fe` with `git grep`, so a reader can re-derive rather than trust:

| What | Measured | Command |
|---|---|---|
| `rackpal`, any case | 4,359 hits in 807 files | `git grep -Iic rackpal` |
| `package:rackpal` | 2,109 lines in 608 files | `git grep -Ic "package:rackpal" -- '*.dart'` |
| `.rackpal` literal | 209 hits in 59 files | `git grep -IFc -- .rackpal` |
| Inside a blockquote | **30 lines in 12 files**, of which **24 in 11** are in swept files | `git grep -Iic "^ *>.*rackpal" -- '*.md'` |

**THAT LAST ROW WAS WRONG TWICE BEFORE IT WAS RIGHT, AND BOTH ERRORS ARE KEPT HERE RATHER THAN
CORRECTED AWAY**, because this ruling authorises a substitution at 4,359 sites and the reader needs
to know how the counting failed rather than only what it settled at.

**First it read 9.** `git grep -Ic "^> .*RackPal"` is case-sensitive, and eighteen occurrences are
the LOWERCASE form inside quotations: `rackpal_core` in docs/03's dependency rule and docs/07 §385,
`packages/rackpal_core/…` in docs/08 §386, `.rackpal` in docs/10 §173. A pattern written against
the name as a reader says it cannot see the name as a machine spells it.

**Then it read 27.** `^>` anchors the quote marker to column zero, and three lines in
docs/m1-implementation-log.md §§1862, 1863, 1865 are indented inside a list. `^ *>` finds them and
returns **30**. That second miss happened *in the same paragraph that was documenting the first
one*, which is the most useful fact in this subsection: a count corrected once is not a count
verified, and the correcting pass inherits the blind spot of whatever it corrected with.

**The number the sweep is actually measured against is 24, in 11 files.** The other six are in
docs/m1-implementation-log.md, which is excluded whole (below), so they are protected by the file
rule rather than by the line rule and must not be counted twice. **Post-conditions on two different
sets are how a sweep passes its own check and still fails**, so the two are separated here: 30 is
the corpus fact, 24 is the obligation.

Those twenty-four are the ones a `sed -i` gets wrong. **Canon quotes rulings, criteria and critiques
word for word, and the house style already protects that: the em-dash sweep left blockquotes alone
"because canon quotes rulings and critiques word for word and editing a quotation falsifies the
record."** The identical argument governs here and is stronger, because a name inside a quotation is
load-bearing: docs/00 §30's *"RackPal is a cable-schedule generator…"*, canon §10's *"RackPal is a
local application"* and docs/12 §4372's DR-006 amendment are all records of **what was said at the
time under the name in force at the time.**

So the rule for the sweep is: **rename the PRODUCT, never the RECORD.** A blockquote, the M1
implementation log (65 hits) and the `.okf` decision bundle (191, of which 95 are the decision
files) are history, and history said RackMate. Everything else, code, identifiers, package names,
paths, live prose, becomes RackPal.

**AND A QUOTED PATH STAYS QUOTED, EVEN THOUGH THE SWEEP MAKES IT STALE.** The twenty-four split
**15 lowercase to 9 cased, with no line carrying both**, so fifteen of them quote an identifier
rather than a sentence. Leaving them means canon will hold
blockquotes naming `rackpal_core` after no such package exists. That is correct and it is the
lesser of the two errors: a quotation altered to stay accurate is no longer evidence of what was
said, and this corpus turns on being able to tell those apart. The practice already exists and is
docs/12 §5.2's, which keeps M3's exit criterion verbatim under a heading saying DR-027 amended it:
**the correction goes in live prose beside the quotation, never inside it.** A reader who needs the
current path reads the sentence under the quote.

**11.95.3 THE FILE FORMAT SURVIVES, AND THAT IS LUCK RATHER THAN FORESIGHT.** Four extensions are
in the corpus, and the split runs cleanly between them: `.rmpj` (451 hits), `.rmdev` (79) and
`.rmlib` (31) are `rm`-prefixed and **do not spell the name**, so they carry over untouched and
**CR-117's byte round-trip is not in play at all**: no fixture is rewritten, no golden regenerated,
no migration written. `.rackmate` (209) does spell it and goes.

The `rm` stood for RackMate and now stands for nothing in particular. **Leave it in this sweep.**

**THE USER WANTS THEM TO MATCH, LATER (2026-08-26), AND THE COST THIS RULING FIRST GAVE FOR NOT
DOING IT WAS WRONG.** The sentence that stood here said re-cutting to `rp` *"would invalidate every
file a user already has"*, citing DR-006's shared-file reality. **Counted rather than asserted, the
tree holds four files carrying any of these extensions**, and all four are the checked-in starter
projects; `.rmdev` and `.rmlib` have **no actual files at all** and exist only as strings in code
and prose. M8 is `NOT STARTED` with no installer, nothing signed and nothing published, so **there
is no user, anywhere, holding a file this would invalidate.** The cost quoted was a real one
described in the wrong tense.

So this is **DEFERRED WITH A TRIGGER, and the trigger is M8**, on canon §10.11's pattern. Before M8
the change costs four regenerated starters, which `tool/generate_starters.dart` already produces,
plus the strings. After M8 it costs exactly what the withdrawn sentence claimed, because that is
the milestone at which files start leaving this machine. **A deferral whose cost rises at a known
event is not the same as a deferral, and writing it as one is how the expensive version gets
chosen by default.** Filed as `#782`.

Not ruled here: which letters. `rp` is the obvious mapping and it is not the only one, and the
choice interacts with `.rmdev` and `.rmlib` as a set rather than one at a time.

**11.95.4 THE WORDMARK CANNOT BE RE-CUT INSIDE THIS REPOSITORY, BY ANYONE, AND IT IS THE LONG POLE.**
`brand.dart` is the wordmark as fixed outlines, and DR-089 §11.88 shipped it that way on two
grounds, the second of which now binds hard: **Nasalization's EULA §4.3 forbids the font file
entering this repository, now or later**, and §4.6 forbids inclusion in Publicly Available Software,
which the GPLv3 release under consideration is in all but name.

Outlines are letterforms. New letterforms spelling RackPal therefore **cannot be produced by anyone
working in this tree**, whatever tooling they have, because the tool that produces them is the font
and the font may not be here. They must be cut outside by a holder of a Nasalization desktop
licence and handed over as paths.

**This makes the wordmark an art-asset dependency with the longest lead time in the rename, and it
is already blocking.** The `app_icon.ico`, the document icons and the window icon sit behind the
same brief. Any of that work already in flight is RackPal-shaped and is now waste; whoever holds it
should be told before they deliver, which is a message the user sends and not this repository.

**11.95.5 THE OS IDENTITY STRINGS ARE FREE TODAY AND DEAR AFTER M8.** `Runner.rc` carries
`CompanyName "com.rackpal"`, `InternalName "rackpal"`, `OriginalFilename "rackpal.exe"` and
`ProductName "rackpal"`. Nothing is signed, nothing is installed, nothing is published, so these
are four string edits. After M8 they are an identity a signature and an install base have been
issued against. **They move in this sweep and not later.**

**11.95.6 THE REMOTE IS NAMED TWICE AND IS NOT PART OF THE SWEEP.** `origin` is
`https://{org}.visualstudio.com/RackMate/_git/RackMate`: the Azure DevOps **project** and the
**repository** both carry the name, as does the area and iteration path this board files everything
under. Renaming those is console work with consequences for every board URL already cited in the
corpus, and it is **deliberately not authorised here.** It is its own decision, and the safe default
is that an internal remote may keep a withdrawn name indefinitely, because a cease and desist
addresses a product in commerce and not a private git host.

**11.95.7 SEQUENCE, AND WHY THE ART GOES LAST.** The search clears (done), this ruling lands, the
mechanical sweep lands as **one commit** with the fifteen gates as its proof (`#781`), and the art
assets land when they arrive. The sweep goes before the art because it is deterministic and gated, and the
art is neither; sequencing them the other way would leave the tree half-renamed while waiting on a
person.

**The sweep's post-conditions**, on the pattern the em-dash sweep established, since a
4,359-site substitution is exactly the shape of change that passes a spot-check and fails in
detail: **the fifteen gates green**; **the nine blockquote lines unchanged**, verified by
re-running the count above and getting nine; **`.rmpj` and `.rmdev` hit-counts unchanged**; and
**every `package:` import resolving**, which the analyzer proves at zero errors rather than a grep
does.

**11.95.8 THE SWEEP FALSIFIED THIS RULING, AND A THIRD PROTECTED CLASS IS WHY.** §11.95.2 named two
things the sweep must not touch: quotation lines and whole record files. It ran, and it rewrote
**this subsection's own parent** into nonsense. The opening read *"The name RackPal is withdrawn and
the product is RackPal."* §11.95.1 read *"a company producing homelab-focused hardware is using
RackPal"*, which is not merely wrong but the reverse of the legal fact it exists to record.
§11.95.3 read *"the `rm` stood for RackPal"* and *"`.rackpal` does spell it and goes."*

**The missing class is prose that ASSERTS A FACT ABOUT THE OLD NAME**, as distinct from prose that
merely uses the product's name. A blockquote was protected because of its marker, not because of
what it contained, and the sentences above carry exactly the same content with no marker on them.
Two further kinds fell to it:

* **Inline quotation.** RJ-017's wording is quoted in running prose in four places, and each became
  *"file-type registration for `.rackpal`"* against a ruling that said `.rackmate`. An inline quote
  is a quotation; only the `^ *>` test could not see it.
* **A prediction, which is the sharpest loss.** `docs/research/critique-completeness.md` D9 reads
  *"no trademark search is mentioned: 'RackMate' is a plausible collision in adjacent hardware/AV
  markets and should be checked before any signing certificate or domain is bought."* **That
  critique is the origin of RJ-017's rule and it was correct**, and the sweep rewrote it to name
  RackPal, converting a record of a right call into a false warning about the name that replaced
  it. A prediction with its subject swapped is worse than a deleted one, because it still reads as
  evidence.

All of it is restored, and the count is the check: after restoration the only strings matching the
withdrawn name outside the record files are the twenty-four quotation lines and the frozen remote
URL, which is what §11.95.2 said the answer should be.

**WHAT THIS COSTS A FUTURE SWEEP, stated so the next one does not learn it the same way.** A
mechanical substitution over a corpus that documents its own decisions cannot be verified by
counting what changed. It has to be verified by reading what a changed sentence now CLAIMS, and the
sentences most likely to be wrong are the ones nearest the subject: the ruling that authorises the
sweep is the single most dangerous file in it. **This one was caught by reading §11.95.3 for an
unrelated reason.** No post-condition in §11.95.7 would have found it, and none is added here that
would, because the honest position is that this class needs a reader rather than a check.

**11.95.9 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not change the file format, the schema version or any
extension but `.rackpal` (§11.95.3). It does not rename the Azure DevOps project, the repository or
the board's area path (§11.95.6). It does not buy a domain: RJ-017 sequences that after the search
and the search is now clear, but a purchase is the user's act and its own decision. It does not
settle the mascot, which is canon §10.12(f). It does not disturb DR-089, whose outlines-not-text
ruling stands unchanged and is the reason §11.95.4 is the long pole rather than a find and replace.
And it does not rule on what the withdrawn name is worth defending: no position is taken here on
whether RackPal was ever infringing, only that the product will not be called it.

### 11.96 DR-097 · The tracker grows a fourth level, and an epic's state follows its criterion

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-28.** The board's hierarchy becomes **Saga → Epic → Story →
Chapter**, a Saga is a **release band**, and an Epic's board state is decided by **§8.1's exit
criterion** rather than by how many children are still open. Four questions were put and four were
answered; the reasoning for each is below rather than in a commit message.

**NOT A §8.3 AMENDMENT.** §8.3 governs moving an item between v1, v1.1, v1.2, v2 and not-doing.
Nothing moves. The scope list is untouched, no exit criterion changes a word, and no milestone gains
or loses a clause. What changes is **the shape of the container the work is tracked in**. It takes a
ruling ID on DR-096's precedent (§11.95): §8.2 wants one for a change this size, and the migration
it authorises would otherwise be a large untraceable diff across every work item in the project.

**11.96.1 THE SHAPE, AND WHAT EACH LEVEL HOLDS.**

| Level | Holds | Was |
|---|---|---|
| **Saga** | A release band: v1, v1.1, v1.2, v2 | did not exist |
| **Epic** | A milestone (M0…M9), or a ruling-born body of scope | Epic, unchanged |
| **Story** | What a milestone decomposes into: M4-A, a clause tracker | `Issue` |
| **Chapter** | The unit of work a Story decomposes into | `Task` |

**11.96.2 A SAGA IS A RELEASE BAND, AND THAT IS WHAT MAKES THE LEVEL EARN ITS KEEP.** A fourth
level whose meaning is "bigger than an epic" is a taller filing cabinet and nothing else. This one
carries **roadmap §2's scope list**, which is the one list §8.3 governs. The consequence is the
point: **moving an Epic between Sagas is the visible act of a §8.3 amendment**, so the thing the
process already required to cost a ruling ID now also costs a drag the reader can see. It also
gives the four scope epics that were impersonating milestones (macOS `#55`, the Store `#100`, the
Plan view `#588`, the community catalog `#592`) a level to sit at that does not imply they are
milestones with exit criteria.

**11.96.3 THE COST IS A TYPE CHANGE ON EVERY WORK ITEM, AND IT IS PAID DELIBERATELY.** Azure DevOps
lets an inherited process restyle, extend and disable a system work item type. **It does not let one
be renamed.** `Story` and `Chapter` are therefore new custom types and every existing item is
converted into one. Measured at the time of the ruling with a WIQL count over
`[System.TeamProject]='RackMate'`: **759 work items**, of which 526 are `Task` and 219 are `Issue`.
The alternatives were considered and rejected in the open: renaming only the backlog *tabs* leaves
the cards themselves reading `Issue`, which is the exact irritation being paid to remove; and
adopting the Agile process buys four levels natively at the price of Microsoft's vocabulary
(`Feature`, `User Story`) instead of this project's.

**11.96.4 AN EPIC'S STATE FOLLOWS ITS CRITERION, NOT ITS CHILD COUNT, AND THE BOARD HAD DRIFTED
FAR ENOUGH TO PROVE WHY THAT NEEDS SAYING.** §8.1 already rules that *"the milestone is the unit of
planning; the exit criterion is the unit of truth"*. The board was not reading it. Measured
2026-08-27, against `docs/12`'s own marks on the same day:

| Epic | `docs/12` said | The board said |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | `CRITERION MET`, 8 of 8, weakest mark `DEMONSTRATED` | `To Do`, 3 of 10 stories closed |
| M1 | `CRITERION MET`, 8 of 8, weakest mark `CONFIRMED` | `To Do`, 1 of 10 |
| M3 | `CRITERION MET`, 4 of 5 with the fifth parked | `To Do`, 17 of 18 |
| M4 | `IN PROGRESS`, clause 1 `CONFIRMED` | `To Do` |

**Three milestones whose criteria were met, and one in flight, all sitting in the same column as M9,
which nobody has touched.** A board on which every epic reads `To Do` conveys exactly as much as a
board with no states at all.

The root cause was one level down and is the more useful finding. **The clause-tracking Stories
were never closed when their clauses were discharged.** `docs/12` §2 has marked M0 clause 1
`DEMONSTRATED` since M0 closed; `#28`, the Story that tracks it, was still open on 2026-08-27, as
were five of its siblings and all eight of M1's. `#32` and `#65` were closed on 2026-08-27 by
`38167ec` and `8af36ed`, **and their child Chapters `#508` and `#514` were left open**, so the same
class of drift was reproduced in the act of paying it down. **Forty-three** items were closed on
2026-08-28 to reconcile the two (fourteen clause Stories, twenty-six of their Chapters, plus `#508`,
`#514` and `#567`), each carrying the `docs/12` row or the closing commit that discharges it, and
**no code changed in any of them**.

**The rule this settles:** an Epic is `Done` when its exit criterion is met. Children still open
when that happens are **re-parented to the milestone that will actually deliver them**, never left
hanging under a closed Epic. `#66`, M1's goal clause *"and it ships to real users"*, is the worked
example: `docs/12` §3 marks it `NOT BUILT` and it is the one M1 row that did **not** close. It
moved to M8, which owns the installer and the signing, because that is who inherits it.

**11.96.5 NO WORK ITEM MAY HAVE NO PARENT.** Twenty-three items sat at the root of the board,
belonging to no Epic and appearing in no rollup, of which **two, `#781` and `#782`, were Chapters
parented to nothing at all**, skipping the Story layer the hierarchy requires. Six that were born of
rulings (`#655` DR-039, `#681` DR-048, `#686` DR-049, `#688` DR-051, `#689` DR-052) are promoted to
Epics, which is the shape they always had; `#687` DR-050 is **not**, because "geometry fills the
room estimate" is Plan view work and belongs under `#588`. The remaining debt, reviews and research
gather under one Epic that is honest about being none of the above. **`#96`, `#97` and `#98` are
post-M2 reviews. M2 closed on 2026-08-01.** They were three milestones overdue and invisible the
whole time, because an item with no parent appears on no backlog.

**11.96.6 THE BOARD IS A SITE OF DR-096'S SWEEP AND WAS NOT COUNTED AS ONE, AND THE SWEEP ALSO
REACHED SOMEWHERE ITS OWN RULING EXCLUDED.** Measured 2026-08-27 over all 759 items: **694 carried
`rackmate-sync` and exactly one carried `rackpal-sync`**, against a convention `CLAUDE.md` already
documented as `rackpal-sync`. A standard written down and applied to one item in six hundred and
ninety-five is not a standard. The tag is an **identifier** and is swept; work item titles and
descriptions that quote the old name are **records** and are not, per §11.95.2.

**The more interesting half is the over-reach.** §11.95.9 rules in terms that DR-096 *"does not
rename the Azure DevOps project, the repository or the board's area path"*. The project is
`RackMate`, its area and iteration paths are `RackMate`, and all three are correct. **`CLAUDE.md`
nonetheless says the project, area and iteration are all `RackPal`**, which cost this session six
failed commands before anyone thought to distrust the document rather than the credentials. A sweep
that renames the product is a mechanical act; a sweep that renames it **inside its own ruling's
list of exclusions** is a demonstration that the exclusion list was never turned into a check. The
line is corrected here, and the general lesson is §11.95.2's own, arriving a second time: the
dangerous sites in a rename are the ones a pattern cannot distinguish from the safe ones.

**11.96.7 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not rename the Azure DevOps project, the repository or
the area path, which §11.95.9 already settled and which this ruling merely stops `CLAUDE.md` from
contradicting. It does not change any exit criterion, any milestone's size or any scope band's
contents: an Epic lands in the Saga it was already in. It does not decide the Kanban column set or
the swimlanes, which are a team board setting, are reversible in a click, and are not worth a ruling
ID. And it does not settle which Saga the promoted Epics of §11.96.5 belong to beyond what their own
rulings already say, DR-052 being explicit about v1.2 and the rest defaulting to v1.

**11.96.8 THE MIGRATION RAN ON 2026-08-28, AND WHAT IT FOUND IS WORTH MORE THAN WHAT IT MOVED.**
`746` items converted, `0` failed. The board now holds **4 Sagas, 20 Epics, 218 Stories and 524
Chapters**, `766` in total, with **zero hierarchy violations and zero items without a parent**,
both re-derived from a fresh query rather than inferred from the conversion log.

**The fourth level immediately found fourteen faults the third level had been hiding.** They are
pre-existing, none was created by this ruling, and not one was visible while the board had three
levels:

| Fault | Count | What it was |
|---|---|---|
| Chapter directly under an Epic | 4 | `#574`, `#576`, `#589`, `#779`, skipping the Story level |
| Story under a Story | 10 | `#96`'s nine bug-hunt findings, and `#690`'s one |

A three-level board tolerates `Task`-under-`Epic` and `Issue`-under-`Issue` in silence, because
nothing in it can express that a level was skipped. **Adding a level did not add rules; it made an
existing rule checkable**, which is §11.94.2's argument arriving in a different subsystem: the
definition already existed and what was missing was a place it had to be true.

`#574` is the sharpest of them. It is DR-027's **parked** AC-018 PRINTS clause, the worked example
§11.94.3 uses to justify parking at all, and it was sitting as a Chapter directly under M6 rather
than as a clause tracker beside every other clause tracker.

**`#779` is a duplicate identifier, found on the way past.** It is titled `M4-K1`, but `#226`
already is M4-K1 under Story `#182`, and `#779`'s subject, *"a structured wiring run cannot choose
its landing port"*, has nothing to do with M4-K's panel auto-layout. The title is **left alone as a
record** and the collision is noted on the item, rather than silently renumbering a Done item and
destroying the evidence that board IDs have been assigned by hand.

**11.96.9 THREE PLATFORM FACTS, EACH OF WHICH COST A ROUND TRIP, RECORDED SO THE NEXT PERSON DOES
NOT REDISCOVER THEM.**

**A project's process cannot be changed over the REST API.** The documented
`PATCH _apis/projects/{id}` with `capabilities.processTemplate` returns `400 "The project update is
invalid"`. This was **isolated rather than assumed**: the identical `PATCH` carrying only a
`description` returns `202`, so the endpoint and the credentials are fine and the capability
specifically is not exposed. It is a web-UI operation, and the four clicks are the only manual step
in this entire migration.

**The process API returns `200` while doing nothing.** Renaming a derived work item type returned
`200` with the name unchanged; renaming a state returned `200` with the state unchanged. **A
success code from this API is not evidence that anything happened**, which is the same lesson the
non-vacuity floors teach about a green test run, and every step of this migration was therefore
re-read rather than trusted.

**A custom work item type is created with the state `To do`, and the system types use `To Do`.**
The casing differs, and ADO will not rename a state, will not accept `To Do` as a new state while
`To do` exists (it compares case-insensitively), and will accept the pair only if the old state is
**deleted first and the new one added second**. Caught before the migration ran. Had it not been,
`766` items would have landed in a state vocabulary that no longer matched `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/12`
or any prose in this corpus, and every one of those documents would have been quietly wrong.

### 11.97 DR-098 · An override says three things, and two of its six fields were saying somebody else's

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-28, before any code**, on DR-077's precedent (§11.76): three of
the questions M4-L could not start without are product decisions rather than authoring, and settling
them first is what stopped the last issue of this shape from building a save nothing read.

**11.97.1 THE CENSUS IS WHY THERE ARE THREE QUESTIONS AND NOT ONE.** `DeviceOverrides` is declared
at `device_instance.dart:38` and `PortOverrides` at `port.dart:34`, both since M0, both
codec-covered, both under CR-117's byte round-trip, and **neither has ever been constructed by
anything but its own class and the codec**. That much `#183` already said. Three things it did not:

| Found | The measurement |
|---|---|
| **Every `overrides` block on disk is empty** | Four starters and six fixtures hold 800+ of them and **zero keys** between them, walking the parsed JSON rather than grepping a field name, because `displayName` also lives inside every `TemplateBody` and the naive grep returns 847 |
| **Two of six `DeviceOverrides` fields have no reader** | `typicalWatts` and `weight` reach `derived/device_loads.dart:154,157`; `accentColor` reaches `draw/scene/device_layer.dart:148` by DR-080 §11.79.4. `displayName`, `typePrefix` and `bodyDepth` reach nothing |
| **`PortOverrides` has no reader at all** | Not one of `label`, `connector` or `signalFamily` is read anywhere outside the codec. `connect_target.dart:238` and `schedule.dart:228` both read `PortDef.label` straight off the template |

**The empty-corpus figure is what makes all three of the rulings below free**, and it is DR-079
§11.78's timing argument arriving a second time in the same words: today this is a field deletion,
and the first customer file carrying a key makes it a migration.

**11.97.2 `null` WAS DOING TWO JOBS AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT STATEMENTS.** The class header rules that
*"`null` is the sparse 'not overridden' semantics (CR-053, AC-012)"*. G4 and CR-114 rule that null
is **unknown, never estimated**. Both are correct about their own subject and they collide on one
sentinel, with a consequence nobody had written down:

> A generic 2U amplifier template declares 30 lb. The unit actually in this rack is a different
> model and its weight is not known. **There is no way to say so.** The instance can restate 30 lb,
> or it can supply a different number it does not have.

`RCK-003` then totals the template's figure as a measurement, and the rack subtotal prints a mass
with no unknown counted against it. **That is the exact fabricated rollup CR-114 exists to forbid,
reached through the one door built to let a person correct the record.** It is also the shape
DR-079 §11.78.2 found on `JacketRating`, where a field mixing four axes could assert `cmp` and
`plenum: false` at once: a two-state field asked to carry a three-state fact.

**11.97.3 THE RULING ON STATE: an override is tri-state, on every overridable field.** An override
says exactly one of:

| State | Meaning | On the wire |
|---|---|---|
| **inherit** | this instance has no opinion; the template's value governs | the key is **absent** |
| **set** | this instance states this value | the key is **present** with the value |
| **unknown** | this instance states that the template's value does **not** govern here, and the true value is not known | named in a present `cleared` list |

**The third state cannot be spelled as an explicit `null`**, because CR-114 rules that unknown
serializes as an absent key and an absent key already means inherit. So the third state is carried
by a **present key with a present value**, a `cleared` list naming the fields, absent when empty.
That keeps CR-117's byte round-trip intact, keeps the encoder's existing skip-nulls behaviour
(which is what produced 800 empty blocks and is correct), and makes the addition purely additive:
no `kSchemaVersion` advance, because a file that carries no `cleared` key reads exactly as it does
today.

**Uniform across all overridable fields, and the uniformity is the ruling rather than a detail.**
Only `weight` and `typicalWatts` feed a G4 rollup today and `bodyDepth` joins them the moment M5
builds `RCK-012`. A tri-state on some fields and not others is a class whose next reader has to
learn which is which, and this repository has already recorded what that costs: §5.3.18's
`PortDef.gender` is a non-nullable enum with a default, so silence there is a positive claim, and
the defence named there was *knowing which fields are shaped that way*. Two shapes in one class is
the thing that makes them unknowable.

**11.97.4 THE RULING ON FIELDS: `displayName` and `typePrefix` are deleted from `DeviceOverrides`.**
Both facts already have an instance-level home that works. `DeviceInstance.name` is renameable and
prints in the equipment list's `DESCRIPTION` column; the designator is allocated from the template's
prefix and `DeviceInstance.designatorLocked` already exists to pin it. Keeping the override beside
each of them makes **two spellings of one fact**, which is DR-079's `Link.plenum` again: a document
that can say a thing twice can say it two different ways, and then a reader must be told which wins.

`bodyDepth` **stays**. It has no duplicate anywhere on the instance, and M5's `RCK-012` (front depth
plus rear depth plus 50 mm allowance against usable depth) is a named consumer that does not exist
yet. It is declared, unread, and **the tri-state above is what makes it honest to leave unread**:
absent means inherit, and nothing is asserted.

`DeviceOverrides` therefore ships four fields: `typicalWatts`, `weight`, `bodyDepth`, `accentColor`.

**11.97.5 THE RULING ON SURFACE: door 1 is a section of the inspector column, not a modal.** The
320px column already exists and already holds the one working device control, the lifecycle picker
(M3-A/7). Two of the four remaining override fields change something the user is looking at:
`accentColor` is the device body fill by DR-080 §11.79.4, and `weight` moves the rack's load gutter.
**A modal over the elevation hides the thing the edit changes**, and the amber scope badge's whole
job is to say what this edit does not touch, which is a claim best read beside the untouched
devices.

It also retires `inspector_panel.dart:21`'s deferral **in the file that wrote it**. That header
rules that *"rendering a plausible-looking device form with no working fields would be worse than
rendering the honest summary"*, and notes that the lifecycle picker does not break the rule because
it is the opposite case. Door 1's fields are the same opposite case: every one of them has a reader
already in the tree.

The builder shell was declined on merit rather than cost. It is a full-screen surface carrying a
port grid and Quick Add, none of which door 1 may touch, so a per-instance mode would ship a screen
whose majority is disabled, and a screen mostly disabled reads as broken rather than as scoped.

**11.97.6 WHAT THIS RULING DOES NOT SETTLE, AND `#233` INHERITS IT.** `PortOverrides` has **no
reader**, so an editor written against it today writes a field nothing consumes: §5.3.13's finding
exactly, one level down. **M4-L4 therefore owes a resolver before it owes a form.** The two call
sites that read `PortDef.label` straight off the template (`connect_target.dart:238`,
`schedule.dart:228`) are its consumers, and they must both come to read the resolved value through
one function, because a port label that differs between the connect picker and the schedule sheet
is a document contradicting itself on the one field an installer uses to find the jack.

No ruling is made here on **which** `PortDef` facts are overridable beyond the three declared, nor
on whether `PortOverrides` takes the same tri-state. Both are `#233`'s to raise, against a resolver
that exists.

### 11.98 DR-099 · Door 2 moves the device it was opened from, and the Device Manager holds one draft

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-29, before any code**, on DR-077's and DR-098's precedent. Two
questions M4-L2 could not start without, both of which are product decisions with a trap on each
side rather than authoring work.

**11.98.1 THE FIRST QUESTION IS ONE AC-041 CREATED AND DID NOT NOTICE.** AC-041 cut the Update
Manager to v1.2 and made v1 **copy-on-place**: `templateRef{templateId, version, contentHash}` is
recorded, the snapshot is embedded, and *"placed instances untouched until opted in"*. That is the
right cut and nothing here reopens it.

What it does not say is what happens to **the instance the gesture was invoked from**. CR-054's
door 2 is *"edit the template, forking version+1"*, and `#231` restates AC-041's clause verbatim. Read
literally, the sequence is:

> Right-click `AMP-1`. Choose **Edit the template**. Change the wattage. Save. The template is now
> v2, `AMP-1` is still on v1, and **nothing in v1 of this product can ever move it**, because the
> mechanism that would is v1.2's.

**A menu item invoked on a device that provably cannot affect that device is not a feature, it is a
misunderstanding waiting to happen**, and the user's next act is to try it again. This is the same
class as DR-077 §11.76's finding, where a template saved in the builder could not reach a rack: the
machinery was right and the route was missing.

**11.98.2 THE RULING ON BINDING: the originating instance rebinds; every other instance stays
pinned.** Choosing door 2 **on a device** is itself the opt-in AC-041 asks for. The user did not
open a library manager; they pointed at one device and asked for its template to change. Copy-on-place
holds exactly where AC-041 put it, on the instances nobody pointed at.

**AC-041 IS NOT AMENDED AND THIS IS NOT §8.3 SCOPE.** No update mechanism is built, no diff, no
per-cable remap, no conflicts-with-local-edits merge: the five things AC-041 cut stay cut. One
device's `templateRef.version` advances at the moment its own user asks, which is a rebind of one
reference and not a package manager. The passive stale-fork badge (CR-062, `fork_status.dart`) is
untouched and still describes every device that did not rebind.

**THE ALTERNATIVE WAS OFFERED AND DECLINED ON ITS COPY.** Leaving everything pinned and explaining
it on save is defensible and is AC-041's letter; it was declined because the sentence it requires
(*"Saved as v2. Devices stay on the version they were placed at until v1.2"*) is a permanent apology
printed at the moment of success, and because the commonest expectation of the gesture would be
wrong every time. Removing door 2 from the device menu entirely was also offered and declined: it
would leave CR-054's three doors unreachable from one place, which is the whole shape CR-054 rules.

**11.98.3 THE SECOND QUESTION IS A DATA-LOSS TRAP, and it is in the app shell rather than the
model.** The Device Manager is one of six views and keeps **one** draft alive across view switches:
`app_shell.dart` records that an `IndexedStack` was tried at DR-091 and reverted, and that the draft
survives on `AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin` instead. Door 2 has to open a template into that one
surface, so a user with unsaved work in it is one menu click from losing it.

**11.98.4 THE RULING ON COLLISION: door 2 refuses, shows the draft, and says why.** It switches to
the Device Manager and, when a dirty draft is open, loads nothing:

> **Finish or discard this template first.**

`TemplateEditSession` already tracks `isDirty` and `editsSinceSave`, so the check costs nothing and
reads a value the session maintains rather than a second notion of dirtiness.

**NO DISCARD PROMPT, AND THE REASON IS WHERE PEOPLE CLICK.** A dialog offering *"discard and open the
other one"* is the shape people dismiss by reflex, and a discarded draft has **no recovery path**:
the session is a deep copy that exists only in memory, so there is nothing for `Ctrl+Z` to reach and
nothing on disk to reopen. A refusal costs a user with a forgotten draft one extra step and can
destroy nothing. A second builder window was declined as the largest change for the least return:
two live `TemplateEditSession`s and two undo stacks would put CR-106's one-machinery-three-stacks
reasoning back on the table for a collision that a guard closes in one branch.

**11.98.5 WHAT THIS RULING DOES NOT SETTLE.** It says nothing about door 3, whose rebind is already
CR-054's own text and which is `#232`'s. It does not decide what the Device Manager shows when door 2
is invoked twice on the same template, because the second invocation finds the first still open and
the guard above answers it. And it does not give the stale-fork badge a surface: `fork_status.dart`
has had its rule since M4-C and a widget is still nobody's, which is recorded here so the next reader
does not go looking for one.

### 11.99 DR-100 · A `.rmdx` carries the body flat, because the sections were an illustration with 21 holes in it

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-29, before any code**, on DR-077 (§11.76) and DR-098 (§11.97)'s
precedent: M4-M2 (`#235`) is a file format, and a format question answered after the writer exists
is a migration rather than an edit.

**A §8.3-ADJACENT AMENDMENT, and it is named as one.** No scope moves and no milestone changes, but
this **changes what two derived documents assert** about a shipped file shape, which §8.3's own
corollary in `getting-started.md` says is the moment to stop and record a ruling. `docs/06` §7.3's
worked example and `docs/02` §6.4 are edited to match rather than left pointing at a shape the codec
does not write.

**11.99.1 THE CENSUS IS THE RULING, AND IT WAS RUN OVER THE ENCODER RATHER THAN THE PROSE.**
`_encodeTemplateBody` (`json_codec.dart:3445`) is the only description of a `TemplateBody` under
CR-117's byte gate. Counted from the function, not from a grep of field names, because
`putIfNotNull` and the three bare `json[...] =` assignments do not match the pattern the always-on
keys do:

| Measurement | Figure |
|---|---|
| Keys `_encodeTemplateBody` emits | **39** |
| Keys docs/06 §7.3's worked `.rmdx` places, sections plus top level | **18** |
| Keys with **no home anywhere in the corpus** | **21** |
| Keys the example **renames** against the encoder | **2** |

The twenty-one: `accentColor`, `alternateMountMethods`, `category`, `connectorProjectionNm`,
`containerUsableDepthNm`, `containerUsableWidthNm`, `containerVented`, `containerWeightCapacityUg`,
`customPanelWidthNm`, `description`, `glyph`, `isContainer`, `maxUnsupportedMassUg`, `model`,
`nominalSpanTwelfths`, `panelGraphics`, `portSets`, `requiresClearanceAboveU`,
`requiresClearanceBelowU`, `submittedBy`, `thermalClass`.

**`model` IS ON THAT LIST AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MAKES THIS URGENT.** It is a required constructor
parameter, always encoded, and DR-056 §11.55.4 rules that it stays undefaulted **specifically so it
prints `—`**. It is the unknown `docs/17`'s clause-2 drill is sent to look for. A codec built from
§7.3's example drops it, and the field that proves G4 works would have been lost on the one path
built for sharing a device.

**11.99.2 THE TWO RENAMES ARE A DEFECT IN THE ILLUSTRATION, NOT A DECISION IT WAS MAKING.** The
example writes `depthNm` where the encoder writes `bodyDepthNm`, and `chassisWidth` where the
encoder writes `chassisWidthNm`. The second is the worse of the two: `"chassisWidth": 432000000` is
a bare integer with **no unit in its key**, in a format whose own ruling exists to forbid exactly
that. CR-063 rules `.rmdx` obeys I-1, and N3 rules the naming. An illustration cannot overrule
either, and nobody was choosing to when they typed it.

**11.99.3 THE SECTIONS' FOOTING WAS THINNER THAN THREE DOCUMENTS MAKE IT LOOK, and tracing it is
what decided this.** The chain is one sentence long. **CR-053's subject is the override key
namespace**, and it **rejected** `design-ux-device-builder.md` §5.1's dotted paths
(`"identity.name"`, `"physical.weightKg"`) in favour of typed classes. The sections survive only in
that rejection's trailing clause, *"`.rmdev`'s `identity.` / `physical.` / `power.` sections are a
file layout only; the codec flattens them onto `TemplateBody`"*, whose whole job is to say the
sections do **not** define an override namespace. It asserts they exist in passing, on the way to
throwing away the proposal they came from.

Everything downstream is a restatement of that clause in a **priority-3 derived document**:
`docs/06` §7.3's example and `docs/02` §6.4. **This is §11.56.5 arriving for the third time**, after
a Dart constructor read as a product rule (DR-056) and docs/06 §5's pseudocode pricing a feature cut
that did not exist (DR-057): *a derived document describing a mechanism is not a ruling about what
the mechanism needs.*

**11.99.4 THE RULING: the file is an envelope over the body the encoder already writes.**

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "kind": "device-template",
  "templateId": "0f3a…",
  "version": 3,
  "contentHash": "sha256:…",
  "body": { "…": "the 39 keys _encodeTemplateBody emits, sorted" }
}
```

**`derivedFrom` moves inside `body`, where the encoder already puts it**, rather than being lifted
to the envelope as §7.3 drew it. It is a `TemplateBody` field; hoisting it would be the twenty-second
invented assignment and would give one fact two homes, which is DR-098 §11.97.4's rule against two
spellings applied to a file.

**THE MEASUREMENT THAT SETTLED IT.** A template snapshot **already on disk** in all four starters is
`{templateId, version, contentHash, capturedAt, body: {…}}`. The ruled `.rmdx` is that shape with
`capturedAt` dropped (a file has no capture time) and `schemaVersion` and `kind` added. **The format
was therefore not designed here; it was recognised.** `.rmda` is an array of these plus a manifest
(DR-015 §11.15.3), so the archive inherits it and no second body shape is invented there either.

**11.99.5 WHAT THE FLAT BODY BUYS, STATED AS A MECHANISM RATHER THAN AS TIDINESS.** `.rmdx` acquires
**no second description of a `TemplateBody`**. The alternative was a 39-row partition table that
must stay **total** as the class grows, because a key no section claims is a key that silently
vanishes from the file, and only a gate written for that purpose would ever say so. That is
precisely the failure `copyTemplateBody`'s own header records about a hand-written clone: *"a clone
drifts the first time somebody adds field 51."* The counter-argument was put and is real: a `.rmdx`
is the unit people email each other, `port_validation.dart:154` already reasons about a hand-edited
one arriving, and sections help a person find a key in a 39-key object. **It was outweighed by the
21 holes**, each of which would have been authored today with no source, and one more owed on every
future field, forever.

**11.99.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not touch the unit regime (CR-063 stands), the
migration chain (`.rmdx` keeps its own, AC-050/A8.2, starting at `schemaVersion` 1 independent of
`.rmpj`'s 2), `contentHash`'s status as a warning and never a load failure (AC-042), or the JSON
depth and size limits every import path owes (AC-058/D8, `#237`). It says nothing about the import
and export **surface**, which is `#236`. And it does not make the sections wrong as **documentation**:
a reader who wants the identity fields grouped is served by docs/06 §3's own headings, which is where
that grouping was always doing real work.

### 11.100 DR-101 · An id collision on import means somebody typed the same name, and only a person knows which

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-29, before any code**, for DR-100's reason one level up: M4-M3
(`#236`) is the surface that first lets a template from outside this machine reach a rack, and the
rule for what happens when it lands on a name you already use is not derivable from the file.

**11.100.1 THE FACT THAT DECIDED IT, AND THE FIRST ANSWER IT OVERTURNED.** `templateIdFor`
(`template_snapshot_commands.dart:68`) derives the id **from the display name**:
`HDMI Matrix 16x16` becomes `tpl.hdmi_matrix_16x16`, and does so identically in every project on
every machine. That was `#232`'s deliberate call, made so *"a person diffing two `.rmpj` files"*
reads what the device is instead of a UUID, and it is not reopened here.

Its consequence for import is what nobody had written down. **A colliding id does not mean "this
template came back". It means "somebody typed the same name",** and between two integrators
documenting the same class of hardware that is close to certain rather than rare. The first ruling
put to the user priced collisions as rare and as mostly the returning-file case; **that premise was
wrong and it was load-bearing**, so the question was put again against the measurement.

**The policy for the local case was already ruled, in the function's own header**, and reading it is
what caught this:

> *"Collisions get a numeric suffix rather than joining an existing id: two devices a user happened
> to name the same thing are two devices, and silently merging them would put one template's ports
> on the other's instances."*

An import that joined an existing id unconditionally would ship exactly that defect, and every
placed instance of the incumbent would take a stale-fork badge (CR-062) pointing at a device that is
not theirs.

**11.100.2 THERE IS NO SIGNAL IN THE FILE, AND THAT IS A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN A SHRUG.** Three
candidate discriminators were checked against the tree and all three fail:

| Candidate | Why it cannot answer |
|---|---|
| `derivedFrom` | Written by **door 3 only** (`template_fork_commands.dart:196`). Door 2 forks `version+1` on the **same** id and leaves it untouched, so the returning-file case carries no lineage at all |
| `contentHash` | Every value in the tree is a labelled placeholder. `#795` is filed and unbuilt, and a placeholder never distinguishes anything |
| The version number | A `.rmdx` carries **one** version, not a chain, so a stranger who iterated their own same-named device to `@4` is indistinguishable from your template returning at `@4` |

**A rule keyed to the version was drafted and rejected on the third row.** It would have merged two
strangers whenever the incomer's version happened to be higher, which is `#232`'s defect reached
through a narrower door rather than closed. This is `a rule you invent must be checked against the
good cases` firing before the rule shipped.

**11.100.3 THE RULING: on collision, and only on collision, ask.** Two buttons, no default action,
no third option:

> A device template named **HDMI Matrix 16x16** is already in this project.
> `[ Add as a new version of it ]`  `[ Import as a separate template ]`

**Add as a new version** takes `nextTemplateVersion` and keeps the id, so placement resolves the
newest and the send-it-back-fixed flow works. **Import as a separate template** takes
`templateIdFor`'s suffix, which is the existing policy unchanged.

**THE PROMPT IS NOT A HEDGE AND IT IS NOT THE DEFAULT SHAPE THIS CORPUS PREFERS.** DR-033 §11.32
rejected a save-flow prompt in terms, because a question asked every time trains the dismissal
reflex and makes the rare bad case routine. **That argument does not reach this one, and the
difference is the trigger**: DR-033's prompt fires on every save, and this one fires only when an
ambiguity actually exists, on a gesture the user just initiated deliberately, with the answer
available to them and to nothing else. **A question with no derivable answer is the one case a
dialog is the right instrument.**

**11.100.4 THE RULING ON PLACEMENT: `File ▸ Export device template…` and `File ▸ Import device
template…`.** Beside `Export PDF…`, which is where every other file operation in this product
already lives and where `docs/17`'s drill already sends people. **Import belongs to no template**, so
a palette card's context menu would split the pair across two surfaces and make one verb learnable
twice. A card-level `Export` was declined for `file_picker.dart`'s own stated reason: *"a second call
site would be a second dialog configuration to keep in sync"*, and `session_layering_test.dart` RULE
7 asserts there is exactly one.

**11.100.5 THE RULING ON COPY: one line, in the import dialog.** *"A device template is data. It
contains no scripts and nothing that runs."* docs/06 §7.3 requires the dialog to say it, and the
failure being answered is a reasonable person hesitating over a file a stranger emailed them, which
is a hesitation that happens **at the dialog** and not six months earlier. A dismissible first-run
card was declined for that timing: it lands when nobody is importing anything, and the person who
dismissed it is exactly the one now staring at a stranger's file. Dropping the sentence entirely was
declined as a scope edit under §8.3 rather than a copy choice, §7.3 having stated the requirement in
terms.

**11.100.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not make `contentHash` real, so **AC-042's mismatch
warning and its badge cannot be exercised until `#795` lands** and `#236` must not be read as having
discharged them. It does not give the stale-fork badge a surface, which §11.98.5 already records as
nobody's. It says nothing about importing a `.rmda` or about several libraries at once, both M4-N's.
And it does not decide what happens when the imported body is **byte-identical** to a version
already held: that is a no-op worth detecting, but detecting it cheaply is `#795`'s hash, so it is
named here and left to it.

### 11.101 DR-102 · The palette answers for the document AND the loaded libraries, and a template in two of them is two rows

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-29, before any code**, on the precedent this milestone has now set
four times (DR-077, DR-098, DR-100, DR-101): the questions a story cannot start without are product
decisions, and settling them first is what stopped the last four issues of this shape from building
a save nothing reads.

**11.101.1 THE CENSUS FIRST, AND ONE OF M4-N's FIVE CHAPTERS IS PARTLY BUILT.** `#241` reads
*"THE ITEM MOST LIKELY TO BE UNDERESTIMATED. Nothing carries this today. It is a field on a RUNTIME
object, NOT on `TemplateBody`, because the same template can legitimately arrive from two libraries
and a field on the body would force a false choice between them."*

**`TemplateProvenance` already exists, on a runtime object, in exactly that shape.** M4-S built it
at `derived/placeable_templates.dart:53`, with two values, `seeded` and `project`, and a class
comment that already reasons about what this build cannot tell apart. **The architectural call
`#241` was going to make is made and shipped**, and what remains is widening it to name a library.
That is the fifth time this milestone a chapter written from an absence has met a filled one, and
the first time the surprise was in the cheap direction.

The other four chapters' premises hold. `#238` is right that there is **no writable library
directory at all**: `data_root.dart` defines the portable and installed roots and no library under
either. `#239` and `#240` are unbuilt and both are now materially cheaper than when they were
priced, because the `.rmdx` codec they were waiting on exists (DR-100) and `rmdx_codec.dart`'s own
header already states the relationship: *"`.rmda` is an array of these plus a manifest."*

**11.101.2 THE QUESTION NO DOCUMENT ANSWERED.** `buildPlaceableTemplates(doc)` is the palette's
single source, and DR-077 §11.76.1 made that its **property** rather than an implementation detail:
the palette lists *the document's own shelf*, and
`rackpal_ui/test/canvas/palette_reads_the_document_test.dart` drives live commands through a mounted
screen to hold it, because the defect it closed was a surface holding a `late final` copy of a
constant.

M4-N makes the palette answer for the document **and N libraries**. That is not a contradiction of
DR-077, whose subject was the in-project case, but it changes what *placeable* means, and no ruling
in this corpus says which way.

**11.101.3 THE RULING ON SOURCE: one merged list, every row carrying where it came from.**
`buildPlaceableTemplates` takes the loaded libraries alongside the document and returns one sorted
list of rows tagged by provenance; `#242`'s filter chips narrow it.

**`#242` is the argument, in its own words**: *"Multiple libraries loaded at once, filtered by which
one a device came from, the user-facing point of the whole subsystem."* Filtering by source only
means anything if the sources are in one list to be filtered. It also keeps **CR-104's one-palette
rule literally true** rather than by interpretation, and keeps placement a single gesture.

**The alternative was real and is recorded rather than waved past.** Keeping the palette on the
document alone, and requiring a library template to be *added to the project* before it can be
placed, preserves DR-077 untouched and makes *place* always mean *place something this document
holds*, which is what AC-041's copy-on-place already guarantees on the wire. It was declined on
cost to the common case: it puts a step in front of every use of a library, and it makes M4-O a
prerequisite for M4-N being useful at all rather than the follow-on the decomposition has it as.

**DR-077's PROPERTY WIDENS AND MUST BE RESTATED WHERE IT IS HELD.** It becomes *the palette lists
the document plus the loaded libraries, and never a constant*. The `late final` defect that test
exists to catch is untouched by the widening; what changes is that a second source must be read
afresh too, and the test file is where that gets said.

**11.101.4 THE RULING ON COLLISION: two rows, each tagged.** A template id present in two loaded
libraries, or in a library and the document, appears **once per source**, distinguished by the tag.

**`#241`'s own sentence is the argument** and it was written before anybody asked this question:
provenance cannot live on `TemplateBody` *"because the same template can legitimately arrive from
two libraries and a field on the body would force a false choice between them."* That reasoning only
holds if both are meant to survive to the screen.

**It is also DR-101 §11.100.1 one level up.** `templateIdFor` derives an id from the display name,
identically on every machine, so a colliding id means **two people typed the same name**, not that
one template is duplicated. Hiding one would be the defect `templateIdFor`'s own header refuses,
reached through the palette instead of through an import.

**A precedence rule was considered and declined**, and the cost is what decided it: it silently
hides a device the user deliberately loaded, and the hidden row reappears when they unload the other
library, which reads as a bug rather than as a rule. **Refusing to load a colliding library was
declined harder**: since ids are name-derived, two independently authored libraries that each
contain an `HDMI Matrix 16x16` could never be loaded together, so the multi-library feature would
refuse its own main use case.

**THIS IS NOT THE DUPLICATE-ROW DEFECT DR-077 §11.76.2 CLOSED**, and the difference is the reason
the tag is load-bearing. That defect was **one** template appearing twice in one search because the
pinned group leaked into the filtered state: two rows, one thing, no way to tell them apart and no
reason for the second. This is **two** things that happen to share a name, each answering for a
different shelf, and the tag is what makes them two things rather than a bug. A row that could not
say which library it came from would be that defect.

**11.101.5 THE RULING ON SHAPE, which is engineering and is written down so it is not re-taken.**
`TemplateProvenance` becomes a **sealed class**, not an enum with a nullable `libraryId` beside it.
Three variants: seeded, project, and one carrying a library's id. An enum plus a nullable field is a
two-field invariant that a constructor cannot enforce and a `switch` cannot exhaust, and this
repository already spells exactly this shape as a sealed class in `Outcome`, `FileContent` and
`FsOp`. `isProjectAuthored` survives as the one question the palette badge asks.

**11.101.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not decide where the library directory lives, which is
derivable from `data_root.dart`'s existing portable-versus-installed rule and is `#238`'s. It does
not touch the `.rmda` format, which DR-015 §11.15.3 already ruled and `#239` implements. It says
nothing about **favourites, smart folders or fuzzy search over port families**, all of which are
M4-O's and none of which this ruling makes easier or harder. It does not decide what happens when a
library fails to load, beyond AC-042's standing rule that a hash mismatch is a warning and never a
refusal. And it does not make the browser a prerequisite: the palette is usable with libraries
loaded and no browser at all, which is the whole reason this shape was chosen over the other.
