### 11.102 DR-103 · Placing a library row copies the template into the project, and the palette says which shelf every row came from

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-30, before any code**, on the precedent this milestone has now set
five times (DR-077, DR-098, DR-100, DR-101, DR-102). DR-102 ruled that the palette answers for the
document **and** the loaded libraries. It did not rule what happens when somebody double-clicks one
of those rows, and the census found that today the honest answer is a refusal.

**11.102.1 THE FINDING: DR-102's palette would list rows it cannot place.**
`buildPlaceFromCatalogCommand` opens with `resolveLatestTemplate(doc, catalogId)` and returns
`CatalogPlacementFailed('Unknown catalog template "$catalogId".')` when that answers null
(`commands/catalog_placement.dart`). It has resolved out of `RackDocument.templates` since M0, and
DR-077 §11.76.3 made that its **property** rather than an implementation detail. A library template
is by definition not in the document. So every library row DR-102 adds would list with a badge, take
a double-click, and answer with a refusal naming an id the user can see on screen.

DR-102 §11.101.3 says the merged list *"keeps placement a single gesture"*, and that is the whole of
what it says about placement. **That sentence is a consequence, not a mechanism.** The mechanism is
ruled here rather than chosen inside a widget.

**11.102.2 THE RULING ON PLACEMENT: the copy happens, and it is AC-041 rather than a new idea.**
Placing a row whose provenance is a library writes that template's snapshot into
`RackDocument.templates` and then places the device, **in one transaction**.

This is neither an invention nor a compromise. **AC-041 already rules that v1 is copy-on-place**:
`templateRef{templateId, version, contentHash}` is recorded and *the snapshot is embedded*, which is
what makes a `.rmpj` self-contained and what §11.35.4 leans on when it says a document RackPal
produces is the user's own work. docs/02's rejected-alternatives table is blunter still: the
alternative to embedded snapshots is *"a live library reference"*, and the cost it names is
*"non-reproducible deliverables; drawings that change silently across machines"* (CR-054, AC-041).
A device resolving out of a `.rmda` on one person's shelf **is** that rejected alternative. So the
copy is not the price of this feature; it is the format's standing promise, and the only open
question was where it gets paid.

**ONE TRANSACTION, AND NOTHING IS BUILT FOR IT.** `DocumentController.transact` already groups any
number of commands into a single undo entry and applies each on `add` so the next one sees it
(`document_controller.dart`, CR-106's third piece). `SaveTemplateToProjectCommand` followed by
`AddDeviceCommand` inside one `transact` is one `Ctrl+Z`, which is what a single gesture owes. A
composite command was considered and is recorded only so that nobody builds one.

**THE PLACEMENT IS BUILT BEFORE THE COPY IS COMMITTED, NOT AFTER.** `buildPlaceFromCatalogCommand`
takes the resolved snapshot as an argument on this path, so a rack with no room refuses **without**
having copied anything. Adding the save first and discovering the refusal second would leave a
template in the project for a device that was never placed, and `transact` commits whatever children
it has: it rolls back on a throw, and a refusal is not a throw. This is the one ordering constraint
in the chapter and it is why the argument exists.

**11.102.3 THE RULING ON THE ID THAT IS ALREADY TAKEN, and it is the common case rather than the
edge.** A library row names `templateId@version`. Three cases, and all three are decidable without
asking the user anything:

| The document at that exact key | What happens |
|---|---|
| Nothing | Copy the library's own `templateId@version` verbatim, then place. The version is **preserved, not reset to 1**, for `buildTemplateImport`'s stated reason: a later `@4` then slots in above it and the chain keeps meaning what it means. |
| A body that hashes identically | **No copy at all.** The document already holds this template; place it. Nothing is announced, because nothing changed. |
| A body that hashes differently | Mint a fresh id through `templateIdFor(doc, displayName)` at version 1, copy that, then place. |

**Row three is not hypothetical and DR-101 §11.100.1 is why.** `templateIdFor` derives an id from
the display name identically on every machine, so two people who both typed `HDMI Matrix 16x16` have
`tpl.hdmi_matrix_16x16` in both libraries, both at version 1. DR-102 §11.101.4 already ruled that
those are **two rows** in the palette; this is the same ruling one step later, at the moment one of
them has to land in a document that holds the other. Overwriting was never available: the key is
what placed devices resolve against, and rewriting it would change what somebody's existing device
IS. Placing the document's version instead would silently give the user the other library's device
under the name they clicked.

**THE COMPARISON IS A RECOMPUTED HASH, NOT THE CLAIMED ONE** (`templateContentHash`, `#795`).
Comparing the two `contentHash` strings would answer "unknown" for every template written before
`#795` and for every hand-authored one, and there is no user to ask mid-gesture. Hashing both bodies
answers the question that is actually being asked, which is whether these are the same device.

**`SaveTemplateToProjectCommand`'s revert stays bounded**, which is the one property that had to
survive. Its own comment rests that on `nextTemplateVersion` having guaranteed the key was free; on
this path the guarantee is established differently and just as strictly, since case one is reached
**only** when `doc.templates[key]` is null and case three mints an id nothing holds. An undo can
therefore still not delete a snapshot somebody else's devices resolve against.

**11.102.4 THE RULING ON WHAT IS SAID: once per template, never per placement.** The status line
names the copy the first time a given library template lands and never again: *"Added HDMI Matrix
16x16 from Shop Kit. Placed MTX-1 at RK-1 U3, front."* Every later placement reads exactly as it
does today.

Silence was declined for the reason this repository keeps re-finding: a project quietly growing a
template is a change to a saved artifact that the user did not ask for in those words. Announcing on
**every** placement was declined for the opposite one: the fact is true once, and a clause repeated
on every double-click is the sentence people stop reading, which spends the warning's value before
the day it matters. **The trigger is the copy actually happening**, so the rule carries no state of
its own and cannot drift out of step with what the document did. Case two of §11.102.3 is silent by
construction, and that is the same rule rather than an exception to it.

**11.102.5 THE RULING ON GROUPING: the category, badged. NOT a pinned group per library.** A
library's HDMI matrix files into `Video` beside the seeded ones, carrying its library's name as the
badge where an authored template carries `PROJECT`.

**The alternative is what is already built, and it was still declined.** DR-077 §11.76.2 gives an
authored template both homes: badged in its category, and repeated in a `This project` group pinned
above the nine. Mirroring that would give every library its own pinned group, and consistency with a
shipped surface is a real argument. It loses on arithmetic. The pinned region sits above the
categories in a panel that is **280px wide by default and legal down to 220** (docs/04 §1), one
library costs one heading, and the user's own goal for this subsystem is *"multiple device libraries
loaded into the device palette"*. At four libraries the nine categories start below the fold, so the
feature's success case is the case that breaks the panel. **The chips in §11.102.6 are what replaces
the pinned group**, and they cost one row of height no matter how many libraries load.

**11.102.6 THE RULING ON THE FILTER: single-select source chips, and `All` is one of them.** A
wrapping chip row under the search box, one chip per SOURCE: `All`, `Catalog`, `This project`, and
one per loaded library. Choosing one narrows the whole panel to that source.

Single rather than multiple, on the story's own words: *"filtered by which one a device came from"*.
Multi-select is the more powerful query and was declined on the state it admits, **zero chips lit**,
which renders as an empty palette that looks broken and needs a rule of its own to prevent. A
dropdown was declined for hiding the source list behind a click, in a feature whose entire point is
that there is more than one source.

**THE SEEDED CATALOG GETS A CHIP, which no surface has offered before.** Once the row exists and
means *where this came from*, omitting the 48 archetypes would leave `All` minus every other chip
meaning something with no name. "Show me only the shipped ones" is a question a person with three
libraries loaded will ask.

**`All` IS A CHIP AND NOT A CLEAR BUTTON**, so the reset is in the same control, reachable by the
same gesture, and readable as the current state rather than as an action.

**THE ROW APPEARS ONLY WHEN A LIBRARY IS ON THE SHELF**, which is narrower than "when there is more
than one source" and is a deliberate narrowing rather than an implementation detail. `All` /
`Catalog` / `This project` on a project with no libraries is a real control and it was still
declined twice over: DR-077 §11.76.2's pinned `This project` group already answers the only question
it could, and **M4's exit criterion clause 2 is a stopwatch drill on this exact panel that has not
been run yet** (`#251`, deferred by the user to end of milestone). Adding a row of chrome above the
search box changes the surface that drill measures, for every user who will never load a library.
The chips appear the moment they have a job, and a session without libraries is pixel-identical to
what shipped before `#242`.

**11.102.7 THE RULING ON A LIBRARY THAT WILL NOT LOAD, which DR-102 §11.101.6 left open in terms.**
A `.rmda` on the shelf that fails to decode appears as a **disabled chip carrying its file name**,
with the fault in its tooltip. Every other library loads.

**This is the case AC-042 does NOT cover, and the distinction is the reason both rules can stand.** A
hash mismatch is a warning and never a refusal, so a mismatched library loads, and its templates are
badged; that rule is untouched here. A file that is not JSON, that is a `.rmdx`, that carries a newer
`schemaVersion`, or that trips AC-058/D8's size cap yields **no templates at all**, and there is
nothing to badge. Skipping it silently was declined as the failure this milestone's own practice
keeps naming: a person put a file in a folder, nothing appeared, and there is no thread to pull. A
footer line reading *"1 library could not be read"* was declined for not saying **which**, which is
the only fact that lets them act on it.

**11.102.8 THE RULING ON SHAPE: `PlaceableTemplate.documentKey` is NULLABLE, and that is the point.**
`PlaceableTemplate.key` reads today as *"the `RackDocument.templates` key this row resolves to"*, and
for a library row there is no such entry. It is renamed `documentKey` and typed `String?`, so the
compiler shows every reader on the day library rows start existing. **A getter that cheerfully spells
`"$id@$version"` for a row the document does not hold is a lookup key that silently misses**, and
`library_import.dart` already calls `doc.templates[row.key]` in precisely that shape.

`isProjectAuthored` survives unchanged, as DR-102 §11.101.5 requires: it is the one question the
palette badge asks, and a library row answers **false** to it, because the shelf it names is not this
project's.

**11.102.9 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not decide **which** libraries are loaded: every
`.rmda` on the shelf is, because `#240`'s import is the only thing that puts one there and a
per-project enable list is a preference nobody has asked for. It does not build favourites, smart
folders or search over port signal families, all of which are M4-O's. It gives a library no rename,
delete or unload gesture, so the file manager remains the only way to take one off the shelf until
M4-O: that is a real gap, and it is named here rather than closed. It says nothing about a library
template colliding with a **placed** device's template, because copy-on-place makes a placed device
immune by construction, its `TemplateRef` resolving the version it was placed from for life
(CR-050). And it does not touch the schematic's library panel, CR-104's other half, which is M2's
surface and lists these same rows through this same widget on the day it exists.

---

### 11.103 DR-104 · The Device Manager tab becomes the browser, the card draws the glyph, and there is one matcher

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-30, before any code**, on the precedent this milestone has now set
six times (DR-077, DR-098, DR-100, DR-101, DR-102, DR-103). M4-O (`#186`) is the library browser,
and four of its questions are product decisions its three chapters cannot start without.

**11.103.1 THE CENSUS, AND FOUR OF THE FIVE PIECES ARE ALREADY BUILT.** `#186` was written in 2026
against a tree that had none of the library subsystem in it. Most of what it names now exists:

| What `#186` asks for | What the tree already holds |
|---|---|
| A list of every template | `buildPlaceableTemplates(doc, libraries:)`, merged and source-tagged (DR-102, `#241`) |
| Search over port signal families | `PortDef.signalFamily` is a `SignalFamilyId` **on the definition**, so "has HDBaseT" is a scan of `body.ports` rather than a resolution against a placed device |
| `Used in this project` | `countDevicesOnTemplate(doc, templateId)`, `derived/template_usage.dart` |
| Somewhere to keep favourites | `AppPrefs`, which already persists per-user collections in this exact shape (`coachMarksSeen`, `portColumnPacks`) |
| The rack elevation strip as a card thumbnail | **Nothing.** `buildRackScene` takes a document and a rack; there is no way to draw one template standing alone |

**The expensive item is the one the chapter did not flag**, and the four cheap ones are the ones it
did. That is the seventh time this milestone a census has moved the cost of a chapter, and the
second time it moved it in both directions at once.

**11.103.2 THE RULING ON THE TAB: the Device Manager becomes the browser, and the editor opens from
it.** `Ctrl+2` lists every template the project can place; a card's `Edit` and a `New device
template…` button are what reach `DeviceBuilderScreen`.

**The tab already carries the name and renders something else.** `app_shell.dart`'s
`_deviceManagerTab` returns `DeviceBuilderScreen` directly: a *manager* that shows one editor and no
list. That is not a defect anybody introduced, it is what the tab could be while the browser did not
exist, and it is exactly the mismatch M4-O closes.

**The plumbing is already there.** DR-099 §11.98.4 routes door 2 into this tab **by template id**,
so *"open the editor on this template"* is a call the shell already makes and already guards with a
dirty-draft refusal. The browser adds a second caller of an existing path rather than a path.

**A split view was declined on width.** List beside editor removes a navigation step and suits
authoring several templates in a sitting. It loses because the window already spends 280px on the
palette and 320px on the inspector (docs/04 §1), and the builder's port grid is the widest surface
in the product. **A modal dialog was declined harder**: a browser with smart folders exists to be
left open, and a modal is the one shape that cannot be.

**WHAT THIS COSTS AND IT IS NAMED HERE RATHER THAN FOUND LATER.** The tab **is** the New-template
entry point today. Making it the browser means that entry point has to be rebuilt inside the
browser, or authoring a new template becomes unreachable.

**THIS CLAUSE WAS WRONG ON ITS FIRST DRAFT AND THE CORRECTION IS THE INTERESTING PART.** It read
*"and `Project ▸ New device template…` must keep working unchanged, because it is what `#251`'s
stopwatch drill uses"*. **There is no `Project` menu.** The application has exactly one, `File`,
with nine items, and no new-template item in it or anywhere else: `Ctrl+2` onto the Device Manager
with nothing being edited renders a blank `DeviceBuilderScreen`, and that is the whole of how a
template is authored today.

The false sentence came from a **doc comment** in `app_shell.dart` that opens *"docs/06's Device
Builder, from `Project ▸ New device template…`"* and documents a method that no longer exists. That
is `don't price a decision off a derived artifact` firing on a ruling rather than on a task, and it
is the second time in this corpus that a comment was read as a product fact.

**The correction makes the browser's own button LOAD-BEARING rather than convenient.** There is no
menu route to fall back on, so `#243` ships the entry point or M4 loses the ability to author a
device. It also means **`#251`'s drill route is `Ctrl+2`**, not a menu item, and the drill's own
first step had to be corrected before it was run.

**11.103.3 THE RULING ON THE CARD: the device's glyph mark and an RU badge, NOT an elevation strip.
This is a substitution for docs/06 §7.1's literal words and is recorded as one.**

§7.1 says *"grid or list, the rack elevation strip as the card thumbnail"*. The card draws
**M4-R's glyph mark** instead (DR-059, DR-083): seventeen marks authored as real geometry, one op
each, which `device_layer.dart` already draws inline on the actual elevation before the designator.

**The substitution loses less than it looks and it is not a downgrade.** The mark IS the device's
visual identity on the elevation since M4-R, so a card showing the mark shows what the rack will
show. What is given up is the RU proportion a strip conveys at a glance, and the RU badge carries
that as a number instead.

**It was decided on cost at the size the surface will meet.** A strip needs a synthetic one-device
rack and a full `buildRackScene` **per card**, re-run on every filter change and every resize, and
the browser is the one surface in this product where the card count is unbounded: the seeded 48,
plus the project's own, plus every loaded library. `measure at the size the criterion will meet` is
already a practice here because a 300-link fixture met its budget and missed by 5.8x at 3,600.
**If somebody wants the strip later, this paragraph is what they are overturning**, and the thing to
bring is a measurement at 200 cards.

**11.103.4 THE RULING ON FAVOURITES: per-user, in `AppPrefs`, and not in the document.** A star is a
fact about the person, not about the project: the twelve devices you actually install are the same
twelve across every job, which is the whole reason a favourite beats a search.

`AppPrefs` needs one field and no new machinery. **The document alternative was declined on what it
costs and on what it does**: a model field, a codec change and a CR-117 byte-round-trip obligation,
in exchange for stars that reset at the start of every job, which is exactly when they are worth
most. **Both-with-project-winning was declined on the surface it needs**, a star whose meaning
depends on which store answered, which is a control that has to explain itself.

**A PROJECT MAILED ELSEWHERE CARRIES NO STARS, AND NOTHING BREAKS.** Favourites key on `templateId`,
the seeded ids are identical on every install, and a starred id that this machine does not hold is
simply not shown. G4's shape on a preference: absent is absent, never a broken row.

**11.103.5 THE RULING ON SEARCH: ONE MATCHER, IN CORE, CALLED BY BOTH SURFACES.**
`device_palette_panel.dart`'s private `_matchesQuery` moves to `rackpal_core` and grows signal
families; the palette and the browser both call it.

**CR-104 is the reason it is not two.** *"One palette widget, shared with the Schematic's library
panel"* is a rule about the widget, and a browser whose search understood more than the palette's
would be the same drift arriving through the matcher instead. Typing `hdbaset` must find the
HDBaseT extender wherever you are.

**It also decouples `#244` from `#243`**, which matters because the browser is the larger chapter:
the smarter search reaches the surface where placing actually happens even if the browser slips.

**THE PALETTE'S SEARCH IS THE SUBJECT OF AN UNRUN DRILL**, so the change is additive only. Every
query that matched before still matches, `#251` measures the same field with the same keys, and the
only difference is that some queries now match MORE. A matcher that narrowed anything would be a
change to the surface under measurement.

**11.103.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not decide grid versus list as the browser's default,
which is a layout preference reversible in a click and belongs to whoever builds it. It says nothing
about which filter chips ship beyond the source chips DR-103 §11.102.6 already ruled: `#243`'s list
(RU height, mount method, has HDMI, has PoE, is passthrough, container, used in this project,
drafts) is a menu to choose from and not a contract, and each chip needs a producer this ruling does
not grant it. It does not give a library a delete or unload gesture, which DR-103 §11.102.9 already
names as an open gap and which the browser is the obvious future home for. And it does not touch
the schematic's library panel, CR-104's other half, which stays M2's surface.

### 11.104 DR-105 · The panel layout is DERIVED, a nudge is the override, and `PortDef.position` cannot say "auto" until it is nullable

**Settled by the user on 2026-08-30, before any code**, on the precedent this milestone has now set
seven times. M4-K (`#182`) is panel auto-layout and the three live previews, and its first chapter
cannot be written without deciding where a layout lives.

**11.104.1 THE CENSUS: A MODELLED FIELD, A CODEC ENTRY, 727 STORED VALUES PER STARTER, AND NO
PRODUCER.** `PortDef.position` is a non-nullable `PanelPosition` with a zero default. It encodes
and decodes (`json_codec.dart`), it round-trips under CR-117, and **nothing has ever written a
non-zero one**. `port_commands.dart` says so in its own words:

> `kUnplacedPanelPosition` · A port with no panel geometry yet. Panel layout is M4-K (`#182`), and
> until it runs every authored port sits at the origin; the catalog's own `PortBuilder` uses exactly
> this value for the same reason.

That is `a modelled field is not a reachable one` for the fourth time in this milestone, and M4-K is
the producer it names. **The inputs are ready**: 47 of the 51 shipped connectors carry a footprint
and the 4 that do not are §5.1's no-cutout kinds, which the algorithm skips by rule; DR-057 §11.56.4
already ruled `pitch ?? (footprintWidth + gutter)` so a sparse pitch is a refinement rather than a
gate.

**11.104.2 THE RULING ON WHERE IT LIVES: DERIVED, and a nudge is a typed override.** The layout is a
pure function of the banks, the ports, the connector footprints and `chassisWidthNm`, computed at
draw time exactly as `buildPlaceableTemplates` computes the palette.

**This is what makes docs/06 §5's non-negotiable true by construction rather than by care.** *"A
template with no layout data is not incomplete"* is trivially satisfied when there IS no layout data
in the ordinary case. It also means a corrected connector footprint reaches every template ever
authored, including ones saved before the correction, which a stored layout could never do.

**The stored alternative was declined on what it cannot buy back.** Writing coordinates into every
`PortDef.position` on save needs no model change at all, the field being already there. It costs the
one distinction the feature rests on: a stored coordinate is indistinguishable from a nudged one, so
`#227`'s `Reset to auto` has nothing to reset TO, and CR-071's whole framing of the interaction as
*nudging rather than placing* stops being expressible.

**11.104.3 THE RULING ON SHAPE: `PortDef.position` BECOMES `PanelPosition?`, AND NULL MEANS AUTO.**

**A non-nullable field with a zero default has already answered.** The origin is a legal panel
coordinate: `{ruOffset: 0, xTwelfth: 0, xFineNm: 0, yFineNm: 0}` is the top-left of the panel and a
person may deliberately nudge a jack there. So a zero-valued sentinel cannot distinguish *never
nudged* from *nudged to the corner*, and `kUnplacedPanelPosition` is that sentinel today. Nullable
is the only shape that carries both facts, and it is **G4's own shape** (CR-114): unknown is an
**absent key**, never an explicit `null`.

`PortOverrides` was considered and is the wrong home. DR-098 and M4-L4 put typed overrides on a
PLACED device's `Port`; a panel layout is a fact about the TEMPLATE, shared by every instance, so an
override living on the instance would let two devices from one template disagree about where the
same jack is.

**11.104.4 THE MIGRATION IS THE COST AND IT IS NAMED HERE RATHER THAN FOUND.** Every file that
exists today writes `position` on every port: **727 of them in each of the four checked-in
starters**, all zero. Read under §11.104.3 without a migration, every one of those becomes *"manually
placed at the origin"*, and the auto-layout would never run for any template anybody has ever saved.

So `kSchemaVersion` goes to **3** with a `migrateV2ToV3` that **drops a `position` whose four
components are all zero**, and the starters are regenerated. The chain is append-only and this is a
new entry, never an edit.

**THE MIGRATION IS EXACTLY CORRECT AND NOT AN APPROXIMATION**, which is worth stating because a
"drop it if it looks like a default" rule usually is one. No producer of a non-zero position has
ever existed, so in every file that can exist at v2 a zero position IS an unplaced port, with no
exceptions to reason about. A genuine nudge-to-origin written after this ruling lands in a v3 file
and is never seen by this step.

**11.104.5 THE RULING ON T2.02: NOT YET.** `panel_layer.dart` lands in `rackpal_core` producing a
`DiagramScene`, printable by construction (CR-086), and M4-K wires it to the **builder's preview
dock only**. Sheet `T2.02 Rack Elevation — Rear` keeps drawing device boxes through
`buildElevationSheet`.

M4-K's four chapters name the builder's dock and never name T2.02. Changing what a shipped sheet
prints changes a deliverable **M6's exit criterion measures**, brings new ANSI B legibility
obligations and regenerates goldens, none of which this story priced. Building the layer in core
costs nothing extra to wire later, and CR-071 part 2 stays owed rather than quietly discharged.

**11.104.6 THE RULING ON `#227`: DEFERRED, AND THE STORY CLOSES WITHOUT IT.** M4-K ships `#226` the
algorithm, `#228` the previews and `#229` the real-scene-builder rule. The nudge canvas stays open.

**CR-071 calls it optional in terms** and docs/06 §5 makes a template with no layout data explicitly
complete, so nothing downstream waits on it: no sheet, no schedule, no export reads a coordinate.
It is also the only remaining chapter that is a whole new interactive canvas, and M4 has two other
stories plus an **unrun exit-criterion drill**. §8.9's rule is what makes this legal: a clause is
discharged or **parked**, and this is parked by ruling id to `#227` under M4-K, not silently
dropped.

**11.104.7 THE RULING ON THE DOCK: all three previews, collapsible.** docs/06 §6's right dock
arrives: the rack elevation strip at true aspect, the schematic symbol, and the rear panel render
with its fill percentage, each individually collapsible and updating on every keystroke.

**The dock's absence was deliberate and its own comment sets the condition for ending it**:
*"There is nothing to put in a 340px dock, so it is not drawn."* All three previews have real scene
builders the moment `#226` lands, `rack_layer.dart` and `symbol_layer.dart` already shipping and
printing, so not one of them is the preview-only widget CR-086 forbids and `#229` exists to prevent.

**11.104.8 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not decide the nudge canvas's own interaction, which
stays `#227`'s and stays as CR-071 describes it. It does not give the rail's `Notes & Publish`
section a home, which is M4-P's. It says nothing about the v1.1 interactive Rear Panel view
(`Ctrl+3`), which CR-071 part 3 already places outside v1. And it does not make the panel-fill
percentage a validation rule: a panel over 100% full is a finding for M5 to rule on, not a refusal
this story invents.

### §11.105 DR-106 · `#227` is un-parked, and the nudge canvas gets its four unruled answers

**Question.** DR-105 §11.104.6 parked `#227`, the optional nudge canvas, and M4-K closed without it
(docs/12 §5.3.26, `v0.4.89`). The user has directed that it be built now. §11.104.8 said in terms
that DR-105 *"does not decide the nudge canvas's own interaction"*, so there are two things to rule:
whether the park lifts, and the four interaction questions CR-071 leaves open.

**11.105.1 THE PARK LIFTS, AND THIS IS AN AMENDMENT RATHER THAN A CORRECTION.** §8.3 requires a
scope change to carry a new ruling ID in its own commit, and this is that commit. Nothing about
DR-105 §11.104.6 was WRONG: the reasons it gave still hold, and they are the reasons the park was
cheap to reverse.

- CR-071 part 1 calls the canvas an *"optional hidden toggle"* in terms, so building it is inside
  roadmap §2's scope list and needs no amendment to that list.
- **Nothing downstream reads a coordinate.** docs/06 §5's non-negotiable, that a template with no
  layout data is not incomplete, held by construction and still does.
- **The expensive half already shipped.** `PortDef.position` is nullable with null meaning automatic
  (DR-105 §11.104.3), an override beats the flow, `PanelSlot.nudged` reports which is which, and
  `buildPanelLayer` already draws a nudged cutout differently. `#227` is UI over a finished model.

**M4-K STAYS CLOSED AND `#227` IS RE-PARENTED RATHER THAN REOPENED.** §8.9 is explicit that
*"closing is the moment that binds"*, and docs/12 §5.3.26 is the record of a story that closed with
three of four chapters and a named park. Reopening it would falsify that record to tidy a board.
`#227` moves to `#804`, a story of its own under M4, so the work lands against the milestone it
belongs to without rewriting a discharged clause.

**11.105.2 THE CANVAS IS A SIXTH RAIL SECTION, `Panel`.** It sits after `Ports`, its head carries
CR-071's `☐ Customize panel layout` toggle, and the canvas fills the main pane at full width.

*Rejected: putting it in the dock's rear-panel pane.* That pane is 340 px and the drawing is
482.6 mm wide; `#802` already records that this window has no narrow layout, and nudging a 10 mm
RJ45 cutout inside a third of a pane is not an interaction, it is a dare.

*Rejected: stacking it under the port grid.* The grid is virtualised and already competes for
vertical room. Two scrollable work surfaces in one pane is how neither gets enough.

**The `AUTO` badge lives on the rail tile**, green, exactly as docs/06 §5 asks, so a template that
never touches this section says so from the rail without the section being entered. The section is
skippable forever and that is a property of the rail, not of a dialog somebody has to dismiss.

**11.105.3 ONE ARROW PRESS IS 1 mm; `Shift` IS 0.1 mm AND `Ctrl` IS 10 mm.** CR-071 names a 1 mm
snap, and the two modifiers are the CAD convention a person arrives already knowing.

**The offset lives entirely in `xFineNm`/`yFineNm` and `xTwelfth` stays 0 for a nudged port.** Two
representations of one position is how they come to disagree, and the twelfth grid is a coarse
authoring lattice rather than a nudge unit. **The corpus reaches the same answer independently**:
all three worked examples in `docs/research/design-data-model.md` carry `xTwelfth: 0` and put the
whole offset in `xFineNm`, at 12.7 mm and 25.4 mm, which are a half inch and an inch. CR-001 is
satisfied by construction, since every step is an integer count of nanometres.

**11.105.7 A `xTwelfth` IS A TWELFTH OF THE PANEL WIDTH, AND THE CODE SAID A RACK UNIT.** This
ruling's first draft asserted *"a twelfth of 482.6 mm is about 40 mm"* as a statement about the
implementation. `panel_layer.dart` computed `kRackUnit.nm ~/ 12`, which is 3.70 mm, under a comment
calling it *"docs/research's twelfth-of-a-rack-unit grid"*. **The corpus says no such thing.** It
declares `{ruOffset:int, xTwelfth:int, xFineNm:Len, yFineNm:Len}` and never says what the twelfth
measures; the confident comment was `#226`'s own invention, which is [a confident paragraph is a
tell] firing on a line of code rather than on prose.

**Ruled: a twelfth of `kPanelWidth`, 40.22 mm.** The pairing settles it. `ruOffset` + `yFineNm` is
coarse plus fine vertically, so `xTwelfth` + `xFineNm` is coarse plus fine horizontally, and a
coarse unit of 3.70 mm sitting beside a nanometre-precision fine field buys nothing: nothing would
ever set it, and a field that exists and means nothing is the state this corpus keeps punishing.

**Corrected while it was still free**, which is the only reason this is a one-line change rather than
a migration: every stored `xTwelfth` is 0, the three corpus examples are 0, no test asserted the
resulting x, and this ruling makes nudging never write the field. It is exactly the position
`BankDef.collapseInSymbol` was in when its default was fixed inert.

*Rejected: 1 mm and nothing else.* This surface exists to fix one jack that is 3 mm out, and it
would also be used to move one 40 mm, which at one step per millimetre is forty keypresses. CR-071
says 1 mm **snap**, not 1 mm only.

**11.105.4 `Reset to auto` TAKES THE SELECTION WHEN THERE IS ONE.** With ports selected it clears
those overrides; with nothing selected the control reads `Reset all to auto` and clears every one.
One button whose label says which it will do before it is pressed, and undoable either way through
the builder's own stack (CR-106's third stack).

*Rejected: always the whole panel.* A person who nudged twelve jacks and wants one back would have
to undo their way there or re-nudge eleven.

**11.105.5 ALIGN IS SIX OPERATIONS AND DISTRIBUTE IS TWO.** Align left, right, top, bottom, centre
horizontally, centre vertically; distribute evenly on each axis. The standard set, which needs no
explanation, and **distribute is the load-bearing half**: it is what turns eight hand-nudged XLRs
into a row rather than eight near-misses, and its absence is what sends a person back to nudging one
jack at a time.

*Rejected: an "align to auto-layout" operation instead.* It is not what docs/06 names, nobody has
seen it before, and it overlaps `Reset to auto` confusingly enough that a person would learn neither.

**11.105.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not touch the v1.1 interactive Rear Panel view
(`Ctrl+3`), which CR-071 part 3 places outside v1 and which this is not. It does not make a
nudged position mean anything to the netlist, the schedule or any export: ports still connect by
IDENTITY (CR-071 part 1), and a coordinate remains a drawing fact. It does not feed T2.02, which
stays DR-105 §11.104.5's. And it does not make an overlapping or off-panel nudge a refusal: the
panel already reports overflow as a finding (DR-105 §11.104.8) and a person who deliberately drags
two cutouts together is describing hardware this model does not know about, not making an error.

---

### §11.106 DR-107 · M4-P's scope, the stripped form, and the panel a field device actually has

**Question.** M4-P (`#187`) opens with three chapters: the stripped field-device form (`#246`), the
media-type editor (`#247`) and connector aliases (`#248`). A census before pricing found three things
the board items do not say, and each needs ruling before code.

**11.106.1 RJ-012 NAMES THREE v1 SURFACES AND THE BOARD NAMES TWO.** RJ-012 ships *"a media-type
editor, connector aliases, and a per-family colour override row in settings"*. `#187` calls these
*"the two extensibility surfaces that DO ship"* and omits the third.

**The third has nowhere to go.** `ProjectSettings.familyColorOverrides` exists and
`signal_style.dart` consumes it; **no file in `rackpal_ui` or `apps/rackpal` references it.** Nor is
it alone: `ProjectSettings` carries roughly twenty fields with no producer, including
`displayUnits` (CR-097, authoritative over any app preference), five `IdFormat`s,
`collisionPolicy`, `ruleOverrides` and `jacketColorConventions`. **There is no settings surface in
the app and none assigned to any milestone**; the corpus's only mention is M1's own deferral list,
item 5, left unowned.

**Ruled: M4-P builds its two named chapters, and the settings surface is `#805`.** RJ-012 therefore
stays **partly unmet through M4**, and this ruling says so rather than leaving it implied. A settings
pane built inside M4-P to hold one colour row would invite the other nineteen fields to arrive
without a design, and M4 is already the milestone that grew from `M` to `L`.

**11.106.2 THE STRIPPED FORM IS ONE BUILDER WITH SECTIONS KEYED ON `mountMethod`.** A body whose
mount method is `notInRack` drops the Physical section's rack fields and shows what AC-031 leaves:
identity and ports.

*Rejected: a separate screen.* Two authoring surfaces would have to be kept in step, and changing a
device's mount method after the fact would mean moving it between them, which is CR-104's *"two
places to add a device"* defect rebuilt in a new place.

*Rejected: disabling rather than hiding.* AC-031 asks for a **stripped** form in terms, and a wall of
greyed-out rack fields on a ceiling speaker is the opposite of stripped.

**11.106.3 AC-031's "location" DESCRIBES THE INSPECTOR'S JOB, NOT THE BUILDER'S.** AC-031 says the
form is *"identity, ports, location; no RU, no rack depth, no thermal class"*. **`TemplateBody` has
no location field and must not gain one.** `locationId` lives on `DeviceInstance`: where a speaker
hangs is a fact about a placed device, and a template is a model of a device rather than an instance
of one. A default location on a template would be data nothing reads, with every in-ceiling speaker
carrying "ceiling".

The sentence is read as descriptive rather than as a section list, which its own shape supports:
the three words that follow it are all REMOVALS. The builder builds identity and ports.

**11.106.4 A FIELD DEVICE HAS NO PANEL, AND THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS CLAUSE WAS WRONG.**

**WITHDRAWN BEFORE IT WAS BUILT, and recorded rather than quietly rewritten.** This clause first
ruled that a body occupying no rack U should take its panel height from its own cutouts, so that
*"a wall plate, a floor box and a structured enclosure then draw what they have"*. The code change
was written, two tests refused it, and the census those failures forced overturned the clause.

**Two facts settle it, and both were reachable before the ruling was written.**

`T2.02` is **`Rack Elevation: Rear`, one per `Rack`** (docs/01 §9.8, docs/00 R7), and CR-071 part 2
makes that sheet the thing `panel_layer.dart` draws for. **A field device is by definition not in a
rack**, so it never appears on it. A panel for a field device is a drawing with no sheet to live on:
a display's HDMI sockets are on the back of a television, and putting them on a 482.6 mm EIA panel
draws something that does not exist.

**And no shipped field template is a plate.** AC-031's ruled 18 are display, projector, projection
screen, four speakers, IP camera, NVR, wireless AP, touchpanel, keypad, volume control, IR receiver
eye, ISP gateway/ONT, OTA antenna and F-type ground block. *"Wall plate, parametric N keystones"*
comes from `critique-domain-realism.md`'s **wishlist**, which AC-031 did not adopt. The case the
clause existed to serve is not in the catalog, and the clause was priced off a critique rather than
off the ruling that answered it, which is [don't price a decision off a derived artifact] firing for
the third time in this corpus.

**Ruled: the existing behaviour stands.** A body occupying no rack U has no panel, and the `Panel`
section and the preview dock are right to say so. `#806`, filed against the plate width, is
withdrawn: `plate_geometry.dart` already carries a MEASURED plate outline (2.75 x 4.5 in), gang
pitch (1.8125 in) and an N-gang width rule under DR-041/DR-042, so *"candidates, none ruled"* was a
census miss as well.

**`PlateGeometry` and `panel_layer` stay separate, and that is not two drawings of one thing.** A
Structure plate is an `Outlet`: a physical cover with keystone straps, keyed on `gangCount`, drawn
at its own 4 units/mm anchor because a rack's 0.495 would render a 14.5 mm nose smaller than its own
label. A rear panel is a rack device's connector field at EIA width. They answer different questions
about different entities, and CR-086 is not in tension with that.

**11.106.5 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not build a signal-family editor, a colour-scheme
editor or a rule editor: RJ-012 rejects all three for v1, and AC-011 withdraws user-authored
validation rules from every document, because rules are Dart functions keyed by `ruleId` and a UI
for them would make the app an interpreter for user input. It does not decide where the settings
surface lands, which is `#805`'s first question. And it does not touch the 18 seeded field templates
themselves, which shipped at AC-031 and are not this story's.

---

### §11.107 DR-108 · The preview dock is drawn at every width, and hiding it is a control

**Question.** `#802` asks the device builder for a narrow-window layout, because docs/06 §6's preview
dock vanishes below `kPreviewDockMinWindow` with no explanation. It offers three candidates and rules
none: a collapsed icon rail the dock expands from, an end-drawer over the grid, or the dock moving
under the grid at narrow widths.

**11.107.1 THE THRESHOLD WAS MEASURING THE PORT GRID'S TOOLBAR, NOT THE DOCK.** Its own doc comment
called the number *"MEASURED, NOT CHOSEN"* and derived it from the archetype bar: *"the port grid's
archetype bar overflows a 434 px slot by 203 px, so the grid needs about 637 to draw its own
toolbar"*. That was true, and it was the only hard width in the pane. **The grid scrolls its own
columns**, so nothing else in it had a floor at all. The dock was therefore being withheld to protect
a `Row` of three buttons, and the number described the bar rather than the previews.

**11.107.2 IT WAS ALSO 23 PX SHORT, IN THE ONLY BAND A PERSON CAN REACH.** Measured across the range
`kMinWindowWidth` (1000) admits: clean from 1000 to 1179, **overflowing by 23 at 1180**, by 13 at
1190, by 3 at 1200, and clean from 1203. The constant was 1180, so the dock was admitted 23 px before
there was room for it. The arithmetic in the comment stopped one term short, and the band it created
sits well above the enforced minimum, unlike the 800 px defect `#803` was filed for, which no window
can reach.

**11.107.3 Ruled: the dock is drawn at every width the app will open, and a labelled toggle on the
port grid's toolbar hides it.** `#803` made the archetype bar and the grid toolbar `Wrap`s, which
removes the floor rather than working around it; measured with the threshold forced to zero, the dock
then draws at 1000 with no overflow at any width down to 700. With no geometric floor left, **a
threshold has nothing to measure**, and a constant that still claimed to measure one would be
fiction. What remains is a preference, and a preference belongs to the person holding it.

**The complaint `#802` was filed for is answered by construction rather than by copy.** It objected
that the dock *"gives way SILENTLY"*. Nothing gives way on its own now, so there is no disappearance
to explain.

**The toggle is on the grid's toolbar and not on the dock**, because a control reachable only while
the dock is drawn cannot bring the dock back. It is labelled rather than iconic: `Hide previews`
while they are up and `Show previews` while they are not, since the second reading has to work for
somebody who never saw them. **The state is per session and is deliberately not persisted**, the same
shape as the grid's column-pack override: a remembered value would mean opening the builder on a wide
monitor and finding the previews gone because of a laptop three weeks ago. It defaults to shown,
which is CR-086's side of it.

*Rejected: a collapsed icon rail, `#802`'s first candidate.* It is the right answer to a question
that no longer exists. The rail earns its complexity only when geometry forces the dock out, and
after `#803` nothing does.

*Rejected: keeping a threshold, re-measured and explained.* It preserves the mechanism that produced
the defect, and the explanatory copy would be a sentence apologising for a decision the app made on
the person's behalf while a control was available instead.

*Rejected: an end-drawer over the grid, or the dock beneath it.* Both re-lay the pane to buy width
that measurement says is not needed, and docs/06 §2's drawing is a three-column window.

### §11.108 DR-109 · Bank collapse reaches the canvas, and the user can undo it there

**Question.** CR-103 collapses banks over eight *"on first layout and in the symbol preview"*. `#229`
built collapse in the shared geometry and turned it on for the preview only. `#801` was filed to turn
it on for the canvas, priced as one argument at one call site.

**11.108.1 THAT ONE ARGUMENT REMOVES 47 OF A SWITCH'S 48 PORTS FROM THE SHEET.** `symbolHitRegions`
emits one region per entry in `RenderedSymbol.allPorts`, and a collapsed bank contributes ONE entry.
A collapsed 48-port switch therefore has one pin, one hit region, and **no way to select, trace or
wire the other forty-seven**. **Nothing in `rackpal_ui` or `rackpal_export` read `isCollapsed` or
`collapsedCount`**, so there was no affordance to get them back, and the PDF backend was equally
unaware. Sixty-five schematic tests failed; they were not stale fixtures.

**11.108.2 THE RULING ALREADY OWNED THE ANSWER AND NOTHING HAD BUILT IT.** CR-103 also says any bank
of two or more ports *"may be collapsed by the user at any time"*, which means nothing unless it can
be un-collapsed. `BankDef.collapseInSymbol` is the TEMPLATE's opt-out, edited in the device builder;
it is not something a person can reach while looking at a drawing.

**11.108.3 Ruled: `#801` ships both halves, and the expansion is an exception set.** `expandedBanks`
threads from `buildSchematicScene` through the symbol tier to `layOutSymbolEdges`, keyed by device
and then by bank key. Auto-collapse stays what a device gets on first layout and the user's choice is
the deviation from it, so the ruling's default survives as the default rather than becoming one of
two equal modes.

**The state is per session and is not a document write**, the same shape as DR-011.4's `holdAt`: a
layout INPUT rather than a value in CR-117's byte surface. The collapsed state is derivable from the
template and the threshold and needs no storage; what a person expands while working is not a fact
about the design.

**A click on a vector pin expands it, and `B` collapses it again.** Selecting a pin that stands for
forty-eight ports means nothing, so the click has no meaning to share. The reverse needed a key
because every modifier on that canvas is spoken for: `Shift` extends a pin selection, `Ctrl`
suppresses the magnet, `Alt` re-answers what is under the cursor. Both directions announce
themselves in the status line, because a person who expanded a bank by clicking it cannot otherwise
guess how to put it away.

**`sizeSymbolForBody`'s DEFAULT moves, rather than its two call sites opting in.**
`symbol_sizing_seam_test.dart` reproduces every symbol in the 300-link fixture through that function
WITHOUT the flag and compares it to the scene; it is the guard against the preview and the sheet
drifting apart (`#229`, CR-086), so the value it exercises has to be the value the sheet uses.
Opting in twice would leave the seam holding only while two call sites remembered to agree, which is
the arrangement that test exists to forbid.

*Rejected: shipping collapse and rewriting the sixty-five tests to work through vector pins.* They
fail because the behaviour is broken, so rewriting them pins a defect as intended behaviour, which
this repository has already found in itself more than once.

*Rejected: parking `#801` until an expand affordance exists.* It was the disciplined call and the
user declined it in favour of building the half that was missing.

*Rejected: collapsing only the unlinked remainder of a bank.* It is an appealing drawing, and it is
not CR-103: the ruling collapses a bank on a count, not on how much of it happens to be patched, and
a symbol that changes shape as cables land is a sheet that will not sit still.

*Rejected: persisting the expansion in the document.* It buys a remembered view at the cost of a
model field, a codec key, a byte round-trip and a migration, for state CR-103 describes as a default
plus a deviation.

### §11.109 DR-110 · `CON-002` is v1.2, and two sentences say otherwise

**Question.** M5-A's census turned up `ConnectorTypeDef.genderApplies`, a field canon §6.3 says
*"decides whether `CON-002` (both ends the same gender) evaluates"*, while docs/02 §5's catalogue of
28 does not list `CON-002` at all. CR-021 rules that *"a rule not listed there does not exist"*, so
the question raised was whether v1 ships a field serving a rule it has not got.

**11.109.1 THE ALARM WAS LARGER THAN THE FINDING, AND THAT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY DROPPED.**
It was put as a possible CR-021 violation. It is not one. docs/02 §5.3's closing sentence defers
*"the remaining `DIR`, **`CON`**, `ELE`, `LEN`, `BUS`, `SER`, `NET`, `PWR` and `RCK` rules"* to v1.2
behind a fixture corpus, and `CON-002` is one of the remaining `CON` rules. **It is deferred scope,
not a missing rule**, and the catalogue accounts for it by name-class exactly as it accounts for the
other several dozen.

**11.109.2 THE FIELD IS NOT ORPHANED EITHER, AND THAT WAS MEASURED.** `genderApplies` has a live v1
consumer that has nothing to do with `CON-002`: `port_table.dart`'s `portGenderApplies` gates the
**GENDER column in the device builder's port grid**, which M4 shipped. CR-059 gives it a second,
the symbol glyph's fill. A field with a shipped reader is a field that earns its place, whatever the
status of the rule it was named for.

**11.109.3 Ruled: the 28 stands, `CON-002` is v1.2, and the two sentences are corrected.** No rule is
added and no rule moves. What changes is prose in two normative places that describe `CON-002` as
though it were live:

- **CR-059** closes *"fixes a concrete bug in a shipped rule"*. `CON-002` was never shipped in v1.
  The ruling's substance is untouched and still governs: three gender values, `jack` and `plug`
  deleted, `genderApplies` on `ConnectorTypeDef`. Only the claim about what was fixed is wrong, and
  §12.14 records it.
- **§6.3** reads *"`genderApplies` decides whether `CON-002` evaluates"*. It will, in v1.2. Today it
  decides whether the port grid draws a GENDER column and whether the glyph fill encodes gender.

**A field may ship ahead of the rule that named it, and this ruling says so in general terms** so the
next census does not re-raise it. The test is whether it has a reader now, not whether every reason
it was introduced has arrived. `PortDef.pinoutVariant` is the precedent pointing the other way and is
worth naming: docs/02 §5.2 says it *"exists solely to make `DIR-003` detectable"*, and `DIR-003` is
one of the six tier-2 rules v1 does ship, so that field is owed a consumer and this one is not.

*Rejected: adding `CON-002` to the catalogue to match CR-059's wording.* It would make the count 29
against AC-040 as amended by DR-020, and it would ship a rule with no fixture pair, which AC-051
forbids in terms. Correcting a sentence is cheaper than moving scope to match it.

*Rejected: deleting `genderApplies` until `CON-002` lands.* It has two readers today and removing it
would take the GENDER column out of a shipped surface to tidy a docstring.

**11.109.6 THE COUNTER-EXAMPLE THIS RULING NAMED IS NOT ONE, AND M5-D MEASURED IT.** §11.109's closing
paragraph offered `PortDef.pinoutVariant` as the field pointing the other way, *"owed a consumer"*,
on the ground that docs/02 §5.2 says it *"exists solely to make `DIR-003` detectable"* and `DIR-003`
is one of the six tier-2 rules v1 ships.

**That reasoning took a sentence at face value instead of reading the data**, which is the failure
this corpus keeps meeting. Every `pinoutVariant` the seed catalog authors is a connector WIRING
pinout: `xantech-stereo` and `mono-tip-sleeve`. Neither encodes the emitter/receiver distinction
`DIR-003` turns on. What does is the family split, `ctl.ir_emitter` against `ctl.ir_receiver`, nine
ports and fourteen, exactly as HDBaseT's own family carries `SIG-001`. `DIR-003` shipped at M5-D
without reading `pinoutVariant` at all.

**So `pinoutVariant` is in the same position `genderApplies` was**, and §11.109's own general rule
governs it rather than excepting it: a field may ship ahead of the rule that named it, and the test
is whether it has a reader NOW. Today it has none. That is a fact to carry into the census that asks
about it next, not a defect to fix here: docs/02 §5.2's sentence is the thing that is wrong, and
correcting a derived sentence is §12's business.

**The ruling's substance is untouched.** `CON-002` is still v1.2, `genderApplies` still has its two
readers, and the general rule still stands. Only the example chosen to illustrate its opposite was
picked without measuring, and the measurement is now on the record beside it.

### §11.110 DR-111 · `#261` is `#322` seen from the other side, and DR-027 already ruled which one owns it

**Question.** M5-B's fourth chapter, `#261`, is *"the acknowledgement reaches `T0.02`"*, and its own
body ends *"coordinate with M6-C"*. `T0.02` does not exist. So either M5-B builds a sheet, or the
chapter is on the wrong side of a seam this corpus has already cut.

**11.110.1 MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED, AND THE MEASUREMENT FOUND SOMETHING SHARPER THAN A MISPLACED
CHAPTER.** `SheetRole` carries three values, front elevation, rear elevation and equipment list.
`sheet_def.dart` names `T0.02` among the nine absent ones and states the reason in its own header:
they *"are M6 and most of them need `Link`s"*, and they are *"absent from `SheetRole` rather than
stubbed"*. That much was expected. What was not is that **`#261` and M6-C's story `#322` are the
same work written twice**, a sentence apart:

> `#261`: *"This is where 'the reason prints' actually happens, a promise three design documents made
> and no sheet list honoured until CR-022. Coordinate with M6-C."*

> `#322`: *"This is where 'the reason prints' actually happens, a promise three design documents made
> and no sheet list honoured until CR-022. ... Depends on M5-B's acknowledgement mechanism;
> coordinate the two."*

Each names the other. **They are one clause with two tickets**, and the dependency `#322` declares is
precisely what M5-B has just delivered.

**11.110.2 Ruled: `#261` is re-parented to `#322` and stays open there.** This adds no seam. DR-027
§11.26 already rules that **M6 owns every rendered sheet** and the earlier milestone owns the
derivation, and it names `SheetRole`'s three values as the evidence, the same three that are still
there. A chapter asking M5 to put rows on a page is on the wrong side of a boundary drawn in 2026-08
and reaffirmed at `#574`, `#653` and `#693`. Parking costs a ruling ID under §8.9 (DR-095) and this
is that ID; the re-parenting on the board is the visible act of it, and M6-C is the **named later
milestone** the rule requires.

**11.110.3 What M5-B owes has been discharged, and this section exists so the park is not read as a
deferral.** DR-027 §11.26.4 is explicit that a milestone handing the later one *"an unordered,
untotalled data structure"* has turned the seam into an excuse. M5-B's half is the **mechanism**, and
it is built and tested:

- `Finding` and `findingFingerprint` (`#258`), the identity an acknowledgement joins on, built from
  stable ids and nothing else so a renumber cannot make rule 42 delete somebody's written reason.
- The acknowledgement at both of CR-019's scopes with RJ-006's reason enforced at exactly one of them
  (`#259`), the writer strict and the reader tolerant.
- `ProjectSettings.ruleOverrides` with a writer, and the three-layer order catalogue then project
  then acknowledgement (`#260`).

**And one instruction that binds `#322` when it is built.** `T0.02` and the issues list must resolve
through `acknowledgementFor` and `effectiveSeverity`, never through a second implementation of the
join. CR-022 makes the sheet and the list two presentations of one answer, and two implementations
are how they come to disagree about the same row in front of a client.

**11.110.4 The derivation half is not parked, and it is not M5-B's either.** `#294` (M5-F1) is *"the
findings list, grouped and filterable: by severity, by rule, by locus"*, which is `T0.02`'s row set in
its other presentation. That is where the ordering is authored, and putting it there rather than in
M5-B is not the excuse §11.26.4 warns about: **the Pull Sheet's rows derive from data that exists,
and `T0.02`'s rows derive from findings that no rule produces until M5-E.** A sort order written at
M5-B would be a design invented for a sheet nobody has laid out, over a list nothing can fill, and
pinned by a test that could only ever assert its own fixtures.

**11.110.5 M5-B's exit is not blocked, and neither is M5's.** §8.9 binds at **closing**, and M5 is
not closing here; opening is soft. What this ruling does is make the eventual close legal, by naming
where the clause went before the question is asked under time pressure.

*Rejected: building an `ExceptionsReport` type in `rackpal_core` now.* It is the DR-027-shaped answer
and it fails on the same fact §11.110.4 turns on. It would fix a sheet's data model a milestone
before the sheet is designed and two before anything can fill it, and the "no entry without a
surface" rule `project_settings_commands.dart` states would be broken from the other end: a reader
with no producer is the `NetworkConfig` defect wearing the opposite sign.

*Rejected: closing `#261` as `Done` on the grounds that its M5 half is delivered.* Its title is *"the
acknowledgement reaches `T0.02`"* and nothing reaches `T0.02`. Marking that `Done` is exactly the
checklist-ticking §8.1 refuses, and the board would then carry no open item for a promise three
design documents made. **The second clause of that sentence is false and §11.110.6 corrects it.**

*Rejected: deleting `#261` as a duplicate of `#322`.* There is no `Removed` state on this board, and
the chapter carries the M5-side reasoning that `#322` does not. Re-parenting keeps both.

**11.110.6 §11.110.2 SAID RE-PARENT AND STAY OPEN, AND THE NEXT LOOK AT THE BOARD SAID CLOSE. The
correction is recorded here rather than written over the paragraph above**, because the mistake is
the instructive part: the ruling above was reasoned from `#322`'s *description* without reading
`#322`'s *children*, which is the shape this repository keeps meeting under other names.

`#322` is already decomposed, into `#323` *"open findings with rule ID, severity and locus"*, `#324`
*"acknowledgements with reason, author and date"* and `#325` *"emit when empty, and say so"*. Those
three ARE docs/08 §2.2 row 3, clause for clause, and **`#324` is `#261`**, not merely adjacent to it.

So the rejected alternative above rests on a premise that is not true: the board does not carry *no*
open item for the promise, it carries **three**, and they are more specific than `#261` is. A fourth
chapter under the same story saying what `#324` already says is noise rather than insurance, and the
person who eventually builds `#324` would have to work out what the extra one wanted.

**Amended disposition: `#261` is closed as a duplicate of `#324`, named by this ruling's own commit
under §8.8.** A ruling is what closed it, and that is the honest entry: no code discharged it and
none was owed. §8.1 is untouched, because §8.1 governs **exit criteria** and this ruling discharges
none; M6's criterion still contains the sheet, and `#323`, `#324` and `#325` are all open. The
M5-side reasoning the second rejection wanted to keep is kept **here**, in the normative record,
which is where §8.2 says a re-litigated decision should have been in the first place.

### §11.111 DR-112 · Tier 1 refuses the gesture, tier 3 reports the state, and the same condition may sit in both

**Question.** M5-C implements `PLC-001..003`, and docs/02 §5.1 cannot be read straight. It lists
`PLC-001` as *"`RailPlacement.ruIndex ∈ [1, rack.heightU]` and the device fits within the rack extent
on that face"*, then closes by repeating CR-017: *"the rack editor's other blocking drop checks are
demoted to warnings, **except** RU-range-free on the same face and fits-within-rack-extent."* Two
sections later, §5.3 lists **both** of those conditions as tier-3 findings: `RCK-001` *"RU overlap on
the same face"* and `RCK-002` *"device extends past `heightU`"*. So one document appears to put one
condition in two tiers, and a third condition, occupancy, is named as blocking without a rule id at
all.

**11.111.1 MEASURED FIRST, AND THE CODE IS FURTHER ALONG THAN THE QUESTION ASSUMES.** The overlap
refusal ships. `catalog_placement.dart` exports `findBlockingOccupant`, a query over one face's
occupancy by RU, and two surfaces consult it: the keyboard nudge, which shakes the selection and
reads the blocker's designator onto the status line (docs/04 §3.4, *"a nudge that would collide never
silently stops"*), and the catalog quick-add's caret path, whose planner returns
`CatalogPlacementFailed`. `PLC-001..003` themselves appear in no Dart file, which
`rule_catalogue_test.dart` already asserts by name.

**11.111.2 THE TWO SENTENCES ARE NOT IN CONFLICT, AND CR-017's OWN ENUMERATION IS WHY.** CR-017 gives
model-level illegality as *"only `TOP-001..005` ... plus placement coherence (`ruIndex` within the
rack; host is a container; no containment cycle)"*. **Occupancy is not in that list.** The
"except RU-range-free" sentence sits in a different bullet about a different thing: the **rack
editor's drop checks**, which are gestures. One ruling, two lists, and reading the second as if it
amended the first is what makes the document look self-contradictory.

**11.111.3 Ruled: the tier is a property of the MOMENT, not of the condition.** docs/02 §5's table
already defines tier 1 as *"the command is rejected"* and tier 3 as *"a `Finding` in the issues
list"*. Those are two different moments, and the same physical fact can be met at both:

- **Tier 1 refuses the gesture.** It stops a person creating the state by dragging.
- **Tier 3 reports the state however it arrived.** Import, a hand-edited file, a rack shrunk under a
  device, or a build that predates the rule.

**So `PLC-001` is bounds-plus-extent exactly as §5.1 writes it, `RCK-002` is the same condition seen
at the other moment, and that is deliberate rather than a duplication to be tidied away.** A
catalogue that refused to name a condition twice would have to choose between refusing the drag and
reporting the import, and G2 requires both: *"a model that cannot draw a mistake cannot document
reality, cannot plan a remediation, and cannot import an as-found survey."*

**11.111.4 The overlap refusal stays unnumbered, and the count stays at 28.** It is not tier 1 by
canon's own definition, because **no `Command` refuses on it**: `findBlockingOccupant` is consulted
by a planner and by a keystroke handler, both of which decline before a command exists. That is the
gesture hesitating, which CR-017 permits in as many words. And an overlap does not make the document
mean nothing: two devices in one U is a clear, physically wrong statement, which is what a tier-3
error is for. Contrast `TOP-001`, a conductor from a port to itself, which means nothing at all.

**§12.6(b) is not being contradicted here and the difference is worth stating**, because its argument
looks like it applies. It ratified `PLC-001..003` on the ground that *"an unnumbered blocking rule
can carry neither a `Finding.ruleId` nor an AC-051 fixture pair"*. That was about conditions **canon
had already named as model-level illegality** and then left without ids. Occupancy was never in that
list, and it carries a `Finding.ruleId` today: `RCK-001`.

**11.111.5 A consequence M5-G has to plan for, stated here so it is not discovered late.** `RCK-001`
and `RCK-002` are now formally unreachable by gesture. Their AC-051 known-bad fixtures therefore
**cannot be produced by driving the editor** and must be authored as documents directly. That is not
a defect in the fixture corpus; it is the corpus testing the reader rather than the writer, and it is
the same shape as `acknowledgement_commands_test.dart`'s tolerant-reader case at M5-B2. A near-miss
that is one RU away from an overlap is still a legal document a gesture could make, so only the
known-bad half needs hand-authoring.

*Rejected: numbering the overlap refusal `PLC-004`.* Honest about what the code does, and it costs
more than it buys: 29 rules against AC-040 as amended by DR-020, an §8.3 amendment, a new fixture
pair obligation, and a second rule id for a condition `RCK-001` already names.

*Rejected: folding occupancy into `PLC-001` by reading "fits within the rack extent" broadly.*
Cheapest and the worst of the three. "Extent" is the rack's physical bounds; stretching it to mean
occupancy makes a catalogue row describe something other than what its rule checks, and CR-021 makes
that table the definition of what exists.

### §11.112 DR-113 · `SIG-001` fires on the joint in front of it, and "switch port" is a path question tier 2 cannot ask

**Question.** M5-D builds the six tier-2 rules, and the flagship one cannot be written from its own
row. docs/02 §5.2 gives `SIG-001` as *"HDBaseT port connected to a `net.ethernet` **switch** port.
The flagship rule: PoH into a switch port"*, and nothing in the model says which `net.ethernet` ports
belong to a switch.

**11.112.1 MEASURED, AND THE ONLY TWO CANDIDATES ARE BOTH WRONG.** In the seed catalog a switch
carries `tags: const ['poe', 'switch']` and a patch panel carries `glyph:
DeviceGlyph.patchPanel`. **A hardware-damage rule may not rest on either.** Tags are free text a
person edits and a community template will spell differently; a glyph is a drawing choice, and
`device_glyph.dart` exists to pick a picture. A rule keyed to a tag is a rule that stops working the
day somebody renames one, silently, with no test able to notice.

**What IS modelled is the opposite fact.** CR-057 gives the patch panel `isPassthrough: true` and a
`passthroughPairs` list, and the seeded panels declare both. So the product can say with certainty
which ports pass a signal through to another connector, and cannot say which ports belong to a
switch.

**11.112.2 THE PATCH PANEL IS NOT A CARVE-OUT, IT IS THE CASE CR-017 ALREADY RULED ON.** Patching an
HDBaseT run into a panel and out the back is ordinary structured cabling, and it is the commonest
layout this product will ever draw. A predicate reading only the signal families would fire on every
one of them.

The reason it must not is not merely that it would be annoying. **It is the same reason CR-017 gives
for demoting two of Class A's members unconditionally**: *"Dante endpoints with no network path"* and
*"AVB traversing a non-AVB switch"* are *"logically unevaluatable at drag time, because the link being
drawn may be the one that completes the path."* HDBaseT into a panel is that exact shape. Whether the
run ends on a switch depends on what is on the far side of the panel, which may be nothing yet, and
may be the next cable the person draws.

**11.112.3 Ruled: tier-2 `SIG-001` evaluates THE JOINT, not the path.** It fires when an HDBaseT port
is connected directly to a `net.ethernet` port that TERMINATES the signal, which the model expresses
as the port's device not being a passthrough. It does not fire on a passthrough connector, and it
asks nothing about what lies beyond one.

This is a reading of §5.2's row and not an amendment to it: the row's *"switch port"* is the trade's
name for the terminating case, and **the catalogue count does not move**. `SIG-001` stays one of the
six tier-2 rules, with the same id, the same severity and the same remedy.

**11.112.4 The consequence is stated rather than left to be discovered: v1 does not catch
HDBaseT through a panel into a switch.** That is the honest position and it is consistent, not a
hole this ruling opens. The rule that WOULD catch it is a path rule, path rules are exactly what
CR-017 sends to tier 3, and docs/02 §5.3's fourteen do not include one: Dante-with-no-path and
AVB-across-a-non-AVB-switch are not in the v1 catalogue either, they sit with the remaining forty
that AC-040 defers to v1.2 behind a fixture corpus. **The same milestone that gains a path evaluator
gains all three of them together.**

*Rejected: firing on any `net.ethernet` port.* It buys the through-panel case at the price of a false
failure on the most common layout in the product, and a rule that springs back on correct designs is
a rule people learn to click past. Roadmap M5's own risk list names credibility as the thing the
catalogue is protecting; the flagship rule crying wolf is how that is spent.

*Rejected: reading the `switch` tag, or the patch-panel glyph.* Both are unversioned free choices
made for other purposes, and `AC-051`'s fixture pair cannot protect a predicate whose input a
community template may spell however it likes.

**11.112.5 THE RULING GENERALISES ONE RULE FURTHER THAN IT WAS WRITTEN, AND ITS OWN NEAR-MISS TEST IS
WHAT FOUND THAT.** §11.112.3 speaks only of `SIG-001`. Building it, the AC-051 near-miss for the
passthrough case went red not on `SIG-001`, which cleared correctly, but on **`SIG-002`**: a patch
panel's RJ45 declares `net.ethernet` and does not list `video.hdbaset` in `acceptedFamilies`, so
patching HDBaseT through a panel sprang back anyway, one rule along, for the same wrong reason.

**A passthrough is a physical joint and not a signal endpoint.** `SIG-002` asks what THE SINK accepts,
and a patch panel is not the sink; it is passive copper in the middle of a run, carrying whatever the
cable carries. Its jack declares `net.ethernet` because that is what the connector IS, not a claim
about what may pass through it, and asking a panel to enumerate every family that runs on RJ45 is a
list nobody can finish. So `SIG-002` skips a passthrough sink as `SIG-001` skips a passthrough
target.

**`CON-001` DELIBERATELY DOES NOT SKIP ONE**, and the line is worth stating because it is the whole
distinction: you really do plug into that jack, so the connectors really must mate. Physical rules
apply at a passthrough; signal rules do not. `DIR-001` and `ELE-006` are unaffected by construction,
neither being a question about what the far end accepts.

*Rejected: deferring `SIG-001` to v1.2 with the path rules.* It is *"the highest-value validation in
the product"* (`seed_registries.dart`, authored for it), the direct joint is the case that actually
damages a switch, and it is evaluatable today. Half a rule that fires on the damaging case beats no
rule at all, provided the half it does not cover is written down. It is, here.

### §11.113 DR-114 · A verdict is not a cursor: the spring-back ring takes the severity hex, `[ Why? ]` waits for its viewer, and a gesture that hesitated has not ended

**Question.** `#278` builds the chip and the spring-back interaction, and it is the first thing in the
product that paints a rule's verdict on a canvas. Three questions had to be settled before a pixel
was drawn: what colour the amber ring and the target flash are, whether `[ Why? ]` ships, and what
state the gesture is in once the wire has sprung back.

**11.113.1 THE COMMENT THAT ALREADY REFUSED THE HEX IS HALF WRONG, AND THE HALVES POINT IN OPPOSITE
DIRECTIONS.** `schematic_canvas_screen.dart`'s `_connectOverlayStyle` declined docs/05 §7's fixed
figures on a stated ground:

> docs/05 §7 gives the illumination figures in fixed hex, `#F0E442` for a compatible port and
> `#E69F00` for one that would spring back, and those are PAL-1 colours belonging to the signal
> taxonomy.

Measured against the palette tables, that is wrong about the first colour and right about the second,
and the correction does not merely repair a comment: it reverses which way the argument runs.

**`#F0E442` is not a signal colour at all.** PAL-2 (§14, docs/05:348) reserves it: *"Yellow `#F0E442`
is reserved for selection and focus and is **never a cable**."* docs/05:284 carries it in the palette
table with the family column reading *(reserved)* and the role reading *"Selection / focus"*. So the
compatible ring was specified in that hex precisely BECAUSE it is the reserved focus colour, and the
comment refused it on a claim the corpus contradicts in the same document, eight rows up from the
sentence it was reading.

**`#E69F00` and `#D55E00` genuinely are cable colours**, `audio.analog` and `audio.digital`
respectively (docs/01 §6.3, §6.4). That half of the comment holds. **But docs/05 §8 already paints
validation in exactly those two hexes**, over cables that may themselves be them:

| Severity | Mark |
|---|---|
| `error` | `#D55E00` chevron-hatch stroked along the run at 0.5x weight, plus a badge at the midpoint |
| `warning` | `#E69F00` 0.6 px dotted parallel line offset 1 gu below the run, plus a badge |

The corpus therefore crossed this line on purpose and stated how it stays legible: the discriminator
between a `#D55E00` cable and a `#D55E00` error mark is **shape and badge**, not hue. That is the same
answer PAL-1 gives for two families sharing a grey, and it is why the collision is survivable here.

**11.113.2 Ruled: cursor chrome takes theme roles, a verdict takes the severity hex.** The line runs
between what the overlay is SAYING, not between which file draws it:

- **Chrome** is the caret ring, the source ring, the rubber band, the multi-draw selection ring and
  the selected cable's pennant outline. Every one of them marks *where the user is* or *what the user
  picked*. They keep `scheme.primary`, `scheme.tertiary` and `scheme.secondary`, and the existing
  argument for that is untouched and correct: a cursor must read in both brightnesses and against
  whatever theme its owner chose.
- **A verdict** is the spring-back ring and the target flash. They state what a RULE decided. They
  take `#E69F00` and `#D55E00`, fixed, the same two figures docs/05 §8 gives the DRC mark that will
  appear on the very same cable the moment the user clicks `[ Connect anyway ]`.

**The reason is continuity of meaning across two surfaces, and it is not aesthetic.** Under a theme
role, a port that would spring back is amber during the drag and `scheme.error` (whatever the user's
theme makes that) in the DRC list four seconds later. The user learns two colours for one verdict, and
the one they learn first moves when they change theme. Under the fixed hex they learn one. **The
compatible ring's `#F0E442` follows the same rule from the other side**: it is PAL-2's reserved focus
colour, so a candidate ring is one of the two things that colour exists for, and taking it is
obedience to the palette rather than a raid on it.

*Rejected: theme roles throughout, for one policy per file.* It is a tidier rule and it buys the
tidiness by making the product's error colour a preference. Consistency inside one file is worth less
than consistency across the two surfaces a user sees three seconds apart.

*Rejected: a derived dark-mode pair.* docs/05:278-279 does publish a dark variant per family, so the
mechanism exists, and a lightened amber would read better on a dark sheet. It is refused HERE because
those variants are registry data the PAL-1 gate checks, and inventing two more outside it would put
uncheckable colours in the one palette three gates exist to keep honest. **If the dark sheet proves
illegible, the fix is a dark variant for the severity pair IN the registry, checked like the rest, and
that is a ruling with a measurement behind it rather than a constant typed into a widget.**

**11.113.3 Ruled: `[ Why? ]` does not ship with the chip.** `design-ux-schematic.md`'s worked chip
carries three buttons, `[ Insert HDBaseT receiver ]  [ Pick a different port ]  [ Why? ]`, and the
third has no destination in this build. AC-058/D1 already adjudicated exactly that button:

> `ux-schematic`'s reason chip has a `[ Why? ]` button that leads nowhere. Rule rationale exists in
> the model (`CompatibilityRuleDef.rationale`, `remedyHint`) with no viewer.

and §10(g) assigns the viewer to **M5-F3**, noting the file it publishes *"deliberately does not
exist"* because canon §5 IS the catalogue. **So the button is a named defect with a named fix in a
named later chapter of this same milestone.** Shipping it now would be building the defect on purpose,
in the milestone that promised to remove it, four chapters ahead of the code that would make it true.

The chip is not thereby silent about why. `SpringBackChip.explanation` is the second line of the
mockup, inline and always present, and it carries the trade reason in the trade's words: *"HDBaseT
uses Ethernet cabling but is not interoperable; PoH may damage the switch."* `[ Why? ]` goes DEEPER
than that, to the catalogue entry, which is the thing that does not exist yet.

*Rejected: shipping it disabled with a tooltip.* It sets the layout now and is honest about the state.
It also puts a permanently dead control on the highest-traffic chip in the editor, and "honestly
greyed" is still a button a user aims at once per rule before learning not to.

**11.113.4 Ruled: a spring-back leaves the gesture ARMED, and that is CR-017 read literally.** The
governing sentence is *"the gesture may hesitate; the document may not lie"*. **A gesture that
hesitated has not ended.** So the wire springs back to the source and stays armed there: `_wireFrom`
holds, the candidate rings stay lit, the caret stays where the user aimed.

This is what makes `[ Pick a different port ]` a real button rather than a relabelled Cancel. It
dismisses the chip and returns the user to the state they were in one frame before the release, still
aiming, with the field of candidates still on screen. Under the alternative it closes a dialog and
leaves them to press `W` again to retry the thing they were just told about, which charges a fresh arm
for every near miss on a gesture the roadmap calls the highest-throughput one in the editor.

**The document is untouched either way, which is the half of CR-017 that does not bend.** Nothing is
written until `[ Connect anyway ]`, and the armed state is screen state exclusively.

*Rejected: full cancellation, matching the tier-1 refusal path.* Tier 1 cancels because there is
nothing to escape to (docs/02:854), which is the exact property tier 2 does not have: a spring-back is
droppable by design, docs/05:476 says so in as many words, and a state machine that treated the two
identically would be discarding the distinction the whole tier exists to draw.

### §11.114 DR-115 · The remedy inserts a device and wires the run into it; the second link is unbuildable for the rule that asks for it

**Question.** `#278` builds `SIG-001`'s remedy. docs/05 §5 (:767) specifies it in one sentence:
*"The `[ Insert HDBaseT receiver ]` remedy chip therefore inserts a device, correctly, and creates
both links in one undo step."* Building it revealed that the second link cannot exist.
