for, and M8 is release engineering with no seat for a model change. **It
is a MAYBE and not a schedule.** If the reaction says it must precede
release, moving one Story between two Epics is the visible act §8.3 asks
for and costs a click (DR-097).

**THIS IS THE RIGHT SHAPE OF RESTRAINT AND IS RECORDED AS SUCH.** An
agent had the five facts, a working branch and momentum, and the
alternative was amending a confirmed acceptance criterion inside a DRC
remedy commit on one session's enthusiasm. §8.3 forbids that in terms,
and the person who would have to live with a half-designed shelf model
asked for evidence first.

**11.127.6 `SpringBackRemedy` GAINS TWO MEMBERS, AND ITS DOC COMMENT'S
OBJECTION IS ANSWERED RATHER THAN OVERRULED.** It holds one member today
and says why: *"Inventing labels for the other five would be putting words
in a designer's mouth and shipping them as though the corpus had said
them."* **That objection was right and is now satisfied**, because the
M5-H2 review is the corpus saying them. It still governs the remaining
three: `DIR-001`, `DIR-003` and `ELE-006` get no remedy here, because
nobody has asked for one.

### §11.128 DR-129 · A code-adjacent finding is a different KIND of row, and the panel had no way to say so

**Board `#840` (M5-M), authorised by DR-127 §11.126.** Settled by the user
2026-09-06, on the twelfth of the M5-H2 review's findings: *"a
code-adjacent finding wants more than a row in a panel."*

**11.128.1 THE CITATION WAS PROSE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM.**
`CODE-002`'s message ends *"Verify against NEC 800.154; 300.22(C) permits
a metal raceway, which this product does not model."* Every word of that
is right, and **the article is findable only by reading to the end of a
sentence** that begins with a cable designator. `RuleMeta` carries
`summary`, `rationale` and `governing`, and `governing` holds this
repository's own ids (`AC-027`, `DR-079`), not the code's.

So there is nothing in the model that says "this rule turns on an external
document", and the panel renders these two rows exactly like a cable being
three metres too long.

**11.128.2 RULED: `RuleMeta` GAINS `codeCitation`, ON DR-125's PRECEDENT.**
That ruling's shape is the one being followed: **the catalogue authorises
the fact and the surface renders it**, rather than a widget inferring
something from a rule id. `CODE-001` declares `NEC 725.136` and `CODE-002`
declares `NEC 800.154`. **Two rules and no others**, which is a checkable
claim and is checked.

`300.22(C)`'s metal-raceway exception stays in the message rather than
becoming a second field. It is an argument about what this product cannot
see, not a citation to look up, and the sentence is where an argument
belongs.

**11.128.3 A DIFFERENT SHAPE, NOT A LOUDER COLOUR.** `ConsoleStatus`
carries five values and `statusForSeverity` maps four; **`caution` has
been defined, themed, and reachable by no finding since M5-F**.
`status_marker.dart` draws it as a **diamond**, where warning is a
triangle.

That is the right instrument, and the reason is the one DR-079 gave when
it demoted both rules to `warning`: **this product cannot see the thing
the code article turns on.** A code row is not a louder warning, it is a
different question, and a shape says "different kind" where a colour says
"different amount". PAL-1's whole argument one domain over is that hue
alone is never the channel.

**THE SEVERITY IS UNTOUCHED.** `Finding.severity` stays `warning`, the
severity filter still finds these rows under Warning, and an override
still moves them. Only the MARKER differs, which is a rendering fact and
not a validation one.

**11.128.4 AND THE PANEL RENDERS `Finding.remedy`, WHICH DR-128 SAID IT
ALREADY DID.** §11.127.5 states that the issues panel *"renders it as a
button"*. It did not. The field shipped, `PWR-003` declared it,
`addOutletsToRack` implemented it, and **`drc_panel.dart` never read the
field**, so `[ Add a rack PDU ]` existed nowhere a person could press it.

**THIS IS THE SECOND TIME IN TWO RULINGS THAT A BUTTON WAS DESCRIBED
BEFORE IT EXISTED.** The first was `SpringBackRemedy`'s two members, and
**Dart's exhaustive switch caught that one within the hour**. This one had
no such backstop: a nullable field a widget ignores compiles perfectly and
tests green, because every test that could have noticed was written
against the model.

**So the gate is the correction.** `FindingRemedy` values are asserted
against what the panel renders, in both directions, exactly as
`SpringBackRemedy`'s pairing now is. **A remedy nothing renders is a
button nobody can press**, and that sentence is now a failing test rather
than a thing I have written twice.

**11.128.5 WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT HERE.** A separate verification
dialog for code rules, recording who checked what against which edition,
was offered and not taken. `AckedFinding` already carries `reason`, `by`
and `at`, so the record exists; what a code acknowledgement wants is a
different QUESTION, and **the place that earns its keep is T0.02, the
exceptions sheet, which is M6-C and not built**. Building the dialog first
would design a form for a page nobody has drawn.

### §11.129 DR-130 · The cabinet head end gets a name and a note, and the note had no producer either

**Board `#839` (M5-L), authorised by DR-127 §11.126.** Settled by the user
2026-09-06, on the eleventh of the M5-H2 review's findings: a cabinet head
end is *"the COMMON residential case rather than an edge"*.

**11.129.1 THE FINDING'S OWN FALLBACK DOES NOT EXIST.** DR-125 §11.124.1
dispositioned this as *"expressible as `OffRackPlacement` with a
`mountNote`, but crude"*. Censused before pricing, as that ruling requires
of itself, and **the crude option is not available either**:

`OffRackPlacement.mountNote` is modelled, serialized under its own key,
round-tripped by the codec, and **written by nothing a person can reach**.
The one occurrence in `commands/` is `location_commands.dart` copying it
forward so a location change does not destroy it, which is a preserver and
not a producer. No widget renders it, no schedule prints it, no exporter
reads it. **Its only writers are `apps/rackpal/tool/starters/`**, the
starter-generation tool, which is why four seeded devices carry sentences
like *"Ceiling mount, rear of room"* and no user has ever been able to
type one.

**SO THE FINDING WAS PRICED AGAINST A WORKAROUND THAT IS REACHABLE ONLY
BY HAND-EDITING JSON.** That is the eighth field this milestone with no
producer, and the first found by censusing a ruling's own escape hatch
rather than by a rule firing. The lesson stands where DR-128 left it: **a
claim about what the product can already express belongs in a test.**

**11.129.2 RULED: A NAMED PLACE, WITH A NOTE. NOT A CONTAINER.**
`mountNote` gains a producer, and the cabinet head end is a `Location`
plus that note. **No cabinet entity, no shelf geometry, no RU grid, and no
elevation.** Three larger readings were offered and declined:

| Offered | Why not |
|---|---|
| A cabinet counted by the power and thermal rollups, as a rack is | Real, and the failure it catches (a sealed cabinet full of gear) is real. It is also a container decision, and containers are what M9 is holding |
| A first-class container with shelf geometry, reusing DR-128's `ShelfPlacement` | Collides head-on with `#844`, which parked exactly this under M9 six commits ago. Building it here would unpark by accident |
| Park everything, fix nothing | Leaves the finding's premise false in the record AND leaves a modelled field unreachable, which is the state that produced the finding |

**11.129.3 WHY THE SMALLEST OPTION IS NOT THE TIMID ONE.** The reviewer's
point is that this case is COMMON, and what a common case needs first is
to be **sayable**: a device in the AV closet on the top shelf should print
that way on the schedule and in the PDF, rather than appearing as a device
with no location. A note reaches every one of those surfaces. **Geometry
reaches none of them without a drawing nobody has drawn**, which is
`#844`'s argument and does not improve by being made twice.

**11.129.4 `PLC-001` STAYS SILENT ON AN OFF-RACK DEVICE, AND THAT IS G4
AND NOT AN OMISSION.** `placement_rules.dart` already makes `PLC-001` and
`PLC-003` unevaluatable for `OffRackPlacement` and `StagedPlacement`, on
the ground that there is no RU to be within. **A cabinet does not change
that**: the rule asks whether a rail position fits inside a rack, and a
cabinet has neither. Making `PLC-001` fire on a cabinet would be
fabricating a rack, which CR-114 forbids in the same breath it forbids
estimating an unknown.

So this chapter adds **no rule**, and the rule count stays at 28 under
CR-021 and AC-040.

**11.129.5 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** Whether a cabinet's outlets, watts
and BTU should roll up the way a rack's do is a real question and is
**explicitly left open**, filed rather than answered, because the honest
version of it needs the container the first table row declined. It joins
`#844` under M9 rather than being half-built here.

### §11.130 DR-131 · The switchable device is the SPEAKER, and one control answers both halves of finding 5

**Board `#838` (M5-K), authorised by DR-127 §11.126.** Settled by the user
2026-09-06 on the fifth of the M5-H2 review's findings: *"`maxTapWatts`
exists on the model; a tap SELECTOR and CV-to-Low-Z switching do not."*

**11.130.1 THE FIELD HAS A PRODUCER AND NO CONSUMER, WHICH IS A SHAPE
THIS MILESTONE HAD NOT YET MET.** Eight producer gaps preceded this one
and every one was a field nothing could write. `maxTapWatts` is the
opposite and is no better off:

| | |
|---|---|
| authorable | **yes**, in the device builder (`port_commands.dart`, `port_grid.dart`) |
| declared on a seeded port | **zero of 727** |
| read by a rule, a rollup, a schedule or an export | **nothing, anywhere** |

So a person can type a tap wattage into the builder and **it does not
participate in one calculation**. `catalog_field.dart` even names the
gap in its own comment, calling `F08` *"the only field source of a
tapWatts selector"*, a selector that was never built.

**11.130.2 THE CORRECTION THAT RELOCATED THE WHOLE PROBLEM.** The
question put to the user assumed a switchable AMPLIFIER and asked how its
mode is recorded. The answer was that the premise is wrong:
*"Amplifiers are very rarely switchable, and if they support both Low-Z
and CV, they almost always have separate outputs instead of a switch.
Speakers are the only CV devices that I've seen with taps/switches for
Low-Z/CV in person."*

**The catalogue already agrees, which nobody had checked.** `A05`, the
only rack-side CV source, declares `cv.a` and `cv.b` as
`audio.speaker_cv` bus nodes at `nominalVoltage: 70` and **has no low-Z
output at all**. The amp side needed nothing; the model had been right
for a reason nobody had written down.

**THIS IS THE THIRD TRADE CORRECTION IN THIS MILESTONE**, after the
passive power strip and the shelf, and it has the same shape every time:
an agent reasoning from what the model could express, rather than from
what an installer touches. Recorded under
`trade-knowledge-beats-workflow-reasoning`.

**11.130.3 RULED: ONE CONTROL ON THE SPEAKER, DOING DOUBLE DUTY.** The
tap selector is a per-instance fact on a CV speaker, and its positions
are wattages **plus a Low-Z bypass**. That single control answers both
halves of finding 5, which is why they are one chapter's design and not
two:

- its **wattage** positions are what a 70V bus sums against the
  amplifier's rating, giving `maxTapWatts` its first consumer;
- its **bypass** position is CV-to-Low-Z switching, and it tells
  `ELE-006` that this speaker is currently a low-impedance device.

The amplifier gains nothing. Two catalogue entries with their own outputs
is the model, and it is the model already shipped.

**11.130.4 `ELE-006`'S FALSE POSITIVE IS REAL AND HAS NO REPRODUCING
CASE TODAY.** The rule fires on `audio.speaker_cv` opposite
`audio.speaker_lowz` and looks at nothing else, so a dual-mode speaker
set to bypass and landed correctly on a low-Z output would be told it is
a near short. **No seeded speaker is dual-mode**, though: `F08` is CV
only and `F07` is low-Z only, so the fault is unreachable with shipped
data.

That is exactly `acceptedFamilies`' position before DR-126, and the
lesson there transfers: **a rule whose fault cannot be constructed from
the catalogue has never been tested against the catalogue.** The fixture
must therefore create the dual-mode speaker deliberately, and AC-051's
pair is a known-bad and a known-good that differ **only in the selector
position**.

**11.130.5 TWO CHAPTERS, IN THE ORDER THE USER GAVE.** The false
positive first, then the selector and the sum. The order is not
arbitrary: the bypass position is what makes `ELE-006` correct, and
building the sum first would add a rule on top of one still crying wolf.

**11.130.6 THE SUM CHECK IS A TWENTY-NINTH RULE AND IS NOT AUTHORISED
HERE.** AC-040 caps v1 at an enumerated catalogue, corrected to 28 by
§12.6(b), and CR-021 rules that a rule not in canon §5 does not exist.
**Chapter two therefore needs its own §8.3 amendment**, which is
deliberately not smuggled into this ruling: DR-127 exists precisely
because "unpriced" was being used to let consequences sit outside the one
scope list. The alternative, expressing the sum as a **rollup** in
`totals.dart` rather than a rule, is genuinely open and is cheaper: it
reports a number with a G4 unknown count and adds nothing to the
catalogue.

**11.130.7 WHICH SPEAKERS ARE DUAL-MODE, ANSWERED BY THE USER RATHER
THAN GUESSED.** Two, and the pairing is deliberate: **`F08` gains a
bypass**, which makes the `ELE-006` fix reachable using an entry that
already exists, and **a NEW template covers the in-ceiling / outdoor /
landscape case** rather than `F04`, `F05` or `F07` changing their ports
under documents that already reference them.

**11.130.8 THE TAP VALUE IS FREE NUMERIC ENTRY WITH BYPASS AS A FLAG,
AND THE REASON IS THAT THE LADDER IS NOT ONE LADDER.** A fixed list was
offered and declined on evidence: *"Episode makes one of theirs with
7.5/15/30/60/Bypass taps, while Beale Street has models that range from
1/1.9/3.8/7.5/15W/Bypass, to the same scheme as Episode."* A per-template
list was also offered and declined, for a workflow reason worth
recording: the tap is **set once at install and not touched**, and
*"if any issues come up it's simple enough to reference the sheets and
make the fix on site"*, so the model buys little by policing which
numbers are legal on which speaker.

So the per-instance state is **two fields on the device**, and G4 governs
the third state:

| `lowZBypass` | `tapWatts` | means |
|---|---|---|
| `true` | ignored | the transformer is bypassed; this speaker is a low-impedance device and `ELE-006` must not fire against a low-Z output |
| `false` | `15` | constant voltage at 15 W, and the figure a 70 V bus sums |
| `false` | absent | constant voltage, tap **UNKNOWN**. CR-114: never estimated, never `0`, and the rollup reports it in its unknown count |

**11.130.9 IT LIVES ON `Port`, BECAUSE `Port.tapWatts` ALREADY EXISTS
AND THIS RULING FIRST PUT IT IN THE WRONG PLACE.** §11.130.8 was drafted
ruling the pair onto `DeviceInstance`, and the fields were written there
before the collision surfaced. **The census that priced this ruling
grepped `maxTapWatts` and never grepped `tapWatts`**, which is
`census-the-field-not-the-name` for the fifth recorded time and the
second where the miss was a NAME rather than a call shape.

`Port.tapWatts` is not merely present, it is **already documented as the
right home**: *"70/100 V transformer tap: per INSTALLATION, not per
template."* And it is the **ninth producer gap of this milestone**,
matching `maxTapWatts`' shape exactly:

| | |
|---|---|
| written by | **nothing.** The codec decodes it and no command, no widget and no builder sets it |
| read by | **nothing.** The codec encodes it |
| said so already | `catalog_field.dart`'s header, in as many words: no rule *"reads `impedanceOhms`/`tapWatts` from at all (AC-031)"* |

So `#838` does not add a tap field. **It gives the one already modelled a
producer and a consumer**, and adds only `lowZBypass` beside it. The
device-level draft is withdrawn: a speaker with two pigtail conductors
has one port SET, and the repo already decided that a per-installation
electrical fact belongs on the port (CR-053, "typed; lives here, not in a
device-keyed map").

**AND THE CATALOGUE'S OWN LADDER IS A FOURTH DATA POINT FOR §11.130.8.**
`F08`'s description hard-codes *"2.5/5/10/15/20 W"*, which matches
neither Episode's nor Beale Street's. A fixed list was going to be wrong
in the shipped catalogue as well as in the field, and that sentence
should be read as an example rather than as a constraint.

### §11.131 DR-132 · A §8.3 amendment restoring `ELE-005`, a rule that already had an id, a severity and a threshold

**Board `#838` (M5-K), amending AC-040.** Settled by the user 2026-09-06,
choosing a rule over a rollup: *"I feel like having a warning for that is
important to prevent blowing speakers out."*

**11.131.1 THE REASON IS THE ONE AC-040 ITSELF USED.** That cut kept
`RCK-012`, `CODE-001` and `CODE-002` because they *"protect the user from
real money"*. Overload a 70 V line and the amplifier clips; **clipped
square waves are what destroy tweeters**, so the loss is not the
amplifier's protection circuit doing its job, it is a van full of
replacement drivers. That is the same test, met.

**11.131.2 IT IS NOT A NEW RULE. IT IS A CUT ONE, AND I NEARLY MINTED A
DUPLICATE.** The plan of record was to add `ELE-007`. Two greps before
writing it found that
`docs/research/design-data-model.md` line 1136 already specifies:

> `ELE-005` **warning**: Σ of 70 V/100 V `tapWatts` on a net > 80% of the
> amp channel rating.

**Every parameter matches what was about to be invented**: the severity
the user asked for, the 80% threshold `PWR-001` independently sets as
this repository's load-headroom convention, and the aggregate. Line 1224
even names the mechanism, that *"each speaker's input `Port.tapWatts` is
per-installation. `ELE-005` sums the net."*

`ELE-007` was also already taken, by a satellite-splitter DC-passing rule
in the same document. **Minting it would have put two different rules
behind one id in one corpus.**

**11.131.3 SO THE AMENDMENT IS NARROW AND SAYS WHAT IT DOES NOT DO.**
AC-040's enumeration governs (§12.6(b)) and it currently lists 28.
`ELE-005` is **added, making 29**. `ELE-004`, cut in the same breath by
the same paragraph, **stays cut**: parallel low-Z impedance is a
different calculation over a different aggregate, nobody has asked for
it, and restoring a neighbour because it is adjacent is how a cut list
unravels. The rest of AC-040 is untouched.

**11.131.4 THE SUM IS OVER KNOWN TAPS AND NEVER OVER ESTIMATED ONES**
(G4/CR-114). A speaker whose tap nobody recorded still draws from the
amplifier, so it cannot be treated as zero, and it must not be guessed
either. The rule therefore fires **only when the KNOWN taps alone cross
80%**, which is the one case that is certain, and **the message carries
the unknown count** so the reader knows the figure is a floor rather than
a total.

That asymmetry is deliberate and is the honest direction: a net whose
recorded taps sit under the line while four taps are blank has not been
cleared, it has been **incompletely measured**, and saying so is worth
more than a number nobody can act on.

**11.131.5 WHAT IT NEEDS, AND BOTH HALVES WERE PRODUCER GAPS.** The
capacity side is `PortDef.bus.maxTapWatts`, **declared on zero of 727
seeded ports**, so `A05`'s two CV outputs must state their rating or the
rule is unevaluatable and silent on the only amplifier that can raise it.
The consumption side is `Port.tapWatts`, which DR-131 §11.130.9 found had
no producer at all and which that ruling's first chapter gave a home.
**The rule is the consumer both fields have been waiting for since M0.**

**11.131.6 AND ITS AC-051 PAIR MUST BE CONSTRUCTED, NOT FOUND.** No
seeded document can currently overload a 70 V line, because nothing
declares a capacity and nothing sets a tap. The known-bad and the
known-good therefore differ **only in one tap value**, on DR-131
§11.130.4's reasoning: a rule whose fault cannot be built from the
catalogue has never been tested against the catalogue.

### §11.132 DR-133 · The validation drawer was specified in the layout table and never built

**Board `#847`, ordered into M5 by the user 2026-09-06** behind `#838` and
`#839`. Settled the same day, and settled mostly by **reading docs/04**
rather than by deciding anything.

**11.132.1 THE ITEM WAS FILED CLAIMING A DECISION THAT WAS ALREADY MADE.**
`#847` said *"mounting it is a shell decision, not a widget one"* and
listed three open questions: where the panel lives, how it opens, and
what it displaces. **docs/04 answers all three**, and the item was written
without reading it closely enough.

§1's layout table carries a row for it, written and never built:

| Element | Default | Range | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Validation drawer** | 28 px | 28 / 320 | Auto-expands to 180 px **once**, on the first *error* per session, never again |

and §8's keymap binds its navigation: **`F7` re-check, `F8` next issue,
`Shift+F8` previous issue**, global. **None of the three is bound in
`keymap.dart`.**

**11.132.2 SO THE THREE QUESTIONS WERE CLOSED, AND ONE ANSWER IS BETTER
THAN WHAT WAS GOING TO BE PROPOSED.** A bottom drawer spanning the shell
is not a fourth column, so it needs neither the unbuilt `PanelHost` seam
nor a share of the 320 px inspector. And **it opens by itself**, which is
a better answer than the keybinding about to be offered: a person who
does not know the validation engine exists cannot press a key to find it,
and **that is precisely the state M5-F's closing sentence claimed to have
ended** (§5.4.6).

**11.132.3 THE ONE THING THE SPEC DOES NOT SAY, RULED HERE.** *"The first
error per session"* leaves open what an error IS at that moment, and the
choice is load-bearing because `RuleOverride` and `AckedFinding` both move
severities.

**RULED: the trigger is a finding whose RESOLVED severity is `error`,
after overrides and acknowledgements.** Not the catalogue's default
severity. A project that has demoted `PWR-003` to advisory has said it
does not want to be stopped by it, and re-opening a drawer for it would
overrule a decision the user recorded, which is RJ-006's whole point in
keeping the acknowledgement machinery.

**A DOCUMENT WITH NO ERRORS NEVER AUTO-OPENS IT**, and warnings never do.
The drawer still shows its 28 px rail with a count, so the engine is
visible without being loud, which is the difference between the drawer
and a dialog.

**11.132.4 SESSION MEANS THE APP RUN, TAKEN LITERALLY.** Opening a second
document does not re-arm it. **The alternative is defensible and is
recorded rather than taken**: a per-document arming would surface the
first error in each job, which is arguably what an integrator opening
four projects wants. It is not what §1 says, and changing it is a ruling
rather than a detail, so it stays as written until somebody has used it.

**11.132.5 THE PANEL IS MOUNTED UNCHANGED.** `DrcPanel` gets a host, not
a rewrite. Everything M5-F built (the grouping, the severity filter,
acknowledge and withdraw, the `Why?` viewer) plus DR-128's remedy button
and DR-129's code-citation row become reachable **by mounting one widget
that already passes its own tests**, which is the whole shape of `#847`:
the thing existed, something read it, and no path a person walks reached
it.

**11.132.6 WHAT THIS DOES TO §5.4.6's CORRECTION.** That section was
amended by DR-129 to say a user *cannot* see the findings. **It becomes
true again on this commit**, and the record should say so in the same
place rather than leaving a reader to work out which of two corrections
is current.
### §11.133 DR-134 · `carriedProtocols` is deleted, and DR-081's cell is built for the field that survives

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-07** (`#846`), on a finding `#841`'s census raised and on a
correction to the reasoning that was offered with it.

**A §8.3 AMENDMENT.** It supersedes **DR-081 §11.80.2 in part**: that ruling gave `carriedProtocols`
and `acceptedFamilies` one multi-select cell between them, and one of the two fields does not survive
to receive it. The cell is still built. **DR-081 is discharged by this ruling rather than narrowed**,
which is the user's choice between the two and is the reason the amendment is worth its own commit.

**11.133.1 THE CASE PUT TO THE USER WAS WRONG IN ITS FACTS, AND IS RECORDED BEFORE THE ONE THAT
REPLACED IT.** `#846` says *"searching the shipped catalogue by protocol matches nothing, and always
has"*, and it was relayed with the recommendation that *"deleting two dead reads and a field is
cheaper and more honest than filling it"*. Measured, both halves are false:

| The claim | What the code does |
|---|---|
| protocol search matches nothing | it matches. `dante` finds the seeded DSP twice over, by the `audio.dante` family on `dante.pri` / `dante.sec` and by the device's own `dante` tag, and `template_search_test.dart:181` has asserted it since M4 |
| two dead reads | neither is dead. `templateHasFamilyPrefix` tests `signalFamily` first and `carriedProtocols` second; the search tokeniser already adds `connector.v` and `signalFamily.v` for every port. Both reads are **widenings of paths that work** |

**A finding about a field is not a finding about the feature it is part of.** The census asked
correctly whether anything outside the device builder reads the field, and answered correctly that
two things do. The error was reading that as *"the feature those two things implement is broken"*,
which is a different claim needing a different measurement, and the measurement was available: a
test names it.

**11.133.2 THE ACTUAL CASE FOR DELETING IT IS BETTER, AND IT IS THAT THE FIELD IS A SECOND COPY.**
docs/02 §6.2's worked example uses `carriedProtocols` for exactly two things, and the corpus already
models both, in fields that have a producer **and** a consumer:

- **eARC over HDMI.** `PortDef.returnChannel` has a builder column (`RETURN`, 88 points), seed data
  (`catalog_audio.dart:224` `ReturnChannel.eArc`, `catalog_field.dart:63` `.arc`), a spring-back rule
  at `spring_back_rules.dart:354` and a schematic consumer. **§6.2's own example carries the eARC
  fact twice on one port**, once in `returnChannel` and once in `carriedProtocols`, and only the
  first of the two is read by anything.
- **Dante over RJ45.** A family on a dedicated port plus a device tag, as §11.133.1 measures.

So the field is not an unfinished feature. **It is a weaker spelling of two facts the model already
records properly**, and the version of each that is read is the version that is not this field.

**11.133.3 IT ALSO HAS NO WRITER, WHICH IS THE PART `#846` GOT RIGHT.** `portWithIdentity` copies an
existing value and the codec reads one off disk. **No gesture in the product sets it**, so every one
of the 727 seeded ports and every port a person has ever authored carries `[]`. `#846`'s claim that
*"the device builder CAN set it"* is false for the same reason DR-081 exists: the cell was ordered
and never built.

**11.133.4 TWO OF DR-081's OWN STATEMENTS ARE CORRECTED HERE, BECAUSE THAT RULING REASONED FROM
THEM.** Neither correction changes what DR-081 decided; both change why.

- **§11.80.5: *"CR-117 holds because the codec writes no key for an empty list, which is its existing
  behaviour rather than a new rule."*** **False, and false when it was written.** `_encodePortDef`
  writes `'carriedProtocols'` and `'acceptedFamilies'` unconditionally, list comprehensions over
  possibly-empty lists, with no `putIfNotNull` and no pruning pass after. **`apartment.rmpj` carries
  737 copies of `[]` for this field** and the other three starters carry their own. This is
  `position`'s defect one field over, which DR-105 §11.104.3 found and fixed in the same file and
  described in the same words: *"the file carried 727 copies of the origin per starter and said
  nothing by it."*
- **§11.80.3: *"Nothing reads `acceptedFamilies` at connect time in v1."*** True on 2026-08-21 and
  **false since DR-126**, which populated eighteen seeded ports. Three call sites read it at connect
  time today: `connect_rules.dart:318` (tier 1), `spring_back_rules.dart:423` (`SIG-002`, tier 2) and
  `insert_converter.dart:156`.

**THE SECOND CORRECTION IS WHY THE CELL IS BUILT RATHER THAN DROPPED WITH THE FIELD**, and it is the
whole of the user's choice. DR-081 could treat the cell as a convenience because nothing consumed the
value. **A field that three connect-time call sites read, with no way for a person to correct it, is
the defect this milestone has now found ten times**, and shipping it knowingly on the day of the
tenth would be worse than the nine that were accidents.

**11.133.5 THE SCHEMA MOVES TO 4 AND `kMinReaderVersion` DOES NOT, AND BOTH HALVES ARE THE CORPUS'S
OWN RULE RATHER THAN A NEW ONE.** The trigger for an advance is written in `json_codec.dart` twice in
the same words: a change is free when *"every file already on disk re-encodes byte for byte"* and
*"byte-invisible to existing files (CR-117)"*. **Removing this key is neither.** Every `.rmpj` on
disk loses one key per port, so `migrateV3ToV4` strips it and re-stamps, on `migrateV2ToV3`'s
precedent and in its shape.

**`kMinReaderVersion` STAYS AT 3, WHICH IS NOT BOOKKEEPING EITHER.** DR-081's v1-to-v2 reasoning
raises the stamp when this build would emit bytes an older reader **throws** on. A schema-3 reader
meeting a schema-4 file calls `json['carriedProtocols'] ?? const <Object?>[]`, gets `[]`, and is
correct: **`[]` is the only value this field has ever held in any file**, so there is nothing an
older reader can lose by not finding it. Raising the stamp would refuse a file that opens perfectly.

**11.133.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not touch `acceptedFamilies`' meaning: **DR-081
§11.80.5's DISTINCTION stands**, an empty list is a statement and not an unknown, and the
multi-select must not introduce a third state to be helpful. **Its WORDING does not survive contact
with the cell**, and that is worth separating from the distinction it was making: §11.80.5 spells the
statement *"this port constrains nothing"*, and `ConnectTarget.acceptsFamily` is
`signalFamily == f || acceptedFamilies.contains(f)`, so the list only ever WIDENS and an empty one is
the NARROWEST state rather than the loosest. The cell therefore reads **`Own family only`**, which is
what the port does; a cell reading *no constraint* would tell an installer the opposite. It does not
prune the empty `acceptedFamilies` key from the encoder, which is a separate question with §11.80.5's
answer pointing the other way and no measurement behind it yet. It does not move `channelIndex`,
which DR-081 put on the port-set surface and which stays there. And it does not add, arm or re-tier
any validation rule.

**11.133.7 ONE CONSEQUENCE THE IMPLEMENTATION FOUND, RECORDED BECAUSE THE RULING DID NOT SEE IT.**
`.rmdx` and `.rmda` carry a `TemplateBody` written by the same `templateBodyToJson`, and a
`contentHash` taken over its canonical bytes. **Those bytes move here**, so every device-exchange
file written before this ruling would import reporting a content mismatch, for a reason that has
nothing to do with its content.

**`kRmdxSchemaVersion` therefore moves to 2**, its own chain being independent of `.rmpj`'s by
AC-050/A8.2, and the step strips the key. **`migrateRmdxToCurrent` shipped EMPTY at M4-M and said
what it was for**: *"the SEAM plus the refusal, so that the first person to bump
`kRmdxSchemaVersion` adds a row to a table that already exists instead of discovering that `.rmdx`
never had a chain and inventing one under deadline."* That person arrived nine days later and it was
a row.

**THE MIGRATION RECOMPUTES THE HASH, AND THAT COST IS TAKEN DELIBERATELY.** A recomputed hash cannot
attest to what the exporter wrote, so a migrated file verifies against itself and nothing more. The
alternative is worse: a warning that fires on every older file is one a person learns to click past,
and the check is then gone for the files it was built for. **Only the migration recomputes**;
a file already at the current version is compared as written, so tamper evidence still means what it
says for everything written from here on.

### §11.134 DR-135 · M5 closes, the Plan view opens over it, and the minor stops being a milestone number

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-07.** Three acts in one ruling because they are one decision: M5
closes, its successor opens, and the successor is the first epic on this board that the version
scheme cannot name.

**11.134.1 M5 CLOSES ON ITS CRITERION, WHICH IS §8.1's TEST AND NOT AN EMPTY BACKLOG.** All three
clauses are discharged (docs/12 §5.4): the AC-051 pair coverage is `DEMONSTRATED` at 29 of 29 with a
gate whose subject is `kRuleCatalogue` rather than any evaluator's enum, the domain-expert sign-off
is `CONFIRMED` on 2026-09-06, and *no rule prevents a PDF being written* is `DEMONSTRATED` by a
sealed `ExportError` with three arms and none of them about a rule. **Every one of the twenty
Stories under epic 23 is `Done`**, including all five DR-127 §11.126 added on the day of the review,
and the count of `Done` Chapters beneath them is **61**, which is where `v0.5.61` comes from and why
closing M5 owes no bump.

**docs/12 §5.4 CARRIED A SENTENCE THAT STOPPED BEING TRUE WHILE IT SAT THERE**, and it is corrected
rather than quietly deleted: *"DR-127 §11.126 amended M5's scope with five items on the day of the
review, four of them unbuilt"*. All four closed between 2026-09-06 and 2026-09-07 (§5.4.12 to
§5.4.15). **The paragraph beside it asked for M5's remaining cost to be re-measured before its
successor opened; this ruling is that measurement**, and the number it found is zero.

**11.134.2 THE SUCCESSOR IS THE PLAN VIEW AND NOT M6, AND THIS IS RECORDED BECAUSE THE REQUEST
ARRIVED NAMING M6.** DR-029 §11.28.4 and roadmap §4 sequence the Plan view between M5 and M6, on the
ground that M6's criterion is that all four starters export a *complete* set and a plan sheet
arriving afterwards would make that criterion run twice. docs/12 §5.4 already states this in the
section a person closing M5 would be reading. **The request self-corrected before any work started**,
which is the outcome that note was written for, and it is kept here as evidence the note earns its
place.

**11.134.3 THE QUESTION THE EPIC EXPOSED, WHICH NO DOCUMENT COULD ANSWER.** docs/14 §14.0 defines the
minor as *"the milestone epic under development"* and its own table spells the rule `M2 ⇒ 2, M3 ⇒ 3`.
**The Plan view is an epic with no milestone number**, and DR-029 §11.28.4 withheld one on purpose,
so §14.0 admits no answer for it: there is no digit to read off a name that has none. A scheme that
cannot number the epic currently under development has stopped doing the one job §14.0 buys it,
answering *is this the one with the plan work in it* without a changelog lookup.

**11.134.4 THE ANSWER: THE PLAN VIEW TAKES `0.6`.** The minor is therefore **the epic's position in
the plan's order, not the digit inside a milestone's name**, and §14.0's table is amended to say so.
The consequence is written out here rather than left to be discovered one bump at a time:

| Epic | Band |
|---|---|
| M5 Validation | `0.5` |
| The Plan view | `0.6` |
| M6 Full sheet set | `0.7` |
| M7 Platform and access | `0.8` |
| M8 Release engineering | `0.9` |
| M9 Beta hardening | `0.10` |

**WHAT THIS COSTS IS THE COINCIDENCE THAT MADE THE SCHEME EASY TO READ**, and the cost is named
because it is real: from `0.7` onwards the minor no longer equals the milestone number, so a reader
who learned the shortcut `Mn ⇒ n` is wrong by one for the rest of v1. That is the price of giving a
band to an epic the plan deliberately refused to number, and the alternative was a scheme with a hole
in it exactly where the current work sits.

**11.134.5 WHY THIS RENUMBERING IS CHEAP AND DR-029's WAS NOT, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING.**
DR-029 §11.28.4 refused to renumber M6 to M10 for this same epic, and the two questions look
identical. They are not, and the difference is entirely in what carries the number. **A milestone
number is written into hundreds of `M6-A1`-shaped task titles, into docs/12 §5.3 to §5.8's headers,
into §12.7's table and into dozens of canon references**, none of which any tool can rewrite safely.
**A version minor is written in six files and one table**, and `version_parity_test.dart` fails the
build the moment one of the six is missed. **The rule that generalises: renumbering costs whatever
the number has been duplicated into**, so the same decision is right in one place and wrong in the
other, and neither answer is evidence for the other. This is
`counts written out in prose are a liability` read from the other end: the reason the version could
move is that it has exactly one gated copy set and no prose copies at all.

**11.134.6 THE VERSION AT OPEN IS `v0.6.0`, DERIVED THE TWO WAYS §14.0 REQUIRES.** The board query
for `Done` Chapters under epic 588 returns **0 of 43**; and the epic's own record has no closed
Chapter, `PLAN-0` (`#589`) being the Story that decomposed it rather than a Chapter that built
anything. **A band's baseline is taken at the transition, not at the first commit inside it**, which
is §14.0's own treatment of `v0.2.0`.

**11.134.7 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** It does not renumber any milestone: **M6 stays M6** and every
`M6-`, `M7-`, `M8-` and `M9-` task title is untouched, which is DR-029 §11.28.4 still standing. It
does not re-price the Plan view: DR-029's `L` at 9 to 13 weeks stands, and §11.36.7 already refused
to re-estimate at decomposition. It does not move scope between release bands, so it is **not a §8.3
amendment** and edits no scope list; it is a process ruling in DR-017's class. It does not touch the
major, which stays `0` until a public release whatever the feature set. And it does not discharge or
park a single clause of the Plan view's own criterion, all seven of which remain `NOT BUILT` or
`UNPERFORMED` (docs/12 §5.9).

### §11.135 DR-136 · A document that carries plan data declares a reader that understands plans

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-07**, on a finding PLAN-C/5 turned up while trying to write the
test its own brief asked for.

**11.135.1 THE FINDING: DR-019 BOUGHT A PROTECTION THAT WAS NEVER DELIVERED.** §11.18.1 identified a
real G5 item and described it precisely: *"`json_codec.dart` decodes `OffRackPlacement` as exactly
`locationId` and `mountNote` and re-encodes exactly those two, so a build that predates the Plan
view, opening a file that has plan pins, silently drops them on save."* §11.18.2(5) bought the
remedy, an `unknown` map on `Placement` and `Outlet`, and M3-I (`#568`) built it.

**IT DOES NOT CLOSE THAT HAZARD, AND BOTH IMPLEMENTING FILES SAY SO IN CAPITALS.**
`placement.dart`: *"RESERVED CONTAINER, NOT A HARVESTER. Nothing collects unrecognised SIBLING keys
... Harvesting siblings would be a different format and would need its own ruling (roadmap §8.3)."*
`json_codec.dart`'s `_unknownBag` repeats it. So the bag preserves what a writer deliberately puts
**inside** it, and `planPin` is a sibling key like any other. An older build still drops it.

**NEITHER FILE IS WRONG.** They implemented a reserved container, said exactly that, and named the
ruling a harvester would need. What went missing is that §11.18.2(5)'s remedy does not reach
§11.18.1's hazard, and nothing between the two noticed, because the field the protection was for
did not exist until PLAN-C. **This is `two documents agreeing is not verification` in its costliest
form: the ruling and the implementation agreed with each other and neither agreed with the hazard.**

**11.135.2 THE RULING.** A document that carries plan data **declares a higher
`minReaderVersion`**, so a build that does not understand plans opens it **read-only** and cannot
overwrite it. The silent loss becomes a visible refusal, which is what this corpus does everywhere
else.

- **`kSchemaVersion` moves to 5.** `kMinReaderVersion` stays at **3**.
- **`minReaderVersion` stops being written unconditionally.** It is `kMinReaderVersion` for an
  ordinary document and **5** for one carrying plan data.
- **Plan data means an underlay or a pin**, and nothing else. Any entry in `document.underlays`, or
  any `planPin` on a `Rack`, an `Outlet` or an `OffRackPlacement`.

**11.135.3 WHY THE SCHEMA MOVES WHEN THE FORMAT'S OWN TRIGGER SAYS IT NEED NOT, which is the part
worth keeping.** `json_codec.dart` states the trigger twice in the same words: an advance is owed
when a change is not *"byte-invisible to existing files (CR-117)"*. **These additions are
byte-invisible.** Every `.rmpj` on disk has no underlays and no pins, so every one re-encodes byte
for byte, and by that trigger alone nothing would move.

**The stamp needs a NUMBER, and that is a second limb the trigger did not have.** A conditional
`minReaderVersion` of 5 written by a build declaring `kSchemaVersion` 4 would make this build refuse
its own file the moment it wrote a pin. So the schema advances **because the format gained a
capability `minReaderVersion` must be able to name**, which is a different reason from bytes moving
and is now written down as one.

**11.135.4 WHAT IT COSTS, NAMED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED.** Two things, and the second is the one a
user will actually meet.

- **Every document re-saved by this build declares schema 5**, so a colleague on an older build
  opens it read-only. That is the standing cost of any schema advance and DR-134 paid it nine days
  ago; it is stated here because this ruling is the one that chose to incur it.
- **A project becomes read-only for older builds the moment somebody drops ONE pin.** That is the
  trade taken deliberately: under DR-006 this is an internal tool whose users share files, and a
  colleague who cannot save is a colleague who asks, while a colleague whose save quietly deleted an
  afternoon of pinning is a colleague who finds out on site.

**11.135.5 WHAT IT DOES NOT RULE.** **It does not make the `unknown` bag a harvester**, and that
stays exactly where `placement.dart` left it: a different format, owing its own ruling. This closes
the hazard by refusing the write rather than by preserving the field, which is a narrower fix and
leaves the general problem open for the ruling that wants it. **It does not extend the stamp to
`Location.riseAllowance`**, which is an ordinary additive optional field on `tia570Grade`'s
precedent (DR-024) and `MediaTypeDef.aliases`'s before it: an older build drops it, as it already
drops those, and a scalar somebody can retype is not a drawing somebody spent an afternoon making.
**It does not add a migration that changes data**: `migrateV4ToV5` re-stamps and touches nothing,
because there is nothing in a v4 file for it to convert.

### §11.136 DR-137 · Underlay members are deflated, because a floorplan is line art and line art is not a photograph

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-07**, on a measurement taken against the first real plan set this
project has ever been given: an 18-sheet residential permit set, ARCH D (36 x 24 inches), supplied
as `docs/reference/House-Plan.pdf` and **deliberately never committed** (§11.136.6).

**11.136.1 WHAT PLAN-B DECIDED, AND WHICH HALF OF IT WAS MEASURED.** `container.dart` stores binary
members uncompressed, and its header gives four reasons. Measurement falsifies two of them.

| The reason as written | What measuring found |
|---|---|
| *"A PNG or JPEG is already compressed; deflating it again buys ~nothing"* | **False.** Every one of the 18 pages deflates: 7.0% to 34.3%, mean **16.0%** over the set. **The floor plans deflate BEST** (A-2.1 at **34.3%**), because a floor plan is mostly white and JPEG's entropy coding leaves that redundancy on the table. The dense structural-notes sheets deflate worst, at 7% |
| *"costs real time at level 9 on a multi-megabyte architectural page"* | **False.** Level 6 on the realistic single import (A-2.1, 286,197 bytes) is **5.7 ms**. Even the pathological case, all 18 sheets at once, is **232 ms**, and AC-006 §5 already moved save to `Isolate.run` |
| *"the underlay's bytes appear VERBATIM, so CR-117 on the zip path does not depend on the deflate implementation for the largest member"* | **True, and it is the only surviving argument.** See §11.136.3 |
| *"the file opens in any zip tool with the architect's original page inside it"* | **Not affected by the choice.** Every zip tool inflates a deflated entry. This reason argued for nothing |

**THE GENERALISATION IS THE POINT AND IT IS NOT ABOUT ZIP.** *"Already-compressed rasters do not
deflate"* is a true statement about **photographs** and a false one about **line art on white**,
and this product receives line art on white. The rule was imported from the domain where it is
right into the domain where it is wrong, and it read as self-evident in both.

**11.136.2 THE CHANGE.** Container members are written with the same deflate level as
`document.json`: the existing `kContainerDeflateLevel`, which is `DeflateLevel.bestCompression`
and therefore **9**. No new constant, and the per-member `CompressionType.none` override is
removed rather than replaced, so "every entry is treated alike" is expressed by the absence of a
branch.

**MEASURED IN THE CONTAINER RATHER THAN IN `zlib`**, because the container is the artifact and the
raw ratio is only a proxy for it:

| `whole_house.rmpj` plus | STORE (before) | DEFLATE (after) | Saved |
|---|---|---|---|
| A-2.1, the sheet a user imports | 331,776 | **234,165** | **97,611** |
| all 18 sheets | 9,769,984 | **8,235,004** | **1,534,980** |

CR-117 was re-checked on the real member rather than on a fixture: the underlay round-trips byte
for byte, and `write(read(bytes)) == bytes` holds on the container that carries it.

**THIS CLAUSE SAID "level 6" IN ITS FIRST DRAFT, WHICH WAS A CLAIM ABOUT A CONSTANT MADE WITHOUT
READING IT**, in the same session that added `a wrong ruling ID resolves` to the bundle for
precisely that shape of error. The measured difference is immaterial and is recorded so the
choice is not mistaken for a considered one: level 9 saves **34.3%** in **6.2 ms** on the realistic
import against level 6's **34.1%** in **5.7 ms**. Level 1 is the only level that trades materially,
at 28.4% in 2.1 ms, and it was offered and declined.

**11.136.3 THE SURVIVING OBJECTION IS ANSWERED BY AN EXPOSURE THAT ALREADY EXISTS.** CR-117 on the
zip path now depends on the deflate implementation reproducing identical output for the underlay as
well as for the document. **That dependency is not new**: `document.json` has been deflated in this
same container since PLAN-B, so a dependency bump that moved the deflate stream already broke the
round-trip. This widens an existing surface rather than opening a new one, and
`container_identity_test.dart` is the thing that would fail, loudly, on the day it moves.

**11.136.4 THE RASTERISATION RESOLUTION IS BOUNDED ABOVE BY THE SOURCE, WHICH IS NOT WHAT PLAN-D/3
ASSUMED.** `#625` frames the resolution as a three-way trade between legibility at working zoom,
AC-006's budget and the asymmetric PDF cost PLAN-A/3 measured. **For a raster-backed PDF there is
no trade.** Every page of this set is a single full-page `DCTDecode` image, 2160 x 1440 px on a
36 x 24 inch sheet: **60 dpi**, with **zero fonts and zero vector content in the entire file**.
Rasterising above 60 dpi upsamples:

| Rasterised at | Pixels | Bytes | Information gained |
|---|---|---|---|
| 60 dpi (native) | 2160 x 1440 | 279.5 KB | the source |
| 96 dpi | 3456 x 2304 | 506.7 KB (1.8x) | **none** |
| 150 dpi | 5400 x 3600 | 1122.6 KB (4.0x) | **none** |
| 300 dpi | 10800 x 7200 | 3614.7 KB (12.9x) | **none** |

**AND 60 DPI IS ENOUGH**, which was checked by looking rather than by asserting. At 1:1 on A-2.1
the room names, the dimension strings (`15'-8 1/2"`), the window callouts (`3052`), the stair
counts (`Up 16R`) and the annotations (`Pocket Office`, `Drop Zone`) are all legible. At the
sheet's 1/4 inch = 1 foot scale, 60 dpi is **15 px per foot**, so **one pixel is 0.8 real inches**.
An installer needs to know which wall a drop is in, not which inch of it.

**So the rule is: never rasterise above the source's own effective resolution.** For a vector PDF
`#625`'s trade is real and stands. For a raster-backed one it is a lookup.

**11.136.5 A PLAN MAKES THE FILE SMALLER, WHICH INVERTS docs/15 §2.** That section rejected base64
on an estimate: *"a 2 MB PNG becomes roughly 2.7 MB of inline text"*, a 35% inflation, and admitted
*"the zip path's real number has never been taken"*. Taken:

| | Bytes |
|---|---|
| `whole_house.rmpj` today, plain JSON | 745,646 |
| the same document plus A-2.1 as an underlay, as a container | **234,165** |

**Adding a floorplan makes the project file 69% SMALLER than it was without one**, because the
underlay flips the format from plain JSON to a container and the JSON then deflates **16.3x**
(745,646 to 45,734). AC-006 re-justified plain JSON against a corrected ~600 KB figure;
`whole_house` is over that today at 728 KB and lands **far under** it the moment a plan is added,
which is the opposite of what the budget was braced for. All 18 sheets as underlays is 8,235,004
bytes, almost all of it image: the document is effectively free inside its own container.

**11.136.6 THE PLAN SET IS NOT COMMITTED, AND THE REASON IS GIT RATHER THAN SIZE.** It carries a
licensed engineer's seal and licence number, the firm's name, the builder's mark and an address
whose redaction covers the address and none of the rest. **DR-036's public GPLv3 release is
pending, and a public release publishes every commit ever made rather than the current tree**, so a
plan set committed today and deleted tomorrow ships anyway. `.gitignore` refuses
`docs/reference/*.pdf` at the top level only, which leaves the seven manufacturer drawings under
`keystone/` tracked. **The measurements above are the artifact**, with the method beside them in
docs/12 §5.9.5 so anybody can re-run them against their own sheet.

**11.136.7 WHAT IT DOES NOT RULE.** **It does not settle PDF rasterisation**, which still needs
pdfium vendored and a page picker built, and `PLAN-D/3` stays open for exactly that. **It does not
adopt the shortcut this file makes visible**: because every page here is one full-page image, the
JPEG could be extracted without rasterising at all, which is faster and lossless and works only
for this structure. A vector PDF breaks it and DR-029 bought PDF import generally, so pdfium
remains necessary and the extraction is at most an optimisation with a fallback behind it. **It
does not generalise from one plan set to all of them**: n is one, the user reports it
representative of what this trade is usually given, and that is trade knowledge rather than a
census. The deflate change is safe either way, since a member that will not compress simply does
not.

### §11.137 DR-138 · The page a PDF already contains is lifted, not re-drawn, and pdfium waits for a PDF that needs it

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-07.** `PLAN-D/1` chose pdfium via `pdfrx` (DR-037 §11.36.8, docs/12
§5.9.4.1) and recorded two things as **UNVERIFIED**: the Dart wrapper's licence, and whether its
build fetches pdfium or accepts a vendored one. Verifying them refuses the choice twice.

**11.137.1 THE LICENCE IS FINE AND THE BUILD IS NOT.** `pdfrx`, `pdfrx_engine`, `pdfium_dart` and
`pdfium_flutter` are all **MIT**, which is clean under DR-036. But **every route obtains pdfium by
downloading it at build time**: 2.3.0 and later through Dart native assets, which
*"downloads binaries from bblanchon/pdfium-binaries"*, and earlier versions through a CMake
download, which is the same mechanism this corpus already records for `printing` (docs/03 §10.1).

**CR-100 REFUSES EXACTLY THAT, IN ITS OWN WORDS**: the pdfium binaries are *"vendored into the repo
rather than downloaded at build time (a network-fetched binary in a signed release is a
supply-chain and reproducibility problem, not just a CI problem)"*. So the package chosen to make
the vendoring *"one problem paid once"* is a package that cannot accept a vendored binary.

**AND A SECOND, INDEPENDENT REFUSAL.** `pdfrx` 2.x requires **Flutter 3.47 / Dart 3.13**; this repo
is pinned at **3.44.4 / Dart 3.12.2** and the pin is a gate. Either refusal alone ends it.

**11.137.2 THE MEASUREMENT THAT CHANGED THE ANSWER.** DR-137 §11.136.7 recorded a shortcut and
declined to adopt it: because every page of the plan set is one full-page image, the JPEG could be
lifted out without rasterising. It was declined as *"at most an optimisation with a fallback behind
it"*. **The fallback has now been priced, and it costs a ruling amendment, a pin bump and a
vendored binary.** That changes what the shortcut is.

**IT IS ALSO STRUCTURALLY DETECTABLE RATHER THAN GUESSED**, which is the half that makes it safe.
All 18 pages normalise to one content stream:

```
q BT N N Td ET Q q N N N N N N cm /imgN Do Q
```

An empty text block, then a single `Do` drawing one image XObject across the page. The test is a
**parse**, not a heuristic: exactly one XObject in `/Resources`, that object is `/Subtype /Image`,
the content stream shows exactly one `Do` naming it, no text-showing or path-painting operator
appears, and the `cm` maps it to the MediaBox.

**11.137.3 THE RULING.** The floorplan import **lifts the embedded image when the page is one
full-page image, and refuses otherwise**, naming what it would take. `PLAN-D/3`'s page picker ships
now over the lifted pages.

**LIFTING IS NOT A CHEAPER RASTERISATION, IT IS A BETTER ONE.** Rasterising a page whose only
content is a JPEG decodes that JPEG and re-encodes the result, which loses a generation and cannot
gain a pixel: DR-137 §11.136.4 already established that rasterising above the source is pure cost.
Lifting is **lossless by construction** and produces the exact bytes the architect's office
exported. So on this input class the pure-Dart path is not a compromise pending pdfium; it is the
outcome pdfium would be used to approximate.

**11.137.4 WHAT IS REFUSED, AND IT IS REFUSED OUT LOUD.** Anything the lifter cannot prove it
understands: a page with vector or text content, more than one image, an image filter other than
`DCTDecode`, or a cross-reference stream, which is where PDF 1.5 and later may hide objects the
lifter would have to decompress to see. Each returns its own error naming the reason, on
`PdfImportNotAvailableError`'s precedent (DR-029 §11.28.5): **a refusal that says "not supported"
would tell somebody the product decided something it has not.**

**11.137.5 WHAT IT DOES NOT RULE, AND THE HONEST WEAKNESS.** **It does not cancel pdfium**, and
DR-037 §11.36.2's page picker is unchanged. A vector PDF, which is what a different office's export
preset would produce, falls through to a refusal and reinstates the manual conversion step for that
file, which is precisely the step DR-029 spent 2 to 3 weeks buying out. **That is the cost of this
ruling and it is not hidden**: pdfium arrives when a real file needs it, at a price this ruling does
not change, and CR-100 will still be waiting with the vendoring problem it has always described.
**n is one.** The user reports the set representative; that is trade knowledge and not a census, and
the refusal path exists because it may be wrong.

**11.137.6 IT DOES NOT MOVE THE STORED FORMAT.** `PlanUnderlay.format` keeps its two values
(DR-029 §11.28.12), the lifted bytes go through `importFloorplanBytes` unchanged, and every control
`PLAN-D/4` built runs on them: sniff by content, the declared-size caps before any decode, and the
alpha flatten. **A lifted page is an untrusted image like any other**, and it is not exempted from
one check on the grounds that this product produced it.

### §11.138 DR-139 · The marquee CR-102 ruled is built once and adopted on all three canvases, and the row that promised it was vacuous

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-07**, on a finding from `PLAN-E/1`'s reuse census.

**11.138.1 THE PROMISE, AND WHAT WAS BEHIND IT.** docs/15 §6's gesture table gives the Plan editor
*"Pan, zoom, marquee-select | Identical to the other two canvases (AC-016 #23, `CanvasIntent`)"*.
Pan and zoom are exactly that, verified by `PLAN-E/1`'s spike, which drives both through the shipped
`ViewportController` without touching it. **Marquee-select is not, because neither of the other two
canvases has a marquee.** CR-102 is normative, rules it left-drag in every view, and specifies the
CAD window/cross convention: left to right selects fully contained with a solid band, right to left
selects intersecting with a dashed band. Nothing implements any of it.

**11.138.2 THE CENSUS THAT FOUND IT LOOKED PAST THE WORD, AND THE WORD WOULD NOT HAVE BEEN ENOUGH.**
Grepping `marquee` over the tree returns comments and nothing else, every one of them saying the
gesture is deferred, and a reader could fairly conclude the machinery was present and merely unbound. **The
finding is one layer down: every `SelectMode` call in `lib/` passes exactly one id.**
`SelectionController` holds a `Set<Uuid>`, supports `add` and `subtract`, and is written against a
multi-selection; `add` and `subtract` are reachable only by Ctrl+click, and **no gesture in this
product has ever put more than one thing into that set at once.**

**A MULTI-SELECTION NOTHING CAN MULTI-SELECT IS INVISIBLE TO A CENSUS BY NAME**, because the type is
present, correct and tested. This is the fourth entry in the running list at §11.36.5 of a design
document and a ruling agreeing with each other without either having read the model, and it is the
first where the disagreement is about a **capability** rather than a field: `MediaTypeDef.maxLength`,
`unknown` on `Placement` and `Location.riseAllowance` were all names that resolved to nothing, and
this one is a name that resolves to something that has never been used.

**11.138.3 THE RULING: BUILD IT ONCE, ADOPT IT ON ALL THREE.** Not on the plan alone, and not
deferred behind a corrected sentence. Three options were put and the other two were declined:

| Declined | Why |
|---|---|
| Build it on the plan only | It is where the gesture pays most, the 60-drop rough-in being the design case, and that is an argument for building it FIRST rather than for building it ONLY. It would also make docs/15 §6's *"identical to the other two canvases"* false in the other direction, which is not an improvement |
| Ship the plan without it and correct docs/15 | Keeps `PLAN-E/2` at its estimate and costs sixty Ctrl+clicks to select a plan's worth of pins, which is the same failure AC-048's bulk-entry bar and DR-020 §11.19.2(5)'s tally surface both already exist to refuse at the other end of the job |

**CR-102's ENTIRE CONTENT IS THAT THE GESTURE IS UNIFORM ACROSS VIEWS.** It exists because two design
documents specified different buttons, and it settled the disagreement by ruling one. Discharging it
three separate times, in three chapters, months apart, is how a uniformity ruling stops being one:
the second implementation copies the first and the third copies whichever it happened to read. **The
cost of building it once is paid at the moment the ruling is easiest to satisfy, which is before any
of the three has one.**

**11.138.4 THIS IS NOT A SCOPE AMENDMENT, AND THE DISTINCTION MATTERS UNDER §8.3.** Roadmap §2 is the
scope list, and marquee is not a line on it: it is behaviour inside editors that are already scoped,
already designed and already ruled. Nothing moves between release bands and no Epic changes Saga.
**What this ruling does is assign never-built work to a named chapter**, which is the ordinary act
§8.8 describes, not the amendment §8.3 governs. A reader looking for a scope change here will not
find one.

**11.138.5 IT IS ITS OWN CHAPTER, `#848` (`PLAN-E/6`), AND DELIBERATELY NOT PART OF `PLAN-E/2`.**
`PLAN-E/2` is *"place, drag and select pins"* and was estimated as that. Cross-canvas work touching
two shipped surfaces carries regression risk that has nothing to do with pins, and folding it into
E/2 would be exactly the invisible growth `PLAN-E/1` exists to expose. **The row grows and the growth
is a line somebody can read**, which is the whole difference between an estimate that moved and an
estimate that was wrong.

**THE RISK WAS STATED BEFORE THE CHOICE WAS MADE**, and it is recorded here rather than softened: the
option chosen is the one that touches the most shipped code, and `PLAN-E/1`'s own brief warns that a
coupling discovered late is what makes this row grow. The judgement is that a marquee expressed
against `CanvasIntentHandler` is small, because the spike showed that interface carries a complete
drag in scene space with no rack or schematic term in it, and that the hard part is CR-102's
window/cross discrimination, which is one comparison on drag direction.

**11.138.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** **Not the band's appearance** beyond CR-102's own solid/dashed
distinction: line weight, colour and whether the band dims what it will catch are UI/UX and are the
user's, unasked here. **Not gesture parity generally**: this ruling is about one gesture that was
ruled and never built, and it does not open a review of what else the three canvases do differently.
**Not the Plan view's own gesture set**, which docs/15 §6 governs and which `PLAN-E/2` builds.

**11.138.7 Derived edits owed and made with this ruling.** docs/15 §6's gesture table splits its
combined row so pan and zoom keep their verified claim and marquee names `#848`; docs/09 §4's Plan
editor checklist row drops *"drag-preview"* from the list of reused machinery (docs/12 §5.9.7.3 records why
it is not reused) and gains the marquee row; docs/12 §5.9.7 carries the
measurement.

### §11.139 DR-140 · The rack is pinned from the unpinned strip, because nothing in PLAN-E pinned it at all

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-08**, on a hole `PLAN-E/2`'s decomposition check found before any
code was written.

**11.139.1 THE RACK CARRIES A PIN, THE DESIGN CALLS IT MANDATORY, AND NO GESTURE PUT ONE THERE.**
docs/15 §3.4 lists three carriers and marks the rack's *"**Not optional to the design.** A home run
is measured *from the rack*. Without the rack pinned, no length on that plan is derivable at all"*.
`PLN-003` exists to say so. The epic's exit criterion requires *"the rack plus every drop of a real
rough-in"* to carry a pin.

**docs/15 §6's gesture table has four rows and not one of them pins a rack.** The palette and
staging-bin drag places a **device**; the drop-table fast path pins an **outlet**; the unpinned strip
lists **devices**; pan, zoom and marquee select nothing new. `PLAN-C` built `Rack.planPin` and
`SetPlanPinCommand` accepts `PinCarrier.rack`, so the model and the command have been ready since
2026-09-07 and **the only missing piece was somebody able to press it.**

**11.139.2 THE SHAPE OF THE MISS, WHICH IS THE FOURTH OF ITS KIND.** This is
*"ask what produces each task's input"* again: five `PLAN-E` chapters between them build a canvas, a
palette drop, a fast path, a strip and a shell home, and none of them creates a rack pin. Each
chapter is coherent; the set has a hole, and the hole is only visible from outside any one of them.
The precedents are M4's five tasks that built a grid and never created a port, `MediaTypeDef
.maxLength`, and `Location.riseAllowance` (§11.36.5).

**IT IS A HARD BLOCK ON THE EXIT CRITERION AND NOT A POLISH ITEM**, which is why it is ruled now
rather than noted. A plan whose rack is unpinned yields no `planLowerBound` anywhere, so `PLAN-G`
derives nothing, `PLAN-H`'s `T1.01` prints callouts with no lengths behind them, and `PLAN-J`'s drill
puts a printed sheet in front of a stranger with the one measurement it promised missing.

**11.139.3 THE RULING: THE UNPINNED STRIP LISTS EVERYTHING PINNABLE, AND THE RACK IS ONE OF THEM.**
docs/15 §6 currently says the strip *"lists devices in this plan's location that carry no pin"*. It
lists **every unpinned carrier** in that location instead: off-rack devices, outlets and racks alike.
Dragging one out of the strip onto the plan pins it, which is the gesture the strip already implies
and which `SetPlanPinCommand` already performs.

Two options were declined:

| Declined | Why |
|---|---|
| A dedicated *"Place rack"* control | Most discoverable for the first pin, which is the one that unlocks every length. But docs/15 §6's layout paragraph says in terms that there is **no fourth region and no plan-specific palette**, and a control that exists only to place one kind of thing is a second mechanism for a job the strip is already shaped for |
| Drag it out of the left-hand location tree | Reuses a region that exists and already shows the hierarchy a rack belongs to. But CR-112 makes that tree **read-only with an "edit in `Project ▸ Locations…`" affordance**, and turning a read-only panel into a drag source changes its character for one case |

**THE STRIP IS THE RIGHT HOME BECAUSE OF WHAT IT MAKES THE COUNT MEAN.** `PLAN-E/4`'s brief says the
strip *"is the difference between a plan that is trusted and a plan that is 80% complete without
saying so"*. A strip that omits the rack is exactly the 80%-complete plan it was built to refuse: the
one absent pin that costs every length would be the one thing the count could not see. **One
mechanism, one place to look, and a count that means "everything this plan still owes."**

**11.139.4 THE COUNT IS THEREFORE A COUNT OF CARRIERS AND NOT OF DEVICES, AND `PLAN-E/4` MUST TEST
IT ON A DOCUMENT WHERE THE TWO DIFFER.** That chapter's own brief already warns about a count that
counts the wrong thing, citing the status bar that read *"0 pathways"* the keystroke after somebody
made one and whose own test pinned the wrong number on a two-pathway document. **This ruling creates
exactly that hazard on purpose**: a plan holding three unpinned devices and one unpinned rack has a
device count of three and a carrier count of four, and a strip built from `doc.devices` alone passes
every test that does not contain a rack. Assert on a document where the two answers differ.

**11.139.5 `PLN-002` AND `PLN-003` STAY AS THEY ARE.** They are separate advisories and they remain
separate: `PLN-002` counts unpinned devices and outlets, `PLN-003` fires on the missing rack pin
specifically, and the reason for keeping them apart is that they have different remedies and
different severities of consequence. The strip is a **surface**, not a rule, and it may show what two
rules report without merging them. Nothing in §9's four advisories changes.

**11.139.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** **Not the strip's appearance**: whether a rack row is visually
distinguished from a device row, and how, is UI/UX and is the user's, unasked here. **Not whether a
rack may be pinned on more than one underlay**, which is the same question every carrier already
answers by holding exactly one `PlanPin`, and which no chapter has raised. **Not the order of the
strip's contents.**

**11.139.7 Derived edits owed and made with this ruling.** docs/15 §6's strip paragraph changes
"devices" to every unpinned carrier and gains the rack's drag; §6's gesture table gains the strip
drag as a row, since it is a gesture and the table is where gestures live; docs/09 §4's `PLAN-E`
checklist row names it; docs/12 §5.9.8 records the decomposition hole and how it was found.

### §11.140 DR-141 · A pin arms one drop at a time, and the fast path is the strip rather than the table

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-08**, on a question `PLAN-E/3`'s brief leaves open and which decides
whether that chapter is worth building.

**11.140.1 THE BRIEF SAYS WHAT THE GESTURE IS AND NOT WHAT FOLLOWS IT.** docs/15 §6: *"Click an
outlet in the Structure editor's drop table, then click the plan. Pins that outlet. This is the fast
path for a 60-drop rough-in."* **What happens after that click is unspecified**, and sixty drops means
sixty pins, so the answer is the difference between a fast path and a shortcut.

**11.140.2 THE RULING: ONE ARM, ONE PIN, AND THE MODE STAYS VISIBLE.** Pinning the armed drop leaves
the mode **on with nothing armed**. The chip stays up saying so and `Esc` dismisses it. Nothing is
ever armed that the user did not explicitly choose.

**AUTO-ADVANCE WAS OFFERED AND DECLINED**, and the reasoning is recorded because it is the more
obvious design: pin, advance to the next unpinned outlet in table order, chip reads *"Next: D-014"*,
sixty drops become sixty clicks with no view change. **It was declined for the failure mode rather
than for the ergonomics**: a mis-click pins the wrong drop **and** advances the queue, so the
recovery is an undo plus a re-arm, and a person going fast is exactly the person who will not notice
which subject the chip had moved to. An auto-advancing queue is a machine for producing confidently
wrong pins on a drawing an installer will trust.

**11.140.3 THE COST OF THIS CHOICE, STATED PLAINLY AND NOT SOFTENED.** Two acts per drop rather than
one, and `PLAN-E/3`'s own brief names the failure it is guarding against: *"an installer closing out
sixty runs wants one table they tab down, not sixty inspector visits."* **Across a tab boundary this
ruling IS sixty round trips**, which is that failure with a different shape, and the chapter's claim
to be *"the reason the feature is usable rather than merely present"* would be false.

**11.140.4 IT IS NOT SIXTY ROUND TRIPS, BECAUSE DR-140 ALREADY PUT THE PICKER IN THE PLAN VIEW.** The
unpinned strip lists every unpinned carrier in this plan's location and a drag out of it pins that
row (§11.139). So the ordinary loop is **pick from the strip, click the plan**: two acts, no view
change, every pin deliberate, and the strip's count shrinking by one each time is the progress
indicator an auto-advancing chip would have had to invent.

**THE TWO CHAPTERS THEREFORE OVERLAP, AND THIS RULING SAYS WHICH IS PRIMARY.** `PLAN-E/4`'s strip is
**the** pinning workflow. `PLAN-E/3`'s Structure-table arm is the **secondary entry point**, for
somebody already in the Structure editor working down a drop list, and it is worth building for that
reason and not as the sixty-drop path. **The brief's own framing is superseded here**: the fast path
is the strip.

**AND THAT REDUCES `PLAN-E/3`**, which is a scope observation rather than an amendment: the chapter
builds an arm controller, one entry point on the drop table and the plan-side pin, and it no longer
has to carry a queue, an ordering rule or a next-subject indicator. Roadmap §2 is untouched.

**11.140.5 THE ARM IS A MODE, NOT A REQUEST, AND THAT IS A DIFFERENT TYPE FROM THE ONE PRECEDENT.**
`SchematicRevealController` is the existing cross-tab mechanism (CR-105's *"clicking it switches to
the schematic with that device selected"*) and it is **one-shot**: `take()` empties it so one click
reveals once. This is not that. The mode outlives the pin, because *"stays on with nothing armed"* is
what keeps the chip up telling the user where to go next, and a mode that ended silently after each
pin would be indistinguishable from one that had failed. **`Esc` is the only thing that ends it**,
which is `PLAN-E/3`'s own requirement that what is armed, what happens next and how to stop are all
visible.

**11.140.6 THE ROW IS NOT THE SUBJECT, AND THE JOIN ALREADY EXISTS.** The drop table's rows are keyed
by `linkId`; a pin hangs on an `Outlet`. The join is `Link.structureOrigin.outletId`, which
`derived/structure_matrix.dart` already walks. Two consequences the chapter must handle rather than
discover: **a link with no `structureOrigin` has no outlet to pin** and is refused by name, and **a
four-gang plate is four rows and one outlet**, so arming any of its rows arms the same subject and
the strip must count outlets rather than rows or its number is wrong in the direction that flatters.

**11.140.7 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** **Not the chip's appearance or wording**, which is UI/UX and is
the user's, unasked. **Not whether the strip is orderable**, which §11.139.6 already left open. **Not
the tab switch**: arming from the Structure editor has nowhere to switch to until `PLAN-E/5` puts the
Plan view in the strip, so `PLAN-E/3` builds the controller and both ends, and the shell wiring is
`PLAN-E/5`'s.

> **AND "BOTH ENDS" WAS WRONG, WHICH A GATE ESTABLISHED RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT.** The drop table's
> half was built: `StructureEditorActions.onPinOnPlan`, threaded to a row, opened by a secondary tap,
> two cases green. `actions_have_callers_test.dart` then refused the whole thing, because **nothing
> in `lib/` supplies one**. That gate exists for M3-H/5, where `OutletsActions.onRemoveGang` had a
> command, an app-side implementation, tests for both and no caller, and it had just caught the same
> shape again.
>
> **The call site could have been reworded until the regex stopped matching**, and that is exactly
> what the gate is built to make somebody notice they are doing. The gesture really is unreachable: a
> menu item that arms a mode whose only surface is a view the shell does not mount is a control that
> does nothing, which is DR-091's own rule one level down. **So the producer moves to `PLAN-E/5`**,
> where the Plan view gets a home and the whole path becomes reachable in one commit rather than two.
>
> **THE GENERAL POINT IS ABOUT THE DECOMPOSITION AND NOT ABOUT THIS CALLBACK.** `PLAN-E/2`, `/3` and
> `/4` all build behaviour for a view `PLAN-E/5` mounts, so each of them ends with code the product
> cannot reach. That is legal and is stated in each chapter, but it means **`PLAN-E/5` is not a small
> wiring chapter**: it is the one that makes three chapters' work true, and it should be read that way
> when it is scheduled.

### §11.141 DR-142 · What the unpinned strip lists, and the two location fields a device already had

**Ruled 2026-09-08 at `PLAN-E/4`'s decomposition.** DR-140 §11.139 settled *what* the strip is for
and left *what it contains* to this chapter. The sentence it left is docs/15 §6's: **"a strip along
the bottom lists everything in this plan's location that could carry a pin and does not, with a
count."** Every clause of that sentence turns out to hide a decision, and the model makes each one
ambiguous rather than obvious.

**11.141.1 THIS CHAPTER'S OWN BRIEF PREDICTED THE SHAPE OF THE MISTAKE AND NOT ITS LOCATION.** The
board item warns, in terms, of *"the count that counts the wrong thing"*, citing the status bar that
read **`0 pathways`** the keystroke after somebody made one because it counted only pathways with
drops in them. DR-140 then supplied a second instance deliberately: a strip built from `doc.devices`
alone gets the count wrong on any document with an unpinned rack. **Reading the model turned up three
more**, and the fourth is a defect already shipped. The warning was right about the class and had no
way to name the members.

**11.141.2 "UNPINNED" MEANS NO PIN AT ALL, NOT "NO PIN ON THIS UNDERLAY".** A carrier has exactly one
`planPin` field, and a `PlanPin` names the underlay it stands on. So a device pinned on `Level 1` and
listed as unpinned while `Level 2` is open is not merely a wrong row: **dragging it out would move
its pin off `Level 1`**, silently, as the answer to a gesture that presented itself as adding
something. The per-underlay reading is only available at all because the model cannot express it, and
a surface must not offer a state the document has no way to hold.

The cost is stated rather than hidden: on a two-plan project, `Level 2`'s strip reads zero while
`Level 2` has no pins on it, because everything is pinned on `Level 1`. **That is the truth**, and the
remedy is the underlay's own emptiness, which is visible on the canvas the strip sits under.

**11.141.3 AN UNDERLAY WITH NO LOCATION HAS NO FILTER, AND ITS STRIP LISTS EVERY UNPINNED CARRIER.**
`PlanUnderlay.locationId` is nullable and the model says why in its own words: *"an underlay with no
location is perfectly ordinary: a site plan depicts no room."* Three readings were available and two
are wrong for reasons worth keeping:

- **Nothing**, on "no location matches no carrier". A site plan would report a count of **zero**
  while nothing on it is pinned, which is the 80%-complete plan this strip exists to refuse, arrived
  at from the opposite direction.
- **Only carriers whose location is also null**, joining unknown to unknown. That is G4's forbidden
  move (`CR-114`): `null` is *unknown*, never a value, and two unknowns are not equal to each other.
- **Everything unpinned**, which is what ships. It is **not** a null-join: an underlay with no
  location is not a plan of an unknown room, it is a plan that is not scoped to a room, and a filter
  that is absent filters nothing.

**11.141.4 A CARRIER WHOSE OWN LOCATION IS UNKNOWN IS A COUNT AND NOT A ROW.** On a plan that *does*
name a room, a device with `locationId == null` cannot be attributed to it. Listing it as a row would
invite pinning a second-floor speaker onto `Level 1` and calling it placed; dropping it silently is
the `0 pathways` defect exactly. **G4 gives the third answer and it is already this repo's rule**:
report the unknown count rather than fabricating a total. `UnpinnedCarriers` therefore carries
`unlocatedCount` beside its rows, and a surface showing the rows shows that number.

**11.141.5 A DEVICE HAS TWO LOCATION FIELDS, AND `PLAN-E/2` LEFT THEM DISAGREEING.** This is a
shipped defect found by reading the model rather than by a failing test, and it is the reason this
subsection exists in a ruling about a strip.

`DeviceInstance.locationId` and `OffRackPlacement.locationId` are **different fields holding the same
value**. The model says so and says why: `AddStructureCommand` writes both, `RemoveLocationCommand`
clears both (DR-021 §11.20.2), and *"clearing one would leave the document disagreeing with itself."*

**`buildPlaceOnPlanCommand` writes one of them.** It hands `AddDeviceCommand` an `OffRackPlacement`
carrying the underlay's `locationId`, and `AddDeviceCommand.apply` constructs its `DeviceInstance`
with no `locationId` at all, because it has never had that parameter. So **every device dropped on a
plan since `PLAN-E/2` has a placement that says `Level 1` and an instance that says nothing.**

It is not inert. `derived/equipment_list.dart` reads `device.locationId`, so **the Equipment List
prints no room for a device dropped on a plan**, and there is no later repair: `locationId` is
deliberately not a `DeviceField` row, so no editing gesture can set it.

The fix is in `AddDeviceCommand` rather than at the call site: **when the placement names a room, the
instance is constructed with the same room**, derived from the command's own field, so a future
caller cannot forget what this one did. Rail, shelf and 0U placements name no room and are unchanged.

> **THE STRIP IS WHY THIS WAS FOUND AT ALL.** A surface that filters carriers by room has to choose
> which of two fields is the room, and asking that question is what exposed a writer that sets one.
> Neither choice would have been safe while the two disagreed: the strip would have been right about
> half the documents either way.

**11.141.6 THE ORDER AND THE RACK'S DISTINCTION ARE THE USER'S, AND A DEFAULT SHIPS RATHER THAN A
BLANK.** §11.139.6 left both open and this ruling does not close them. What ships is **rack first,
then outlets, then off-rack devices, each band by designator**, which is `pinsOnUnderlay`'s existing
