### §11.150 DR-151 · The bar is drawn, the uncalibrated sheet says so itself, and a placeholder string reached a deliverable

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-09**, at `PLAN-H/4`'s census.

**11.150.1 A PLACEHOLDER REACHED A CLIENT DELIVERABLE, AND THE GATE THAT EXISTS FOR THAT CLASS
CANNOT SEE A SHEET.** `PLAN-H/1` shipped `kPlanSheetScaleNote = 'PLAN SCALED TO FIT · SEE BAR'` on
`T1.01`, and there was no bar. It was written as a forward pointer to this chapter and it printed as
a instruction to a reader.

`unbuilt_copy_accuracy_test.dart` exists for exactly this failure and its own header says so: *"the
app's honest-absence copy is a factual claim about this codebase, so it is tested against this
codebase."* It scans `rackpal_ui` and `apps/rackpal`. **A sheet string lives in `rackpal_core` and is
invisible to it**, which is a gate's scope being narrower than its subject for the fifth time in this
epic, and the first where the surface it misses is *printed and handed to somebody*. In-app copy is
wrong until somebody clicks away; a sheet is wrong in a folder on a job site.

**The fix is this chapter, and the finding is the gate's reach.** `PLAN-H/5` inherits nothing here;
what is recorded is that sheet copy has no honest-absence gate, and that the two surfaces differ in
consequence rather than in kind.

**11.150.2 THE BRIEF'S PLAN FOR THE UNCALIBRATED CASE DOES NOT REACH THE READER.** `#643`: *"an
uncalibrated underlay gets no scale bar at all, not a bar with a guessed figure on it. G4, and
`PLN-001` is what tells the user why."*

`PLN-001` is a **finding**. It lands in the validation drawer and, at M6, on `T0.02 Exceptions and
Acknowledgements`. **A person holding the printed `T1.01` has neither**, and `SheetRole` has four
values today, none of them `T0.02`. The half of the brief that is right is that no bar may be drawn;
the half that does not work is who explains it.

**11.150.3 RULED: THE SHEET SAYS IT ITSELF.**

> `NOT TO SCALE · PLAN NOT CALIBRATED`

The drafting term for the fact, and the cause in the product's own words. **`NOT TO SCALE` is the
part that matters to the person holding it**, because it names the one thing they must not do with
the sheet, and the plan still locates every drop: pins and callouts work uncalibrated, which is
docs/15 §1's first job.

*The full `PLN-001` sentence with its count* was refused, and it was the closest call: DR-146
§11.145.6 put that sentence in core precisely so surfaces cannot drift. **But its count is a
designer's number.** `39 pins carry no measurable position` tells the person at the desk what a
calibration would buy; the installer holding the print can already find all thirty-nine, and a
sheet is read by the second person. *`NOT TO SCALE` alone* was refused for leaving a designer who
picks the sheet up unable to tell an uncalibrated plan from an unscalable one.

**11.150.4 RULED: ALTERNATING SEGMENTS, ENDS LABELLED.** Four equal divisions, filled and hollow
alternating, `0` at the left and the round total at the right.

**The alternation is the feature and not the decoration.** A plain rule can be read only at its full
length; a divided one can be read by eye at a quarter, a half, three quarters. It survives greyscale
by construction, being black and paper rather than two greys, which is the property AC-054's print
tests and PAL-1 gates everywhere else.

*Every division labelled* was refused on the sheet rather than on the principle: four more text runs
at 6.5 pt under a drawing, and on a 20 ft bar at ANSI B the intermediate numbers crowd each other.

**11.150.5 THE BAR'S LENGTH IS A ROUND NUMBER IN THE PROJECT'S UNITS, AND IS NEVER REFUSED FOR
SCALE.** A ladder of round values in `ProjectSettings.displayUnits` (CR-097 makes that field
authoritative), and the largest whose drawn length fits the budget wins. **When none fits, the
smallest is taken anyway**: a bar that is longer than a quarter of the sheet is still true, and a
bar refused for being awkward is a sheet with no bar on a plan that has a scale. The only refusal is
§11.150.3's.

**THE ARITHMETIC WAS ALREADY SEAMED.** `PlanSheet.factor` was carried out of `PLAN-H/1` with a doc
comment naming this chapter: *"the scale bar needs exactly this number times the calibration to know
how long a real foot is on this page, and a second fit computed there would be a second answer to one
question."* Points per nanometre is `factor / PlanScale.nanometresPerPixel`, computed once.

**11.150.6 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** Not a north arrow, which has no field on `PlanUnderlay` to
read. Not the per-plan device schedule (`PLAN-H/5`). Not the bar's own type size as a final figure,
which is `kCalloutTextPt`'s question and `PLAN-J`'s print to settle. And **not a gate for sheet
copy**: §11.150.1 records that the absence exists and prices nothing, because the honest scope of a
new gate is a question for whoever has met the failure twice rather than once.

---

### §11.151 DR-152 · The plan schedule projects the plan's own derivations, and it is set in columns because one column fails the exit criterion

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-09**, at `PLAN-H/5`'s census. `PLAN-H`'s last chapter, and the
fourth of its five briefs to describe something the tree does not hold.

**11.151.1 THE DERIVATION THE BRIEF NAMES DOES NOT CONTAIN THE ROWS.** `#644`: *"It is a PROJECTION
of the derivation the equipment list already uses, not a second table builder."*

**`EquipmentList` is one row per `DeviceInstance`** and its own header says so. A plan pins three
carriers (docs/15 §3.4) and **two of them are not devices**: an `Outlet` and a `Rack` appear in that
derivation nowhere at all. On the rough-in the exit criterion describes, outlets are most of what is
pinned, so the named source holds a minority of the rows.

**The principle the brief is protecting is right and the pointer is wrong**, which is the same shape
`#642` had one chapter earlier. CR-107 is the ruling behind it, and it is worth quoting because it is
about exactly this table: two entities carrying the same facts *"is guaranteed to diverge within one
week of real use: the drop schedule says 78 ft and the wiring schedule says 90 ft, and nobody knows
which to bill against."*

**11.151.2 RULED BY CONSTRUCTION: IT PROJECTS THE PLAN'S OWN DERIVATIONS.** The row subject is **a
pinned carrier**, and `PLAN-H/3` already built that set: `planPinsFor` enumerates it and
`planPinLabelsFor` resolves what each one prints. The schedule reuses both rather than walking the
three collections a third time.

Each column then reads what already exists: `Location.name` for the area, the callout's own
designator for the reference, and for the description whichever derivation owns that carrier:
`EquipmentRow` for a device, `plateFillOf` for an outlet, the rack's own height for the rack.
**Nothing here re-derives anything**, which is what "not a second table builder" was asking for.

**AND THE REFERENCE COLUMN IS THE JOIN.** It is the string the pill on the drawing prints, from one
function, so a reader going from a callout to a row cannot meet two spellings of one designator.

**11.151.3 RULED: EVERY CALLOUT RESOLVES, INCLUDING THE RACK.** The schedule's job is to turn a pill
into a thing. A reader who finds `RK-1` on the plan and nothing in the table beneath it has hit the
one dead end this sheet exists to prevent, and **the rack is the thing a stranger needs to find
first**. It costs one row.

*Drops only* was refused although it is truer to the sheet's name and to the standard's sample;
*a rack row set apart in its own band* was refused for adding a grouping concept to a table that has
none.

**11.151.4 RULED: THE BAND IS SET IN COLUMNS, AND THE MEASUREMENT IS WHY.** Measured on the real
sheet rather than estimated: `T1.01`'s drawing area is **1122 × 567 pt**, a schedule row is 12 pt and
its header 14.

| Rows | One column | Plan keeps |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 254 pt | 313 pt |
| 40 | 494 pt | 73 pt |
| 60 | 734 pt | **does not fit** |

**A single column fails the exit criterion's own scenario.** DR-037 §11.36.1 asks for *"the rack plus
every drop of a real rough-in"*, and sixty is the number this corpus has used for a rough-in since
AC-048. A layout that cannot print sixty rows is a layout that cannot meet the criterion it is under.

The band is 1122 pt wide and a four-field row needs roughly a quarter of it, so **four blocks sit
side by side**: sixty rows cost 194 pt instead of 734 and the plan keeps 373, more than half the
sheet. It is also how a floor-plan device schedule is actually set.

*Cap and count* was refused because forty references on the drawing would resolve to nothing.
*Let the plan shrink* was refused because at forty rows the plan is a 73 pt strip and at sixty it is
gone, which turns a locator into a table with a picture stuck on it.

**11.151.4a AMENDED THE SAME DAY: FOUR BLOCKS AND NOT THREE, BECAUSE THE CAP WAS MEASURED.** This
clause was ruled as *"three columns"* on a drafted claim that the cap then held *"roughly 180 rows"*.
**It held sixty.** The arithmetic multiplied rows-per-block by blocks in the wrong direction, and the
number went into a normative clause without being run.

Sixty is the exit criterion's own figure, so the overflow this clause calls a last resort fired on
the sixty-first drop of an ordinary house. Measured at `kPlanBandColumnMinPt`:

| Blocks | Block width | Cap | Plan keeps at 60 rows | DESCRIPTION |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 365 pt | 60 rows | 313 pt | 37 characters |
| 4 | 270 pt | 80 rows | 373 pt | 27 characters |

**Four blocks give the plan MORE of the sheet at every row count**, not less, because the band takes
what it needs: sixty rows over four blocks is fifteen rows down rather than twenty. What narrows is
the fields, and those are already named below as `PLAN-J`'s print to settle.

Ruled by the user on the measurement: four blocks. The refused readings are recorded for the same
reason the rest of this section records them. *Raise the ceiling to 0.55 of the drawing area* would
have capped at 72 and changed nothing on a sheet of sixty or fewer, but past 68 rows the table takes
more than half the sheet and the plan becomes the strip this clause already refused. *Leave the cap
at sixty and correct only the prose* was refused because a cap standing exactly on the criterion is a
cap that omits a row from the scenario it was measured against.

**A COUNTED OVERFLOW SURVIVES AS THE LAST RESORT.** Four blocks at the band's cap hold **eighty**
rows, a third more than the criterion asks for. Past that the sheet prints what fits and **states how
many it did not**, because a table quietly shorter than the plan above it is the failure this whole
chapter is about (G4).

**11.151.5 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** Not the column widths as final figures, which are `PLAN-J`'s
print to settle along with the callout and bar type sizes. Not a per-plan footage or count strip,
which nothing asks for. Not whether `T6.30`'s equipment list should gain outlet rows, which is a
question about that sheet and is M6's. And not the sheet's behaviour past the overflow cap beyond
stating the count, since a plan that reaches eighty pinned carriers is already half again the
criterion's own rough-in.

---

### §11.152 DR-153 · The rasteriser is built, the deferral ends on trade evidence, and the vector is kept rather than discarded

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-09**, immediately after `PLAN-H` closed. DR-138 §11.137.5 deferred
pdfium *"until a PDF needs it"*, DR-145 §11.144.5 kept the deferral when one did, and DR-148
§11.147.2 kept it a second time and wired the debt into the exit criterion. **This is the ruling that
ends it**, and it ends on the one thing all three said they did not have.

**11.152.1 THE EVIDENCE THE CORPUS WAS MISSING IS A POPULATION, AND IT CAME FROM THE TRADE.**
DR-145 §11.144.3 measured two real plan sets at opposite ends, one all raster and one all vector, and
refused to generalise from them in terms: *"nothing here says how the two classes are distributed
across the trade."* DR-138 §11.137.5 said the same thing more bluntly: *"**n is one.**"*

The user has now supplied the distribution. **Raster sets are the more common of the two and vector
plots are by no means uncommon**, and many plans arrive as CAD plots. That is trade knowledge rather
than a census, which is exactly what DR-138 said it was waiting for, and it settles the question both
prior rulings parked: the refused class is ordinary rather than exceptional. **DR-145 §11.144.4's
*"half the ordinary path is bought"* is no longer a note about a possibility.**

**AND THERE IS A SECOND REASON, WHICH IS ABOUT THE OUTPUT RATHER THAN THE INPUT.** The user's other
ground is that vector scales better on a sheet somebody is presented with. That is a print-quality
argument and it is independent of coverage: it would be true even if every plan imported today. It is
why §11.152.6 keeps the source page rather than discarding it, and it is not by itself an argument
for building a passthrough now (§11.152.7).

**11.152.2 THE MECHANISM IS UNCHANGED, BECAUSE BOTH ORIGINAL REFUSALS STILL HOLD.** Re-checked
rather than assumed. `pdfrx` and its siblings obtain pdfium by **downloading it at build time**,
which CR-100 forbids in its own words, and 2.x requires **Flutter 3.47** against a repo pinned at
3.44.4 by a gate (DR-138 §11.137.1). `printing` fetches the same way (docs/03 §10.1). Either refusal
alone still ends it, and both stand.

**A pure-Dart renderer is refused on the file itself.** DR-145 §11.144.7 put it on the record as *not
costed*; costing it is one measurement, and it is in that same ruling's table: **the CAD plot carries
39 fonts**. A renderer for that page is a font rasteriser plus a path engine plus a clipping model,
which is a research project wearing a chapter's clothes.

**Ruled: a direct FFI binding over a vendored pdfium**, which is what DR-138, DR-145 and DR-148 each
named and none built.

**11.152.3 RULED: WINDOWS X64 IS VENDORED NOW, PINNED BY VERSION AND CHECKSUM, AND A PERSON PLACES
IT.** One `pdfium.dll`, its release version and SHA-256 written into the tree, and a script that
verifies the checksum rather than trusting the download. macOS binaries when macOS work starts
(DR-009), because an unused binary is an unverified one.

**THE AGENT CANNOT FETCH IT, AND UNDER CR-100 THAT IS THE POINT.** The vendoring step is the
supply-chain boundary that ruling describes, so it is a human act by construction rather than by
accident. Everything above the binary is built and gated without it; the tests that need it are red
until it is in the tree, which is the honest state for a suite that cannot run.

**11.152.4 RULED: THE NATIVE DEPENDENCY IS A LEAF PACKAGE AND `rackpal_core` NEVER SEES IT.**
`rackpal_pdfium`: pure Dart, `dart:ffi`, no Flutter, depended on by `apps/rackpal` alone. The
importer calls it through an injected function, which is the seam `PdfImageResolver` and
`FlutterImageResolver` already are.

**The property being protected is not tidiness.** `rackpal_core` has zero native dependencies, and
its 4,464 tests run on any machine with a Dart SDK and nothing else. A binding inside core makes a
missing DLL a red core suite on somebody's laptop, which is a worse failure than the one it saves.

**11.152.5 RULED: 300 DPI OF THE PAGE'S OWN SIZE, WITH A PIXEL BUDGET THAT STEPS DOWN RATHER THAN
REFUSES.** This discharges the question DR-145 §11.144.7 opened and DR-148 §11.147.5 left owed: *"a
rule for a raster source and a vector source has no such ceiling."*

Measured rather than chosen by feel. `T1.01` fits the plan into **15.6 x 7.9 in**, so:

| Source render | Pixels on ANSI B | Effective on the sheet |
|---|---|---|
| 200 dpi | 3400 x 2200, 7.5 MP | 218 dpi |
| **300 dpi** | **5100 x 3300, 16.8 MP** | **327 dpi** |
| 600 dpi | 10200 x 6600, 67 MP | 654 dpi |

300 is the rung that prints above 300 on the sheet, which is where a laser stops being the limit.
600 is refused as a default rather than as an idea: an ARCH D sheet at 600 is **311 MP** against a
120 MP cap and a 20,000 px dimension cap, so it could never be the rule for both real sheet sizes.

**THE BUDGET IS WHY THIS IS A RULE AND NOT A NUMBER.** ARCH D at 300 dpi is 78 MP and a 311 MB
bitmap, which is inside the caps and outside what a desktop should allocate in one block. So the
target is 300 dpi and the effective figure **steps down to fit a pixel budget**, rather than a large
sheet being refused. A refusal here would reinstate the manual step for exactly the drawings most
likely to be a whole floor.

**Stored as PNG.** Line art deflates and a JPEG of line art rings around every wall, which is the
domain half of the borrowed rule DR-137's own census got wrong once.

**11.152.6 RULED: A RASTERISED PAGE KEEPS ITS SOURCE, A LIFTED PAGE DOES NOT, AND THE ASYMMETRY IS
THE ARGUMENT.** A lifted page's stored bytes **are** the source (DR-138 §11.137.3: lossless by
construction), so copying the PDF beside it would store the same drawing twice. A rasterised page has
thrown the vector away, and only the source can bring it back.

So the container keeps the originating PDF page for pages it rasterised. **The cost is one copy of a
file the user already has** and the purchase is that §11.152.7 stays open without re-importing a
single plan, which is the half of this decision that cannot be made later.

**11.152.7 RULED: VECTOR PASSTHROUGH IS NOT BUILT NOW, AND `PLAN-J` DECIDES WHETHER IT IS BUILT AT
ALL.** Embedding the architect's own page into the exported `T1.01` is the best possible print and it
is a different job:

- **It needs an object-graph copier**, which is a second and larger PDF reader than
  `pdf_page_lift.dart`, whose header says in terms that it *"is not a PDF reader and must never
  become one."*
- **It collides with the screening.** `kUnderlayInkRetained` is 25% applied per pixel (DR-149
  §11.148.4). A vector page cannot receive that: it needs a constant-alpha overlay, which is a
  different mechanism from the image alpha `PLAN-H/2` asserts against, and it would need its own
  ruling.

**The drill is the evidence and it is already scheduled.** `PLAN-J` prints `T1.01` on a greyscale
laser at ANSI B. A 327 dpi screened underlay either survives that or it does not, and building a
subsystem before the print would be a spend against a guess.

**11.152.8 AND `PLAN-K` IS THE GATE ON `PLAN-J`, WHICH REVERSES THE LETTER ORDER.** DR-148 §11.147.3
bound the drill to the CAD plot, so `PLAN-J` cannot run until this work lands. `PLAN-I` is
independent of both and its order is unchanged. **This is not an §8.3 amendment**: DR-148 §11.147.3
already ruled that the exit criterion covers this input, so the scope list does not move.

**11.152.9 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** Not the page picker's behaviour when every page is refused,
which is still DR-145 §11.144.7's and is now less likely to arise. Not the licence census CR-100 says
a vendored pdfium reopens; that is the vendoring chapter's own work and belongs beside the binary.
Not whether the raster prints well enough, which is §11.152.7's and `PLAN-J`'s. Not macOS. And not
text on the sheet remaining selectable or searchable, which no criterion asks for and which only a
passthrough could offer.

### §11.153 DR-154 · The plan advisories are a second band, the count they must not join is already wrong by one, and the pair gate follows the rule rather than the list

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-10**, at `PLAN-I`'s census. DR-144 §11.143.8 left `PLN-001`'s
*"wording, its severity or its band"* to this chapter and this is that ruling. The census found the
band's subject in worse shape than the brief describes.

**11.153.1 THE COUNT THE CHAPTER IS ABOUT IS ALREADY WRONG BY ONE, IN SIX DOCUMENTS.** `#645` opens
with *"THE COUNT IS THE TRAP AND IT HAS BITTEN THIS CORPUS FIVE TIMES. AC-040 pins v1's catalogue at
27 and DR-020 made it 28 (8 tier-1 + 6 tier-2 + 14 tier-3)."*

**It is 29.** DR-132 §11.131 restored `ELE-005` by a §8.3 amendment at `#838`, and the tree moved with
it: `rule_catalogue_test.dart` asserts **8 + 6 + 15 = 29** and PARSES docs/02 §5's table to check the
ids one by one, which is the mechanism that keeps the code and the normative catalogue in step.

**What that mechanism cannot see is prose.** The table has twenty-nine rows and the sentence above it
says twenty-eight, and so does every other sentence that restates the total: across docs/00, docs/02,
docs/05, docs/09, docs/10 and docs/11, including a box in an ASCII diagram. The number is correct in
every place a test can reach and wrong in every place only a person can.

**AND NO COUNT OF THE WRONG COUNTS IS WRITTEN HERE EITHER**, which is not a joke at this ruling's own
expense so much as its point. The first draft of this clause said six documents, then twelve places,
and both were wrong by the time the sweep finished. The sweep is one commit and `git show --stat` is
what counts it; a number here would be a seventh copy of exactly the thing being fixed.

**docs/12 IS LEFT ALONE.** Its entries record what was true when the work happened, and a milestone
board rewritten to agree with today is a board that can no longer be read as evidence.

**THIS IS THE SIXTH INSTANCE AND IT ARRIVED INSIDE THE WARNING ABOUT IT**, which is worth recording
plainly: a brief that opens by naming a trap walked into it, because the brief was written from the
prose. The remedy is the corpus's own and is applied here: the derived sentences are corrected to
**cite the tier arithmetic rather than restate a total**, so the next rule moves one number in one
place. No new ruling authorises the count itself; DR-132 already did.

**11.153.2 RULED: THE PLAN ADVISORIES ARE A SECOND BAND, NOT FOUR MORE ROWS.** `PLN-001` to
`PLN-004` live in `kPlanRules`, bound to **docs/15 §9** exactly as `kRuleCatalogue` is bound to
docs/02 §5, by a test that parses the table and compares ids.

The reason is CR-021's and not tidiness: *"a rule not listed there does not exist"*, and the catalogue
docs/02 §5 governs is the v1 DRC catalogue that AC-040 sized and AC-051 gates. A plan advisory is not
one of those and must not be counted as one, so it needs its own list and its own normative table,
each with the same binding.

**AND ANY DOCUMENT QUOTING A TOTAL SAYS WHICH BAND IT COUNTS.** A bare *"29 rules"* becomes a sentence
that is true today and silently wrong the first time this band grows.

**11.153.3 RULED: ONE LOOKUP, ONE EVALUATOR, ONE ACKNOWLEDGEMENT MECHANISM.** The band is separate;
the machinery is not. `kRulesById` spans both lists, `evaluateDocument` runs both maps, and a
`PLN-*` finding passes through the same three steps in the same order: the project's override, then
`off`, then the acknowledgement.

**A SECOND EVALUATION PATH IS THE THING `drc.dart` ALREADY FORBIDS** in its own header: a predicate
that resolved its own severity *"would be a second copy of that order, and the three steps have to
happen in exactly this one."* CR-019 says the same about the mute: **one** `AckedFinding` mechanism,
not a per-rule opt-out and not a second one for a new band.

**11.153.3a AND TWO SWEEPS THAT SAY "EVERY RULE" MEANT ONE CATALOGUE (`PLAN-I/2`, `#646`).**
§11.153.3 is a claim about machinery, and the tests that would have failed if it were false were
written before there were two bands. `rule_exception_test.dart`'s *"every tier-2 and tier-3 rule can
be acknowledged"* and `severity_resolution_test.dart`'s *"every rule that files a finding has one"*
both loop over `kRuleCatalogue`. Neither reached a `PLN-*` at all, so §11.153.3 shipped asserted by
two tests that could not see the band it is about.

**Both now loop over `kRulesById`, and both COUNT the plan rules they reached**, because a loop over
an empty band passes silently: the guard is the same one `corpusGaps` carries, one file along.

**THE SECOND ONE IS NOT COSMETIC.** `projectSeverity` returns null for a rule it cannot find and
`evaluateDocument` DROPS a finding on a null rather than defaulting, which is G4 doing its job one
layer up. A plan rule missing from `kRulesById` would therefore not throw and not warn. It would
never fire, and the only thing standing between that and a silent release was a sweep that stopped
at the other catalogue.

**AND THE MECHANISM IS NOW PROVED END TO END, NOT ONLY AT ITS GATE.**
`evaluateAcknowledgement` admitting a `PLN-*` id says the door opens. What
`plan_acknowledgement_test.dart` adds is a real acknowledgement demoting a real finding on a document
where all four are open at once, the project-wide `"*"` mute reaching an instance nobody named and
not reaching the other three, and the acknowledgement still winning over an override.

**THE FINGERPRINT IS THE PART THAT COULD HAVE GONE WRONG QUIETLY.** Every `PLN-*` message embeds
`underlay.name`, and an underlay is renamed by typing in a text field. Had the name reached the
fingerprint, renaming `Level 1` to `First Floor` would leave every acknowledgement about that plan
matching nothing, and rule 42 would collect them on the next load and report them as stale: the
exact failure `finding.dart` refuses designators for, arriving through a field nobody had thought of
as an identifier. It does not, and that is now asserted rather than inherited.

**`PLN-002`'S FINGERPRINT DOES MOVE, AND THAT IS THE SAME RULE RATHER THAN AN EXCEPTION TO IT.** It
targets the carriers as well as the plan, on the contract `PWR-003` and `LNK-020` already wrote out:
acknowledging *"1 device is not on the plan"* is not an acknowledgement of two. The other three are
about the plan itself and adding an outlet leaves them alone.

**11.153.4 RULED: THE AC-051 PAIR GATE FOLLOWS THE RULE, NOT THE LIST.** AC-051 is written about
rules and not about a catalogue: *"No rule ships without its pair."* So each `PLN-*` rule gets a
known-bad fixture producing exactly that finding and a known-good near-miss producing none, and the
gate reports **per band** rather than adding four to twenty-nine.

`#645` says the gate *"applies to 28 pairs and this does not move it"*, and that is honoured on the
number: the DRC band's pair count is untouched. What the brief does not say, and what this rules, is
that the new band is gated too. **A rule shipped without its pair is the failure AC-051 exists to
prevent, and it does not become acceptable by being filed under a different heading** (`PLAN-H` found
five gates in this epic whose scope was narrower than their subject; this is the first chance to
avoid a sixth by construction).

**11.153.5 RULED: `PLN-004` IS A WARNING AND THE OTHER THREE ARE ADVISORIES.** docs/15 §9 grades it a
warning and `#646` says all four are advisory; the user settled it on the difference in what the four
sentences claim.

`PLN-001`, `PLN-002` and `PLN-003` say **you have not done this yet**: nothing is calibrated, these
drops are not pinned, this plan has no rack to measure from. `PLN-004` says **what you are looking at
may not be what you measured**: the bytes under a calibration and a set of pins have changed, so
every pin may be in the wrong place and every length derived from them wrong.

**IT STILL BLOCKS NOTHING** (CR-022, G3) and it stays acknowledgeable and overridable like any other
row. AC-042's *"a mismatch is a warning and never a load failure"* is honoured exactly: the file
opens, and the finding says why it might not be what its owner thinks.

**11.153.5a AND "IT STILL BLOCKS NOTHING" IS NOW PROVED RATHER THAN RESTATED (`PLAN-I/2`, `#646`).**
`#646` asks this epic to prove its own four *"before that milestone exists"*, naming M5-I as the
milestone-level version that has not run. **M5-I HAS RUN**, at `c500cf5`; the correction does not
retire the task. `findings_never_block_export_test.dart`'s three groups sweep `kRuleCatalogue`, which
has been one catalogue of two since §11.153.2, so **not one of them reaches a `PLN-*`**. The brief is
stale on the timing and exactly right on the obligation, which is the third `#645`/`#646` sentence
this epic has found describing a tree that moved under it.

**A COMPLETE SHEET SET IS READ OFF THE PAGE, NOT OFF A COUNT.** Four blank pages satisfy a
`sheetCount` of four, and `T1.01` is the sheet these four rules are about: a plan whose advisories
held it back would still have exported the elevations and the schedule and reported the same number.
So the proof parses the PDF and finds the sheet number, the role's own title and the pinned drop's
callout, and it is mutation-tested by making `planUnderlaysWithPins` return nothing.

**THE WARNING GETS ITS OWN CASE, AND THIS CLAUSE IS WHY.** `#646` opens *"all four are `advisory`"*
and §11.153.5 made one of them a warning. A run that scoped the three advisories off and left the
warning open is precisely the case that sentence would have skipped, and it is the one somebody would
most expect an exporter to refuse.

**ACKNOWLEDGING CHANGES NOTHING**, which is CR-022 from the other side. An acknowledgement is for
whoever reads `T0.02`; it is not a key that unlocks the exporter, and a product where muting a rule
made an export succeed would have taught people to mute rules.

**AND THE ABSENCE NAMES WHAT RETIRES IT**, which is the practice `#646` asks for by name.
`T0.02` is M6's, so *"the reason prints on the exceptions sheet"* cannot be proved today and asserting
it would be vacuous in the same shape `#310` refused for the `ISSUED FOR CONSTRUCTION` stamp. The
guard is that `SheetRole` has no `exceptions` value: M6 landing one fails that test, and whoever lands
it writes the real assertion in its place.

**11.153.6 RULED: EACH RULE STATES ITS COUNT.** *"N pins carry no measurable position"*, *"N devices
in Level 1 are not on the plan"*. G4's discipline in a findings list: a rule that fires without
saying how much has told somebody there is a problem and left them to count it themselves.

`PLN-001`'s sentence already exists and is not rewritten here. `unmeasurablePinsSentence` was built at
`PLAN-F/3` and DR-146 §11.145.6 put it in core *"precisely so surfaces cannot drift"*; this chapter
reads it rather than composing a second one.

**11.153.7 RULED: `PLN-002` COUNTS THE LOCATION'S SUBTREE.** An underlay's `locationId` is *"the
`Location` this depicts, usually a floor"* (docs/15 §3.1), and the drops on a floor are filed in the
rooms under it. Counting only the exact location would make the rule silent on every plan filed the
way the trade files them, which is the shape of a rule that exists and never fires.

**11.153.7a AND THE SHIPPED STRIP ALREADY MADE THE OPPOSITE CHOICE, WHICH THIS CLAUSE DID NOT CHECK.**
§11.153.7 was ruled from docs/15 §3.1 alone. `unpinnedCarriersFor` scopes with `where == scope`, an
exact match, and `PLAN-E/4` shipped it that way: **on a `Level 1` plan an outlet filed in `Great Room`
is neither in `rows` nor counted in `unlocatedCount`**, but dropped by a comparison. There is no case
in `unpinned_carriers_test.dart` for a child room, so nothing said so.

That is a defect in the strip and not merely a difference of opinion, on the strip's own stated
standard: `unlocatedCount` exists so the count is never *"the `0 pathways` status bar: a number that
flatters by counting only what it can see"*, and this path counts nothing and reports nothing.

**Ruled by the user: both widen, to one scope.** A carrier is on this plan's floor when its location
is the underlay's location or any descendant, `LocationTree.subtreeOf`, which
`location_removal.dart` already uses for the same question about the same tree. **The strip is
`PLN-002`'s remedy surface**, so the two must count one population: a person reading *"12 devices in
Level 1 are not on the plan"*, opening the strip and finding it empty is the two-answers failure
CR-107 keeps naming, one layer down.

**THIS AMENDS DR-142's STRIP CLAUSE** on the scope only. The order, the `unlocatedCount` and the
rack-leads default are untouched.

**AND THE ORDER OF THE TWO FINDINGS IS THE LESSON.** A ruling drafted from a design document, checked
against the shipped code twenty minutes later, disagreed with it. The corpus already carries that
practice by name; this is its instance in a ruling rather than in a task.

**11.153.8 WHAT THIS DOES NOT RULE.** Not the issues-list surface, which is M5's and which renders
whatever `evaluateDocument` returns. Not whether `PLN-*` ever becomes v1 scope rather than v1.1;
docs/15 §9 calls them v1.1 rules and nothing here moves that. Not the remedy actions a `PLN-*`
finding might offer, which nothing asks for. And not `T0.02`'s rendering of an acknowledged plan
advisory, which is M6's sheet.

**11.153.8a THE ISSUES-LIST SURFACE COULD NOT RENDER WHAT `evaluateDocument` RETURNED, AND §11.153.8
IS THE CLAUSE THAT SAID IT COULD (`PLAN-I/2`, `#646`).** That exclusion reads *"Not the issues-list
surface, which is M5's and which renders whatever `evaluateDocument` returns."* It does not.
`locusLabel` resolves a `Finding.primaryEntityId` through four collections, `Link`, `Rack`,
`DeviceInstance` and `Circuit`, and returns null for anything else. Every `PLN-*` finding points at a
`PlanUnderlay`, so **all four grouped under `No single location`**: the panel told a person that the
most locatable object in their document had no location, and offered them nothing to click.

**THE GUARD THAT PROMISED TO CATCH THIS SAT THROUGH IT.** `findings_view.dart`'s header said a fifth
`primaryEntityId` type would be *"a test failure, not a blank cell"*, and the test carrying that
promise asserts `locusLabel` returns null for a hand-written stranger id. **That is a statement about
an id no rule produces**, and it cannot see a type that rules DO produce, which is the only way a
fifth type was ever going to arrive.

**AND IT WAS THE SIXTH, NOT THE FIFTH.** `ELE-005` has pointed at a `Net` since `#838` and had no arm
either, so that rule's findings had been unclickable for three epics with the promise sitting above
them the whole time. **Neither was found by looking; both were found by the census that replaced the
sentence**, on its first run, one of them in work this epic had nothing to do with.

**Ruled: the census is taken over the corpus, not over a sentence.** Every AC-051 fixture already
evaluates a real document, so `FixtureOutcome` now reports the label the panel would print for every
finding produced and `violationOf` fails on a null. Both halves of every pair, because a near-miss
document still produces its neighbours' findings and a finding nobody can click is broken whichever
fixture made it. A seventh type is a test failure for real this time, because the thing that fails is
a run of the rules rather than a claim about them.

**A NET PREFERS ITS DESIGNATOR AND FALLS BACK TO ITS NAME**, which is what `ELE-005`'s own message
does: a group header reading `Net 12` over a row reading `SPK-A carries 260 W` is two names for one
thing on one screen. **An underlay has no designator at all**, and that is not an inconsistency to
paper over: a plan is a drawing of the building rather than equipment in it, so its locus is the name
its own `T1.01` title block prints (docs/15 §8).

**WHAT §11.153.8 MEANT SURVIVES.** The issues list is still M5's, its rendering is still not this
ruling's to design, and nothing here adds a `PLN-*` remedy action. What it may no longer say is that
the surface renders whatever the evaluator returns, because for the whole of `PLAN-I/1` it did not.

### §11.154 DR-155 · The Plan view's walkthrough clause is parked on M6, because the Pull Sheet does not print

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-11**, from *"defer 649 to M6"*, after this task reported that the
clause names an artifact the product has no way to produce.

**§11.154.1 The tension, and it is not a matter of appetite.** The Plan view epic's exit criterion
(docs/09, DR-029) says: *"A person who has never seen the building is handed the printed `T1.01` and
the printed Pull Sheet, and locates every drop without asking a question."* **The Pull Sheet does
not print.** `SheetRole` has four values, `devicePlan`, `rackElevationFront`, `rackElevationRear`
and `equipmentList`; the Pull Sheet exists only as a derivation, `SchedulePreset.pullSheet` sorted
`roomThenPathway` and rendered on screen by `ScheduleScreen`, and `rackpal_export` does not
reference `ScheduleView` anywhere. There is no tabular export either: `EXP-A` is DR-049's and is
unstarted.

**So the clause could not have been discharged at any point in this epic's life**, and no amount of
drilling would have changed that. It is not a clause the Plan view failed to reach; it is a clause
that named somebody else's sheet.

**§11.154.2 THIS IS DR-027's SEAM REACHING A SECOND CRITERION, NOT A NEW DECISION.** §11.26.2 ruled
that M6 owns *"the `SheetRole`, the layout, the initial boxes and the page"* of the Pull Sheet, and
§11.26.3 gave the reason in terms that apply here word for word: **a milestone cannot discharge a
clause about a sheet it does not own**, and reading such a clause loosely enough to call it met
*"would be precisely the checklist-ticking §8.1 refuses."* docs/12 already records the split. The
Plan view's criterion was written a month later naming both printed artifacts, and one of them had
been M6's since 2026-08-09.

**§11.154.3 The ruling.** `PLAN-J/3`'s walkthrough is **parked on M6** under roadmap §8.9, which
requires a park to be reassigned by ruling ID to a named later milestone with its structural reason:
this is that ID and that reason. Board `#649` moves from `PLAN-J` to **`M6-J`**, the story that
already holds this epic's physical print tests on real hardware.

**AND M6's CRITERION DOES GAIN A CLAUSE**, which is where this differs from DR-027. That ruling
found M6's *"all four starter projects export a complete set"* already contained the sheet, so
nothing was owed. A **walkthrough** is a demonstration rather than an export, and no M6 clause
contains it. M6 therefore owes: the stranger test, run against the printed `T1.01` and the printed
Pull Sheet together, once the Pull Sheet renders.

**§11.154.4 WHAT DOES NOT MOVE, so this is not read as deferring the hard part.** The print itself
stays. `PLAN-J/2` still demands a real greyscale laser at ANSI B with every callout legible over the
screened underlay (AC-054), and `PLAN-J/1` still demands a real plan and a real rough-in rather than
a synthetic fixture. **The stranger test moves because its second artifact does not exist, not
because it is inconvenient**, and the half of it that `T1.01` alone can answer is already inside
`PLAN-J/2`'s legibility clause.

**§11.154.5 Scope.** **A milestone-boundary amendment; no change to roadmap §2's contents**
(§11.26.5's own words, and for the same reason). Nothing leaves v1 and nothing joins it. One clause
moves from the Plan view epic's criterion to M6's, and the Plan view epic's remaining criterion is
discharged by `PLAN-J/1` and `PLAN-J/2`.

### §11.155 DR-156 · A command reports whether it applied, and a transaction may take its label from its first child

**Settled by the user on 2026-09-12**, closing `#863` and `#866`. Both were filed rather than fixed
in flight because each changes the `Command` protocol every command in this product implements, and
roadmap §8.3 makes that a ruling rather than a commit.

**§11.155.1 RULED: `apply` RETURNS WHETHER IT CHANGED THE AGGREGATE, AND A REFUSAL NEVER REACHES THE
UNDO STACK.**

A command that self-refuses inside `apply` still becomes a child of its transaction, so the
transaction is recorded, the epochs bump over a document that did not change, and the next `Ctrl+Z`
calls `revert` on a command that never applied. Probed on the shipped `SetPlanPinCommand`:
`canUndo` is true after a refusal and the undo throws
`StateError: revert called before apply()`.

**THE CONCEPT WAS ALREADY IN `_commit` AND COULD NOT SEE THIS CASE.** It reads
`if (b.children.isEmpty) return; // no-op edits add no history`. What was missing was any way for a
command to say it declined, so a refusal was indistinguishable from a write. `TxnScope.add` now
drops a child that returned false, and that existing guard handles the rest.

**THE RETURN TYPE RATHER THAN A SECOND MEMBER, AND THE USER CHOSE IT.** A `bool get applied` beside a
`void apply` was offered and refused: it is two members that can drift, and a default of `true` is a
hole every future refusing command falls into silently. **`bool apply` has no default to fall
through.** The compiler stops at every implementation and each author decides.

*Measured, not estimated:* **78 `apply` implementations across 40 files, of which 24 carry a refusal
path today.** The ticket said twenty-nine, counting `_applied` bits rather than refusal paths; the
two questions are different and the second is the one this clause is about.

**THE `StateError` IN `revert` STAYS.** It catches *revert called before apply*, which is a real
programming error, and softening it would trade a loud bug for a silent one. The defect was never the
throw; it was that a refusal reached the stack at all.

**§11.155.2 RULED: A TRANSACTION'S LABEL MAY BE DEFERRED TO ITS FIRST CHILD, AND IS THEN READ AFTER
`apply`.**

`DocumentController.run` is `transact(c.label, (tx) => tx.add(c))`. Dart evaluates `c.label` before
the closure runs and the closure is what calls `apply`, so a command that decides its label from what
it found in the document is asked for that label while the document still holds the old state.

**THE AFFECTED SET IS THREE COMMANDS AND THEY ARE NAMED HERE**, because a fix cannot be tested
against *"every second act"*: `SetPlanPinCommand` (`movePlanPin`), `SetRoomOutlineCommand`
(`reshapeRoomOutline`) and `SetPlanScaleCommand` (`recalibratePlan`). Two further commands look
dynamic and are not: `SetRoomEstimateCommand` and `SetEntityPropertyCommand` both discriminate on
state known at construction, so their labels were always right.

`transact`'s label becomes **nullable, meaning the first child names this entry**, resolved at commit
after every child has applied. `run` passes null. **A caller that names the act still wins**, which
is what keeps `Undo Import CSV` from becoming `Undo Set Property`.

> **THE OBVIOUS MIRROR WAS DRAFTED AND REJECTED, AND THE REASON IS RECORDED BECAUSE IT IS NOT
> OBVIOUS.** `Transaction.mergeKey` already forwards to a single child, with a comment explaining
> that the wrapper `run` adds would otherwise make every `mergeKey` declaration dead code, and the
> same three lines would have fixed this. They would also silently override a caller who named the
> act, and shipped code shows the cost: `LEN-A/4`'s outline close names its own transaction and adds
> **one child or two** depending on whether the estimate auto-filled, so one gesture would produce
> two different menu entries depending on a derivation nobody can see.

**§11.155.3 Why one ruling and not two.** The two defects are one subject: what a command tells its
transaction, and when the transaction listens. `TxnScope` is shared by both undo stacks, so the
refusal fix lands **once**; `TemplateEditSession` carries its own `_TxnBuilder` and `_commit`, so the
label fix lands **twice**. That asymmetry is only visible from a census and is why one is recorded
here rather than assumed symmetrical.

**§11.155.4 What it does not rule.**

- **Whether `revert` should also report.** It should not: `revert` is only ever reached by a command
  that applied, which is exactly what §11.155.1 makes true.
- **Whether a refusal should be shown to a person.** `onRefuse` already exists at the UI layer and
  several commands already word their own refusals. Whether the machinery should surface one that
  nobody worded is a separate question with no ticket.
- **Three call sites that pass a command's own `.label` into `transact`** carry the defect's shape
  with no symptom, because the commands they pass have static labels: `app_shell.dart` and
  `pathway_actions.dart` (both `commands.first.label`) move to the deferred form, and
  `rack_canvas_screen.dart` keeps its explicit label because it names its transaction after its
  **second** child deliberately.

### §11.156 DR-157 · A rack height with no side is incoherent, and placement says so instead of quietly putting the device somewhere else

**Reported by the user on 2026-09-12**, running the `PLAN-J` demo project: *"I can't seem to
actually see rack devices as I populate a rack. They act as though they are present, but don't
appear to do anything."* Devices they had AUTHORED failed; seeded catalog devices worked.

**§11.156.1 What was measured.** A probe built the exact body the device builder permits,
`{frontU: 2, side: none}`, and ran `buildPlaceFromCatalogCommand` against a rack. The result is
`CatalogPlacementReady` carrying an **`OffRackPlacement`**. The placement succeeds, reports success,
and puts the device somewhere the person is not looking. Nothing is drawn in the rack because
nothing is in the rack.

**TWO SURFACES DISAGREE ABOUT ONE FACT.** The builder's save gate requires `frontU > 0` or
`zeroUVertical` or `notInRack`, and **never consults `side`**. `buildPlaceFromCatalogCommand`
requires `side != OccupancySide.none`, and **checks it before it ever looks at the height**. `side`
defaults to `none`, so a body the builder calls complete is one placement routes off-rack.

**§11.156.2 RULED: A BODY WITH A RACK HEIGHT AND NO SIDE IS REFUSED BY NAME.** `frontU > 0` or
`rearU > 0`, with `side == none` and a `mountMethod` other than `notInRack`, is an incoherent
occupancy rather than a field device. Placement refuses it and the reason names the height and the
field to change.

**THE DISTINGUISHING FACT IS THE HEIGHT, NOT THE SIDE**, and that is what keeps AC-031's eighteen
shipped field templates landing exactly where they always did: they are `{front: 0, rear: 0, side:
none}`, and a body with no rack height at all is a field device by construction. `notInRack` remains
the explicit escape hatch at any height, because saying *"this does not go in a rack"* is a coherent
answer.

**§11.156.3 It is the guard beside it, catching up.** `catalog_placement.dart` already refuses
`deviceH <= 0`, and its comment says why in terms this ruling adopts: the device *"is never painted,
cannot be clicked, cannot be selection-chromed, and landed on the REAR face while the user was
looking at the front. A reported success for a device that does not exist on screen is the worst
possible outcome of the three."* The `side == none` path produced the same outcome and slipped past
that guard **by returning before it**.

**§11.156.4 NOT A REGRESSION, and the check was worth running.** The disagreement predates DR-156 and
nothing in that work is involved. It was found while auditing DR-156's sweep against this report, and
the audit did find three real defects of its own; they are not these.

**§11.156.5 RULED: THE BUILDER DERIVES THE SIDE AS THE HEIGHT IS TYPED.** Settled by the user on
2026-09-12, from three options.

**A SAVE GATE WAS TRIED FIRST AND WAS WRONG.** Requiring a side before `Save` lights broke the
existing case asserting AC-049's *"three required fields (name, RU height, designator prefix) then
ports, then done"*, and **that case was right**: a fourth interaction is precisely the stall AC-049
exists to prevent. The attempt is recorded because the reasoning is what stops somebody trying it
again.

**Typing a front height IS saying the device mounts on the front**, so the answer is to read it
rather than ask for it a second time. The derivation is unambiguous and was already spelled out in
this repository's own test fixture before anybody needed it as a rule: both heights is `both`, a rear
height alone is `rear`, otherwise `front`.

**IT ONLY EVER FILLS A BLANK.** A person who has chosen a side keeps it whatever they type
afterwards, and one who has said `notInRack` is not contradicted. The write rides in the field
edit's own transaction, so a height and the side it implies are one undo entry: it is one act to the
person who typed it.

**The rejected third option was to leave the builder alone** and let §11.156.2's refusal be the whole
remedy. It was refused because it leaves a template that can be authored, saved, and taken by no
rack, with the person finding out at placement time rather than at the moment they could fix it.

---

### §11.157 DR-158 · A template is removed from a project as a whole, and it takes the devices standing on it

**Reported by the user on 2026-09-12**, running the `PLAN-J` demo project: *"I also have no way to
delete device templates, or to delete floor plan pages."* The floorplan half is `#870` and needed no
ruling: the command existed and nothing built one. This half needed one, because **nothing existed at
all**: there is no `RemoveTemplate` class anywhere in the tree, and `doc.templates.remove` appears
only inside revert bodies undoing a save or a fork.

**THE RULE WAS ALREADY WRITTEN AND THE SURFACE WAS MISSING.** docs/06 §7.1: *"Library operations
(delete a template, import, set favourite) are not undoable and are therefore individually
confirmable or trivially reversible."* That sentence governs the **shelf**, which is M4-N and does not
exist. What this ruling governs is the **per-project embedded snapshot**, which has existed since M0
and is what `TemplateRef` resolves against (CR-054).

**§11.157.1 RULED: THIS IS A DOCUMENT EDIT AND IT IS UNDOABLE.** `SaveTemplateToProjectCommand`'s
header already made this argument for the other direction and it holds in both: *"CR-106's 'library
operations are not undoable' is about acts on the SHELF and there is no shelf here."* A snapshot in
`RackDocument.templates` is project data, it is persisted in the `.rmpj`, and removing it is an edit
to the project. It therefore goes on the document's undo stack like every other edit, and the
confirmation can honestly say so.

**§11.157.2 RULED: THE UNIT IS THE TEMPLATE ID, NOT THE SNAPSHOT.** Every version of the id goes, in
one command.

The product already thinks in ids everywhere the user can see: `buildPlaceableTemplates` reduces to
the newest version per id, the palette and the browser each list one row per id, a placement gesture
carries an id and never a version (DR-077 §11.76.3), and `countDevicesOnTemplate` counts by id
because *"a count that split by version would understate what the badge is reassuring the user
about"*. **A removal that took one snapshot would be the first gesture in the product to address a
version**, and its visible effect would be a row that disappears and then silently comes back at the
previous version. Versions are an archival mechanism CR-050 keeps resolvable; they are not a thing a
person picks between.

**§11.157.3 RULED: PROJECT-AUTHORED ONLY.** Settled by the user on 2026-09-12. The control is offered
on rows tagged `This project` and on no others.

A library row is somebody else's shelf and this project does not hold it. A **seeded** row is
removable in the narrow technical sense, because the 48 catalog snapshots are written into the
document once at creation (`blank_document.dart`) and would not grow back. It is refused anyway: the
seeded set is what the build ships and is identical in every project, so a per-project hole in it is
a difference carried in the file forever, discovered later by somebody who did not make it, and
repairable by nothing in the product. Pruning a palette down to what a shop installs is a **filtering**
question and belongs to the shelf (`#817`), not to a delete.

**§11.157.4 RULED: THE DEVICES GO WITH IT, AFTER A CONFIRMATION THAT COUNTS BOTH.** Settled by the
user on 2026-09-12, from three options. The alternative recommended here was a refusal naming the
count, and it was not taken.

`DeviceInstance.templateRef` is **the only referent in the entire model**: no other field anywhere
points at a template. So the cascade has exactly one edge, and the choice is what to do along it.
Removing the template while leaving the devices was never on the table, because CR-054 says a
`TemplateRef` *"ALWAYS resolves to one"* and a device whose snapshot is gone has no body, no
footprint and nothing to draw.

**THE BLAST RADIUS IS THE COST AND IT IS STATED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED.** A template delete becomes a
device delete, behind a small control, and those devices take their cables with them under DR-013
§11.13.1. What makes it acceptable is the same thing that makes every other destructive gesture in
this product acceptable: the dialog names what goes, in the units it goes in, and one undo puts all
of it back.

**§11.157.5 THE CONFIRMATION COUNTS THREE THINGS, IN THREE UNITS.** On `LocationRemovalPlan`'s
reasoning, restated once more because this is the fourth plan to need it: numbers in different units
are not summed. **Templates** removed, **devices** removed, **cables** cut. A device is a thing that
leaves the project; a cable is a row that leaves the schedule, which is the deliverable and is what
makes DR-013 §11.13.2 expensive.

**AND A TEMPLATE NOTHING STANDS ON IS STILL ASKED ABOUT**, which is where this departs from
`confirmUnderlayRemoval` and `confirmDeviceRemoval`. DR-013 §11.13.2's last sentence exempts the
*consequence-free* delete, and this one is not: authoring a device template is minutes of work that
exists nowhere else in the project, so removing an unused one still destroys something the person
cannot get back by any route but undo. The prompt is shorter when nothing stands on it; it is
not absent.

**§11.157.6 ONE TRANSACTION, ONE UNDO.** The gesture is a `Transaction` holding one
`RemoveDeviceCommand` per device and then the template removal, which is exactly the shape
`_deleteSelection` already uses for a multi-device delete. Each `RemoveDeviceCommand` plans itself
against the aggregate as it stands when it applies, so the plans compose correctly in sequence: a
cable between two departing devices is removed at the first of them, and a net carried only by
departing cables is collected at the last one that could still have carried it.

**§11.157.7 The count the dialog states must be the count the edit delivers, and that was already
broken elsewhere.** `#873`, found while building this: `DeleteDeviceDialog` summed one
`DeviceRemovalPlan` per selected device, and a cable landing on two selected devices is in **both**
plans while the transaction removes it once. Selecting both ends of a run said two cables and removed
one. The arithmetic was wrong, not the plans; `cablesAcrossPlans` is the union and lives in core
beside the planner. It is named here because this ruling's dialog counts the same way and would have
inherited the same defect.

---

### §11.158 DR-159 · Undo is document-global, it says what it will take back, and the builder keeps its own stack

**Reported by the user on 2026-09-12**, running the `PLAN-J` demo: *"Undo doesn't appear to work
anywhere across the program currently."* It was recorded as a side observation during `#869`'s
investigation and not followed up. Found again by a `#871` shell case that pressed `Ctrl+Z` on the
Device Manager and watched nothing happen.

**§11.158.1 What was measured.** `UndoIntent` and `RedoIntent` have **exactly one handler in the
entire tree**, inside `RackCanvasScreen`'s own `Shortcuts`. The application has **one menu**, `File`,
and no Undo item anywhere in it. The strip is **seven** tabs. Undo works on one of them.

**AND THE INTENT WAS ALWAYS RIGHT; ONLY THE INSTALLATION POINT WAS WRONG.** That handler's own
comment reads: *"the key is DOCUMENT-GLOBAL. Undo and redo must keep working from the palette, the
inspector and the toolbar; scoping them to the canvas would reintroduce the exact defect
app_shell.dart's header post-mortems for `Ctrl+S`."* The registry row says the same thing from the
other side, and names *"promoting it to `KeyScope.global`"* as a rebinding owed a ruling. This is that
ruling.

**§11.158.2 TWO COUNTS IN THIS REPOSITORY SAID TWO TABS AND IT WAS SIX.** `rack_canvas_screen.dart`
and the keymap registry each carried *"`Ctrl+Z` still reaches nothing at all on the Schematic and
Schedule tabs"*, written when the strip had four. DR-091 reordered and extended it and `PLAN-E/5`
added Plan; neither number moved. **The first draft of this ruling said six tabs and it is seven**,
which is the same failure a third time, in the document about the failure. The tabs are not counted
here: `ShellView.values` is the list, `app_shell.dart` builds the strip from it, and a count in prose
is a liability.

**§11.158.3 RULED: THE BINDING IS `KeyScope.global`.** The document is global, so its keys are too,
which is `buildFileActions`' own post-mortem applied to the pair of keys it did not cover. Installed
at the app root beside the File and view actions, above the root focus scope, because a `Shortcuts`
below it only ever sees keys pressed while focus is inside its own subtree.

**THE TEXT-FIELD GUARD LIFTS UNCHANGED**, and that is a fact rather than a design: it already reads
`FocusManager.instance.primaryFocus`, which is a global query. A person typing in a field gets their
typing back, everywhere, as they do today on the rack.

**THE SCHEDULE TAB IS READ-ONLY** and still gets the key. Nothing under `schedule/` constructs a
command, so there is no edit to take back from there; the edit a person wants back was made
elsewhere on the same document, and a key that declined on the deliverable view would be a second
rule to explain.

**§11.158.4 RULED: THE RACK KEEPS ITS OWN HANDLER, AND THAT IS NOT A DUPLICATE.** Flutter resolves an
`Action` from the focused context upward, so the nearest one wins. The rack's does something the
global one cannot: `undoLast` returns the selection as it was, and restoring it is what makes undo of
a delete put the selection back rather than leaving the user staring at an empty inspector. The
global handler is the fallback for every surface that has no selection of its own.

**§11.158.5 RULED: THE DEVICE BUILDER KEEPS ITS OWN STACK, AND `Ctrl+Z` REACHES IT THERE.** Settled by
the user on 2026-09-12.

CR-106 makes the builder a full-window editor over a `TemplateBody` with an undo stack that dies with
the window, and `KeyScope.builder`'s own note already refuses to share a scope with the canvas
because *"a scope shared with the document's canvas would say the two stacks were one thing."* The
builder has had Undo and Redo **buttons** since M4-A/4 and no key binding at all, so `Ctrl+Z` was dead
there too, on a second stack.

**SO ONE KEY MEANS TWO THINGS ON ONE TAB**, depending on whether the browser or the editor is showing,
and that is the cost of the choice rather than an oversight. It is mitigated by §11.158.6: the menu
says which stack it is about, so the mode is read rather than felt.

**THE ALTERNATIVE WAS ONE KEY, ONE STACK, ALWAYS THE DOCUMENT'S**, and it was refused because
`Ctrl+Z` while editing a template would silently undo something in the project behind the window. A
larger blast radius, invisible from where the person is standing, is the shape DR-013 §11.13.2 exists
to prevent.

**§11.158.6 RULED: THE EDIT MENU IS BUILT, AND IT NAMES THE ACT.** docs/03-architecture.md §13.3 has
specified it since M0: *"The Edit menu shows a localized 'Undo Move device'; the log shows the stable
enum name."* It was never built, and `LabelKey` has **101 values whose comments argue about what that
menu should say**. `commitPortSort` exists rather than reusing `reorderPorts` because *"'Undo
Reorder' in front of somebody who has just been through a confirm dialog names the wrong act"*;
`clearRoomEstimate` is separate from `setRoomEstimate` because the opposite act must not be named;
`drawRoomOutline` and `reshapeRoomOutline` are one command with two labels chosen at apply time. That
is a great deal of careful reasoning about a surface that does not exist.

**A KEYBOARD-ONLY BINDING IS INVISIBLE**, which is why fixing the key alone was refused. A person who
does not already know the chord has no way to learn that the product has undo at all.

**§11.158.7 THE MAP IS EXPLICIT AND GATED, NOT DERIVED.** A label could be de-camel-cased from the
enum name, and `removeTemplateFromProject` would read *"Remove Template From Project"*. That is worse
than useless for the values above, whose whole point is that the obvious wording names the wrong act.

So `rackpal_ui` holds one `LabelKey` to text map, and **a parity gate fails when a value has no
entry**. Not a fallback: a default is a hole a future `LabelKey` falls into silently, which is the
argument DR-156 §11.155.1 already made about `applied`. The gate is the same shape as registry
parity and AC-051's pair gate.

**IT IS NOT LOCALIZED, AND THIS RULING DOES NOT PRETEND OTHERWISE.** docs/03 §13.3 also says
`AppLocalizations` from the first commit with one locale and `l10n.yaml` in CI. **There is no
`l10n.yaml` in this tree and no `AppLocalizations`**, so the map holds English strings and the
localisation half of that paragraph stays owed. Saying so here is the point: a menu built against
half a specification must record which half.

**§11.158.8 RULED: AN EMPTY QUICK-ENTRY BOX HANDS THE KEY BACK TO THE DOCUMENT.** Settled by the user
on 2026-09-12, after the per-tab sweep this ruling required found the fix incomplete on one tab.

**THE COMPLAINT SURVIVED INSIDE ITS OWN FIX.** The Structured Wiring tab's `Add drops` box carries
`autofocus: true`, because typing a drop is what somebody comes to that tab to do, and `_submit`
refocuses and clears it after every entry. So a text field held focus there permanently,
`DefaultTextEditingShortcuts` sits nearer a focused field than the app's own `Shortcuts` and claimed
`Ctrl+Z` for `UndoTextIntent`, and with nothing typed there was nothing to restore. The key did
nothing at all, on the one tab whose primary verb is bulk data entry.

**THE CONDITION IS THE WHOLE DESIGN.** A box with text in it has typing worth taking back and keeps
the key, which is the general rule and stays the general rule. An **empty** box has none, so it
forwards. Dropping the autofocus was the alternative and was refused: it buys a flat rule by taking
away the reason the tab is fast.

**AND THE SHELL'S OWN TEXT-FIELD GUARD IS REMOVED, NOT WEAKENED.** The first draft of
`undoFromShell` copied `RackCanvasScreen`'s `!_textFieldHasFocus`. That copy is **redundant**,
because a focused field's nearer binding consumes the key before `UndoIntent` is ever raised, so
reaching this method already proves no field claimed it; and it is **harmful**, because it would have
caught the forward above and thrown it away. A guard that re-asks a question the dispatch has already
answered can only get it wrong.

---

### 11.159 DR-160 · Removing a Structure body or an outlet, and what each takes with it

**The question.** `#872`'s reachability gate found `RemoveOutletCommand` and `RemoveStructureCommand`
declared in `structure_commands.dart` with real reverts, eight and nine test constructions between
them, and **no caller anywhere in `lib/`**. `AddStructureCommand` and `AddOutletCommand` are both
wired, so the Structured Wiring tab could create a panel and a wall plate and could never take either
back: a wrong drop or a duplicate panel was permanent for the life of the project unless the person
noticed in time to press `Ctrl+Z`. That is the shape `#674`, `#870`, `#871`, `#875` and `#879` each
found, and it is the sixth instance.

**11.159.1 RULED: BOTH ARE REACHABLE FROM THE STRUCTURE EDITOR.** Where they are created is where
they are destroyed, which is docs/04 §3.1's rule and the answer `#871` already gave for a template.
Nothing else in the product shows a Structure body or a plate as an object a person owns.

**11.159.2 RULED: REMOVING A PLATE TAKES ITS HOME RUNS, AND THE MODEL IS WHY.** Settled by the user
on 2026-09-13, against the alternative of leaving the cables and blanking their box.

`RemoveOutletCommand`'s own doc comment argues the other way: *"silently deleting a user's home runs
because they removed a wall plate is a much larger edit than the gesture asked for. A caller that
means both composes a `Transaction`."* Both halves of that stand. This ruling supplies the caller the
sentence asks for, and §11.159.5 is what makes the larger edit legitimate rather than silent.

**BLANKING THE BOX WAS THE TEMPTING ANSWER AND IT IS A TRAP.** `StructureOrigin.outletId` is
nullable, and DR-046's reasoning gives the null a real meaning: *"nobody has said"* which box, as
distinct from `boxless`, which is *"there is no box"*. So a drop whose plate was deleted and whose
`outletId` was cleared would be a legal document saying something true. It would also be
**unrepairable**: `StructureOriginField` lists seven editable properties and `outletId` is not one of
them, `AddHomeRunCommand` sets it at creation, and no surface in the product can move a drop onto a
different plate. The cable would sit on the Structure table with an empty box column forever, looking
like an oversight, and the only way out would be to delete it and type it again. Deleting it now, in
one undoable step, with the count stated first, is the smaller loss.

**11.159.3 RULED: REMOVING A STRUCTURE TAKES ITS PLATES AND EVERY HOME RUN OUT OF IT.** Here there is
no choice to make, and recording why is the point of the clause.

`Outlet.structureBodyId` is non-nullable and `final`. `StructureOrigin.structureBodyId` is
non-nullable and `final`. Neither an outlet nor a home run can be repaired to point at a surviving
panel or at none, so leaving them behind does not produce a document saying something true: it
produces two classes of entity naming a body that is not there. G4's whole discipline is that an
absent value has exactly one meaning, and a dangling id has none.

**REFUSAL WAS NOT RECONSIDERED.** DR-013 §11.13.3 settled it for the device delete in terms that
reach here verbatim: CR-017 reserves refusal for the five tier-1 topology rules, whose escape docs/02
§5 gives as *"None. There is nothing to escape to."* Wanting a panel gone is not that.

**11.159.4 THE CASCADE IS ASYMMETRIC AND THAT IS THE MODEL SPEAKING.** A plate's drops go because
they cannot be re-homed; a body's plates and drops go because they cannot exist without it. Those are
different reasons reaching the same act, and a later reader who makes `outletId` editable should
revisit §11.159.2 and must not touch §11.159.3.

**11.159.5 THE PLAN IS COMPUTED ONCE AND THE CONFIRMATION STATES IT.** DR-013 §11.13.2 and DR-021
§11.20.3, which `delete_location_dialog.dart` and `#871` both already obey: the number the person
answers and the set the edit removes are ONE object, because two walks over the same document asking
the same question is how a dialog and its edit drift apart. `planOutletRemoval` and
`planStructureRemoval` live in `derived/structure_removal.dart`; the dialogs read them and
`addOutletRemoval` / `addStructureRemoval` consume them.

**THE UNITS ARE PLATES, CABLES AND PINS**, and the third is not decoration. `Outlet.planPin` is
walked-site work: somebody stood in the room and dotted the floorplan, `plan_length.dart` derives a
cable length from it, and it travels with the outlet when the outlet goes. A count that named only
cables would understate what a pinned plate costs.

**AND THE PLAN IS TAKEN TWICE, WHICH IS THE ONE PLACE THAT RULE BENDS.** The document is not frozen
while a confirmation is open, and `#877` MEASURED that rather than assuming it: `Ctrl+Z` reaches
`undoFromShell` from inside a modal route, because DR-159 §11.158.4 put undo on `KeyScope.global`
with its `Shortcuts` above the `Navigator`. Probed on the plate dialog, the document went from two
links to three with the confirmation still up and still saying one. So the edit re-plans after the
await and removes **what is actually there**, which is DR-158's recorded choice and is the smaller of
two costs: the alternative leaves the restored drop naming a plate that is gone, which is the state
§11.159.2 exists to prevent. A dialog that dismissed itself when the document moved would be better
than both and is not ruled here.

**A PLATE WITH NOTHING ON IT IS NOT ASKED ABOUT.** `needsConfirmation` is false for an outlet with no
drops and no pin, exactly as it is false for a bare leaf location, and for DR-013 §11.13.2's own
reason: a prompt for a consequence-free delete is the nag that teaches people to click through
prompts, including this one on the day it matters. **A Structure body is always asked about**, even
an empty one, because it is the container the tab is named for and re-creating one is a different
order of work from re-typing a drop.

**11.159.6 RULED: WHERE THE TWO CONTROLS LIVE.** Settled by the user on 2026-09-13.

**THE PLATE GETS A TRASH ICON ON ITS ROW IN THE LEFT RAIL** of the `[ Outlets ]` tab, which is where
a person already picks one, and which is the shape the user chose for `#871`'s template removal the day
before.

**THE STRUCTURE GETS AN OVERFLOW MENU IN THE EDITOR HEADER**, after `Connector aliases…`. The largest
delete in the product does not sit as a fourth text button in a row of three benign ones. **A trash
icon beside the body picker was refused on a defect**: `_EditorHeader` builds that picker only when
`doc.structures.length > 1`, so a one-panel project would have had no control at all, and a one-panel
project is both the ordinary case and exactly the case where somebody wants a wrongly-created panel
gone.

**11.159.7 ONE TRANSACTION, ONE UNDO, AND IT NAMES THE GESTURE.** DR-158 §11.157.6's rule. The
transaction's label is `removeOutlet` or `removeStructure` and never `removeLink`, because what the
person did was get rid of a plate or a panel and the cables are a consequence of it. DR-013 §11.13.4
binds the revert: every `Link`, `Net`, `Outlet`, `StructureBody` and `DeviceInstance` that applying
removed comes back with the SAME ids, so delete-then-undo is not a lossy round trip through the
entities CR-117's byte gate is about.

**11.159.8 Scope.** **No scope change.** Both commands are M3-A/1 work that shipped without a caller;
this rules how they are reached and what they take, inside scope M3 already owns. Board `#877` cites
it, and `#872`'s exemption list loses both rows.

---

### 11.160 DR-161 · What the reachability gate counts, and when an exemption may be permanent

**The question.** `#872`'s gate reported twelve unreachable `Command` classes. Two of its rows turned
out to be about the GATE rather than about the tree, and they fail in opposite directions:
**`SnapshotCommand` does not exist** and was counted anyway, and **`AddLinkCommand` exists, is used
twenty-one times, and is not reachable by design**. Both were filed as tickets against the code
(`#880`, `#881`) on the gate's own word. A gate whose output is read as a fact about the product must
be right about what it is counting.

**11.160.1 RULED: THE GATE COUNTS DECLARATIONS, AND A COMMENT IS NOT ONE.**

`snapshot_command.dart` **declares nothing**. Its own header says so in as many words: it *"exists,
per the directory tree in docs/03-architecture.md §2.2, purely as a marker for where that lands; it
deliberately defines no class so nothing here reads as more built than it is"*. What the file holds
is a SKETCH of the class, indented inside a `//` comment, written at M0 to record what building it
would need.

The gate's own pipeline already knew better and applied the knowledge unevenly: step 2, the
declaration scan, runs over `_strip`ped text with comments and string literals removed; step 1, the
Command inventory, ran over the RAW file. So the inventory admitted a class the declaration scan
could never match, it was correctly found to have no construction site, and it was filed as a
capability awaiting a decision. **Measured over the three scan roots: 73 commands raw, 72 stripped,
one phantom, and stripping loses nothing.** Step 1 now strips, and a named case pins the answer.

**THIS IS THE SECOND TIME THIS CENSUS COUNTED A COMMENT.** `#872`'s own record lists, as attempt 2 of
three, *"counting any MENTION in another lib file let a name in a COMMENT count as reachable"*. That
was fixed on the EDGE side and the same mistake survived on the NODE side, which is the shape worth
naming: a bug found in one direction of a scan is a reason to check the other direction, not evidence
that the scan is now clean.

**11.160.2 RULED: AN EXEMPTION MAY BE PERMANENT, AND IT MUST SAY WHY IN A SENTENCE.** Settled by the
user on 2026-09-13.

`_exempt` held one kind of row: a command name against the board item that will retire it, and a test
refusing any value that does not look like one, *"a list of names is a place to hide; a list of due
dates is a debt somebody can collect."* That rule is right for a debt and has no room for a command
that is deliberately not reachable.

**`AddLinkCommand` IS SUCH A COMMAND, AND THE CENSUS IS WHY.** It mints a `Link` with two open ends
and an implicit `Net`, needing no device, no port and no panel, which its M0 header states as the
design: *"which keeps this command usable anywhere in a command sequence rather than only after a
device has been placed."* Nothing in docs/ asks for a gesture that creates an unattached cable, and
there is no picture of one: the schematic draws links between ports and such a link has none, so it
would surface only as a schedule row with both ends unbound. Meanwhile twenty-one test sites use it,
and nine of them could not be rebuilt cheaply: the two `allocateNetNameFor` properties (a revert
frees the name, a redo reuses it) have **no other coverage**, and `command_roundtrip_test`'s
thousand-sequence CR-117 sweep has **no other link-creating step**.

So it stays, in a **second map** whose values are sentences rather than board items, and whose format
test refuses anything shaped like a board item for the same reason the first map refuses anything
that is not.

**11.160.3 THE STALENESS CHECK BINDS BOTH MAPS, AND THAT IS THE PRICE OF THE CARVE-OUT.** A permanent
exemption is a standing claim that no person can reach the command, and the day somebody wires one
that claim is false. Both maps therefore fail when a row becomes reachable and when a row names a
class that no longer exists. **The permanence is in the reason, not in the checking.**

**11.160.4 WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO.** It does not delete `snapshot_command.dart`. The file is a marker
that names two things building it would need (`RackDocument.restoreEntities` and an encode/decode
dispatch table `json_codec.dart` deliberately does not export), and that record is worth more than
the tidiness of removing it. It also does not rule on whether snapshots are in scope, which `#880`
asked for: **there was never a question, because there is no class.** docs/03 §5.5 deferred the shape
and nothing has since claimed otherwise.

**11.160.5 Scope.** **No scope change.** Both tickets close as corrections to a gate, inside scope
M5 already owns. Board `#880` and `#881` cite this.

---

### 11.161 DR-162 · Taking something off the plan, and putting the pages in order

**The question.** `#872`'s gate found `ClearPlanPinCommand` and `ReorderPlanUnderlayCommand` declared
in `plan_commands.dart` with real reverts, six test constructions between them, and no caller.
`SetPlanPinCommand` and `RemovePlanUnderlayCommand` in the same file both have callers, so the
missing halves are the ones that UNDO a placement rather than make one. **A rack pinned to the wrong
room could only be fixed by pinning it somewhere else**: there was no way to say it is not on the plan
after all. And docs/15 §6's gesture table has a row for every way to CREATE a pin and none for
removing one.

**11.161.1 RULED: `Delete` AND `Backspace` CLEAR THE PIN, ON THE SELECTION.** Settled by the user on
2026-09-13, against a visible control instead of a key and against having both.

The rack canvas and the schematic already bind both keys to `DeleteSelectionIntent` under one label,
*"Delete the selection"*, which `KeymapConflictKind.meaningDrift` holds identical across scopes. The
plan is the third canvas and takes the same pair.

**THE COST IS REAL AND IS STATED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER.** On the rack that key removes a
device from the project; here it removes only a pin, and DR-011.6's note already refused to widen
`meaningDrift` for per-scope labels because *"a keyboard-only user cannot see a scope boundary"*. The
reason it is nonetheless right is that **the label names the SELECTION, and the selection is a
different kind of thing on each canvas**: devices on the rack, cables on the schematic, pins here.
*"Delete the selection"* is true in all three, and a person looking at a plan is looking at pins.

**11.161.2 THE CARRIER SURVIVES, AND THE STRIP IS WHAT SAYS SO.** This is what makes §11.161.1 safe
rather than merely consistent. A cleared pin puts its carrier straight back into the unpinned strip
along the bottom, which docs/15 §6 calls *"the difference between a plan that is trusted and a plan
that is 80% complete without saying so"*. So the visible answer to *"did I just delete my rack"* is a
row appearing three inches below the pointer, in the same frame.

A rack that is neither pinned nor listed would be the state that makes this key frightening, and
`unpinned_carriers.dart` makes it unreachable: **"unpinned" is no pin AT ALL**, so the moment the pin
goes the row is owed.

**11.161.3 A MULTI-PIN SELECTION IS ONE UNDO STEP.** CR-102's marquee can take several pins at once,
and DR-158 §11.157.6's rule applies unchanged: undoing a marquee clear one pin at a time is not
undoing a marquee clear. The label stays `clearPlanPin` for one and for many, because what the person
did was take things off the plan.

**AND A SELECTION WITH NO PINS IN IT DISABLES THE ACTION** rather than running an empty transaction.
`_PlanGatedAction` declines by being disabled, which is the shape this canvas already uses for
`PlanCancelIntent`, and `#863` is why it matters: a transaction whose only child declines to apply
leaves an undo entry that throws.

**11.161.4 RULED: PAGES REORDER BY A DEDICATED DRAG HANDLE.** Settled by the user on 2026-09-13,
against dragging anywhere on the row and against a pair of up/down buttons.

The rail's rows already carry tap-to-open, `Calibrate` and `Remove`. **Whole-row drag was refused
because those controls live inside the drag target**: a slow tap becomes a drag and a missed button
press reorders the set. **Up/down buttons were refused on a measurement**, not a preference: the row
overflowed by 126 pixels at 240 wide when it held one button, and the `Wrap` that fixed it is what
two more would have to negotiate with.

`port_grid.dart` already reorders with `ReorderableDragStartListener` and records why
`onReorderItem` beats the older `onReorder`; this is the second use of the same mechanism.

**11.161.5 A REORDER IS ONE FIELD WRITE, NEVER A RENUMBER.** `orderBetween` mints a `FracIndex`
between the two neighbours, which is docs/06 §4.6's rule for the port table restated for a rail of
pages, and `ReorderPlanUnderlayCommand` already takes exactly one id and one order. **Where
`orderBetween` returns null the reorder is REFUSED in words**, because the one shape it cannot answer
is reachable only from a hand-edited file and renumbering the whole rail behind somebody's back is a
larger edit than the gesture asked for. `nextOrder`'s own header carries that argument.

**11.161.6 WHAT BUILDING THIS FOUND, WHICH THE TICKET DID NOT NAME.** Two things, and both are
older than `#878`.

**THE PLAN CANVAS NEVER TOOK FOCUS.** `rack_canvas_screen.dart` calls `_canvasFocus.requestFocus()`
in eight places; this one called it nowhere and relied on `autofocus: true`, which wins only while
nothing else has claimed focus. That is true in every case in its own test file, where the canvas is
the whole tree, and false after one click anywhere else. `Shortcuts` sits above the focus node, **so
